6
Conclusion
In conclusion, we introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework which augments prompt optimization to select which agentic tasks should shape prompt optimization.
A Curator is used to agentically select and filter out tasks based on whether they can provide noisy or reliable training signals.
Furthermore, the Curator can retrieve and provide prior successful trajectories for failed tasks and gives them to the prompt optimizer to act as an anchoring context for reflections.
We show that this technique achieves consistent performance improvements over GEPA and ACE by up to 21.2% on Webarena, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and
τ
\tau
-bench.
We further extend our method to Meta-Harness and show that this agentic curation idea can even improve harness code as well.
AI use statement
LLMs are a core component of our paper.
Our method uses LLMs to curate data, retrieve robust successful trajectories, and propose improvements to prompts used by an LLM agent.
These LLM-generated artifacts are part of the system being studied and developed in the paper.
Furthermore, standard LLM tools were used for simple writing assistance such as grammar and formatting.
Ethics statement
This work presents a generic method for improving prompts for LLM agents, rather than a system designed for a specific domain.
Potential positive impacts include making agentic systems more reliable, adaptable, and accessible to researchers and practitioners.
Potential negative impacts are indirect: stronger LLM agents could be misused in harmful ways, or could cause harm if deployed in high-risk environments without proper human supervision.
We emphasize that optimized agents should be evaluated in the intended environment and used with appropriate human oversight, monitoring, and controls.

Appendix A
Details about Motivating Experiments
A.1
Selection of Dataset Composition
Before constructing the experimental datasets for the motivating examples, we use logs from several preliminary GitLab experiments to identify tasks corresponding to different labels. For
Easy
tasks, we select tasks that already achieve consistently high success rates with the seed prompt. For
Optimizable
tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve consistent success with the optimized prompt from at least one preliminary GEPA run, and then select, from this subset, those with the lowest success rates under the seed prompt. For
Impossible
tasks, we select tasks with the lowest success rates across all rollouts. For
Flaky
tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve roughly 50% success with both the seed prompt and the optimized prompts returned by the preliminary GEPA runs. We then manually inspect these tasks and prioritize cases where the LLM-as-a-judge produces inconsistent success and failure judgments despite similar or identical end states, particularly when even the best attainable end state does not yield consistently successful judgments.
A.2
A Concrete Example of Negative Transfer
We trace an accepted prompt mutation from iteration 7 of the
Optimizable
+
Impossible
condition. Two tasks from the
Impossible
partition had failed under the parent prompt. For “View the
split_silence.py
example for audio processing,” global search returned no useful result, and the evaluator suggested manually browsing projects and groups. For “Expand a subgroup in the hierarchy list to view nested subgroups,” the actor searched public groups containing no expandable subgroup, and the evaluator suggested checking the actor’s own groups instead. Both tasks are considered
Impossible
because their underspecified intents identify neither a target repository nor a group, leaving the actor to explore without direction, frequently exhausting its step budget before succeeding and making the tasks difficult to optimize through prompting. Reflection converted this feedback into a stronger exhaustive-search instruction:
Exhaustive Exploration:
Global code search is often limited or disabled. If a search yields no results, manually navigate through groups, projects, and repository file trees. Always check “Your groups”, “Your projects”, and your personal dashboard before defaulting to public “Explore” tabs, as task resources are usually associated with your account.
Its exhaustive-search instruction caused a regression on the
Optimizable
task “Check the guide to WCAG documents and standards.” Immediately before the mutation, the actor recognized The A11Y Project on its starting page, opened the repository, used
Find file
to search for
WCAG
, and reached
src/posts/wcag2-documents.md
in five actions. With the mutated prompt, instead of opening the visible A11Y Project directly, the actor first filtered its personal projects, then traversed Explore, Topics, Help, global search, and group pages. After eventually returning to the A11Y Project, it inspected the README and Wiki and manually traversed the repository tree. It exhausted all 30 actions in the
src
directory without reaching the guide.
The exhaustive-search instruction caused the regression by replacing the short repository-level search path with broad exploration across site sections and the repository tree. Nevertheless, the aggregate minibatch score increased from 8 to 9, so the mutation was accepted as candidate 5. This example provides a concrete mechanism for the trend in Figure
2
: feedback from difficult tasks can elicit an overgeneralized search strategy whose aggregate gain masks a regression on a solvable task.

B.2
Curator Prompts
The Curator agent in the full method makes task-selection and success-selection decisions jointly in one LLM call. For readability, we separate the shared task-selection prefix from the success-selection instructions appended when success evidence is enabled.
Task-Selection Instructions
You are a task curator allocating evaluation budget during text optimization. Judge this task independently: no other task is visible. Decide whether another rollout is currently useful for learning a better prompt or obtaining information about the task.
Use these definitions:
Mastered:
Multiple stable, clean successes across separate rollouts. The agent must complete the task correctly, not merely benefit from evaluator luck, leaked state, or an accidentally correct final page. There must be no recent regression. One success is not sufficient evidence of mastery.
Prompt-sensitive:
Before/after evaluation pairs show that prompt changes can improve the behavior, including partial behavioral correction even when the binary score does not change. Run these tasks.
Operationally impossible:
The available tools or UI genuinely lack the required capability, supported by the action schema, trajectory-derived diagnostics, reference evaluation, or evaluator evidence. A single unsupported actor claim is insufficient; repeated independent attempts consistently identifying the same missing essential capability are meaningful evidence.
No current optimization signal:
The same failure mode persists across multiple materially relevant prompt mutations, with no behavioral progress or new diagnostic information. Do not infer this merely because several mutations failed when they did not address the observed failure.
Flaky or uninformative:
Materially similar behavior and ending states repeatedly receive inconsistent outcomes without a credible relationship to prompt changes. Do not infer flakiness from one disagreement.
Evaluator-broken:
There is explicit evidence of an incorrect label, stale or contradictory target, or an evaluator expectation inconsistent with the user request. A brittle, unusually strict, or difficult evaluator is not necessarily broken.
Infrastructure failure:
Timeout, reset, network errors, or local-state/file collisions caused by missing resets provide no evidence about prompt quality. Do not interpret them as agent failures.
Uncertain:
Run rather than skip. A rollout has information value: use it to test uncertain mastery, suspected flakiness, possible regressions, or ambiguous failure mechanisms.
Run unseen or underexplored tasks and tasks with credible prompt-sensitive failures. Skip only when the history provides strong evidence that another rollout currently has little optimization or diagnostic value. A
mutation_comparison
records paired before/after evaluations even when the proposed mutation was rejected. Use an improved after result as evidence that the task may be prompt-sensitive, but when
mutation_accepted
is false, do not assume that behavior belongs to the current prompt or that the task is now mastered. A skip is revisited in a later epoch; it is not a permanent retirement. In the reason, cite the specific historical evidence supporting the decision.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that GEPA-Curator can identify tasks whose outcomes are unlikely to provide reliable optimization signals. Many of the tasks diagnosed as impossible or flaky are affected by inherent limitations of the execution harness or environment, or by faulty or underspecified task descriptions. By withholding these tasks from the corresponding training batches, GEPA-Curator prevents their potentially misleading outcomes from influencing those optimization steps.
Importantly, an impossible or flaky diagnosis does not permanently retire a task. The diagnosis may be uncertain, and subsequent prompt updates or further actor exploration may reveal that a task previously considered impossible is solvable. The Curator therefore reconsiders skipped tasks in subsequent epochs.
To analyze this behavior, we divide the complete training epochs into three phases and measure the consecutive skipped epochs preceding each rerun. As shown in Table
12
, impossible tasks are deferred the longest, with their mean skip streak increasing from 5.50 to 8.75 epochs.
Mastered tasks are also deferred longer over time because repeated stable successes reduce the expected value of additional rollouts, although they are periodically revisited to detect regressions.
Flaky tasks are revisited more frequently to resolve uncertainty.
Thus, curation adjusts task frequency rather than permanently excluding tasks.
Furthermore, skip streaks generally increase as task histories accumulate, making the Curator more confident that rerunning a task at the current stage is unlikely to provide new information for prompt optimization.
While the Curator diagnosed 75 of the 1,581 training tasks (4.7%) as impossible or flaky at least once during optimization,
its effect on optimization is non-trivial.

article.headline: GEPA-Curator：用任务策展改进提示优化
article.lede: GEPA-Curator 在优化前筛选任务并检索历史成功轨迹，多个智能体基准上最高较 GEPA/ACE 提升 20.7%
article.problem: 现有反思式提示优化器假设失败轨迹含有可泛化信号，但智能体失败也可能源于工具缺失、执行框架限制、随机性或评审噪声，未必该归因于提示。仅靠验证集门控在变异后筛选，无法阻止噪声进入反思。因此需要先策展任务与上下文。
article.method: GEPA-Curator 作为外循环 harness 维护每任务历史，包含任务策展与先验成功检索两个组件。任务策展优先探索不足任务，并临时跳过稳定成功、外部原因失败或评估不一致的任务，跳过任务会在后续 epoch 重访。先验成功检索为失败任务选择性提供过去可信成功轨迹，作为反思时的对照上下文；两者只作为额外元数据输入现有优化器，不改变优化器本身。
article.results: WebArena 上，以 Gemini 3.1 Pro 为优化器时 GEPA-Curator 总体成功率 82.1%，高于 GEPA 的 78.7%（seed 72.4），聚合提升 3.4%，单站最高提升 7.4%；以 Claude Opus 5 为优化器时总体 84.5%，高于 GEPA 的 79.5%（seed 73.1），聚合提升 5.0%。附加基准上，Gemini 优化器下平均较 GEPA 提升 14.3%、较 ACE 提升 5.0%；Claude 优化器下平均较 GEPA 提升 8.1%、较 ACE 提升 12.6%，其中 ALFWorld 98.4%、AppWorld Test-N 68.8%、Test-C 46.4%、τ-bench 82.9%（与 GEPA 持平）。GitLab 消融中完整方法 88.6%，仅任务策展 84.2%，仅成功检索 84.7%，GEPA 82.8%。效率版非 WebArena 总成本 173.98 美元，低于 ACE 的 768.69 美元，平均准确率高 9.2%，总优化成本约为 GEPA 的 1.31 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把“从哪些经验学习”提升为自改进智能体的核心问题，提示优化器可通过外挂策展减少噪声失败导致的错误更新。对构建更可靠的多轮智能体有实用意义。
article.limitations: 方法建立在简化的贪心 GEPA 上并去掉了 Pareto 候选选择，Curator 本身依赖 LLM 判断，可能误判或过度弃权。QA 类基准收益有限，HotpotQA 上还比 GEPA 低 1.3%，实验也限于有限基准和两种优化器模型。
article.figure_caption_zh: 系统示意图：Curator 作为外循环读取任务历史，筛选小批量任务并检索历史成功轨迹，再交给提示优化器执行和反思。

figure.caption: system diagram. The prompt optimizer takes in a minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories. The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer. The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal ( {sec:task_curation}). The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as a trusted reference example ( {sec:success_retrieval}). Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds.

Timestral
Abstract
We introduce
Timestral
, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters.
Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M  and Timestral-123M  take the top two places on every metric.
We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context.
This report describes the model design and its benchmark results.
Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face
1
1
1
https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/timestral
and inference code on GitHub
2
2
2
https://github.com/mistralai/timestral
.
Webpage:
https://mistral.ai/news/timestral
1
Introduction
Figure 1
:
Forecast error against parameter count on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench (lower is better; fev-bench skill scores are shown as one minus the skill score).
The dashed and solid curves show the Pareto fronts without and with Timestral, respectively.
All four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front across the six panels.
\Acp
tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem
(
Ansari et al., 2024
;
Das et al., 2024
)
.
Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates
(
Khwaja et al., 2026
;
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Podest et al., 2026
;
Meyer et al., 2026
)
.
These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use.
Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0
(
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Xia et al., 2026
)
sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two.
Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass.
To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively.
cpm
(
cpm
), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3
(
Auer et al., 2025
;
Khwaja et al., 2026
;
Jain and Sen, 2026
)
, achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence.
The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking.
Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden.
We introduce
Timestral
, a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters.
All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost.
Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through
dhf
(
dhf
), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality.
The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context.
Timestral-209M  sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench.
As shown in
Figure
1
, all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics.
Timestral-123M  already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters.
This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them:
•
dhf
.
We introduce
dhf
, a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens.
dhf
preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking.
•
Covariate conditioning within
dhf
.
We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention.
This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values.
•
A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost.
We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters.
The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval
(
Aksu et al., 2024
)
, TIME
(
Qiao et al., 2026
)
, and fev-bench
(
Shchur et al., 2026
)
.
2
Background
We first describe
tsfm
within the framework of
pfn
, which interprets forecasting as amortised posterior inference (
Section
2.1
).
We then review how current
tsfm
model dependencies across variates and over time, and the drawbacks that motivate the design of Timestral (
Section
2.2
).
2.1
Time Series Foundation Models as Prior-Data Fitted Networks
Synthetic data has become a standard ingredient of
tsfm
training, and its share has generally grown.
TimesFM mixes 20% synthetic series built from ARMA processes, seasonal patterns, trends, and steps
(
Das et al., 2024
)
; Chronos samples 10% of its training series from KernelSynth, a Gaussian-process generator
(
Ansari et al., 2024
)
; and TiRex draws about a third of its training series from an extended KernelSynth generator
(
Auer et al., 2025
)
.
More recent models rely on synthetic data more heavily: 57.5% of Toto-2.0’s pretraining mix is generated with TempoPFN’s generators
(
Khwaja et al., 2026
)
, and Chronos-2 learns its multivariate and covariate capabilities from synthetic data only, with a variant trained without any real data performing only slightly worse than the full model
(
Ansari et al., 2025
)
.
At the other end, time series
pfn
such as ForecastPFN, Mamba4Cast, TimePFN, and TempoPFN are trained exclusively on synthetic data
(
Dooley et al., 2023
;
Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024
;
Taga et al., 2025
;

)
.
Timestral follows this direction: it is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and a significant part of our effort went into designing the generating processes.

The composition of the training data is therefore a central design choice for

This decoupling has the following advantages.
First, how often each forecast distance is trained can be tuned without side effects on the context.
Second, missing data can be simulated independently of the forecast distances: optional missing-data augmentation hides variable-length gaps at arbitrary time steps rather than whole patches, which is closer to realistic missing-data distributions, and the hidden values are still scored as targets.

3.2
Multivariate and Covariate Modelling
Each variate of a multivariate series is represented by its own sequence of tokens and has one of three roles: target variate, past-only covariate, or known-future covariate (
Figure
4
).
Every variate has context and prediction tokens, but only the outputs at prediction tokens of target variates are used as forecasts.
Roles are not embedded in the tokens and enter the model only through the attention masks and the choice of normalisation (
Section
3.3
).
Along time, target variates and past-only covariates are processed causally, as described in
Section
3.1
.
The context tokens of known-future covariates instead attend over the entire window, including the forecast horizon, where they hold the known future values.
Normalisation follows the same distinction (
Section
3.3
).
Similar to Chronos-2 and Toto-2.0
(
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Khwaja et al., 2026
)
, variate attention exchanges information between the variates of a series at the same patch position, among context tokens and among prediction tokens.
It uses no positional encoding, so the order of the variates does not affect the forecasts.
To prevent future information leakage, known-future covariates attend only to each other.
Otherwise, a known-future covariate could read the value of a target variate or past-only covariate at patch
i
i
and, through its temporal attention, carry it back to earlier patches, from which it would reach the forecast of patch
i
i
.
Past-only covariates do not attend to target variates either; this is a modelling choice that treats covariates as exogenous, so that their representations do not depend on target values.
Forecasts can thus use future values of known-future covariates, but never future values of target variates or past-only covariates.
During training, some variates in a random subset of multivariate series are assigned the role of past-only or known-future covariates, while the others remain target variates.
These covariates are inputs only and are not scored, so ordinary multivariate series become forecasting tasks with covariates.

We describe the data and training setup shared by the four Timestral models, then report their forecasting performance on public benchmarks.

All four Timestral models are pretrained exclusively on synthetic data with a context length of

Training data.
The synthetic corpus includes both univariate signals and multivariate examples, covering temporal dynamics and cross-series dependencies.

Conclusion
We introduced Timestral, a family of four foundation models with 5M to 209M parameters for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting.
dhf
separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that observed values serve both as forecast targets and as context for later forecasts, and longer forecast distances are trained without masking context.
Role-aware attention masks let prediction tokens use known-future covariates at every forecast origin, while forecasts never use future values of target variates or past-only covariates.
The models are pretrained exclusively on synthetic data and then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context.
Timestral-209M  ranks first among the models compared on every reported metric of GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench using a single checkpoint.
It leads by a wider margin on IND-Eval.
Timestral-123M  ranks second, ahead of every model outside the Timestral family, and all four sizes lie on the Pareto front of accuracy against size.
Accuracy still improves from 123M to 209M parameters, which motivates training larger models.
Beyond standalone forecasting, Timestral can be embedded in existing monitoring pipelines or combined with language models in agentic workflows.
A further direction is to use the context representations as embeddings for tasks such as classification and anomaly detection.

A.2
IND-Eval
Benchmark.
We additionally evaluate Timestral on IND-Eval
(
Haugland et al., 2026
)
, a public benchmark for forecasting in complex physical systems.
It comprises 187 tasks covering applications in energy, manufacturing, and transport.
Compared with general-purpose forecasting benchmarks, it emphasises finer sampling resolutions and multivariate targets.
Evaluation.
All IND-Eval results reported here come from our own evaluation runs, using publicly released checkpoints and inference code from the model authors’ public repositories under the official benchmark protocol.
We re-evaluate TimesFM-3, Chronos-2, and TiRex-2, the three models studied by
Haugland et al. (2026)
, and extend the comparison to t0-gamma, t0-beta, all five released Toto-2.0 sizes (4M, 22M, 313M, 1B, and 2.5B), and Granite-PatchTST-FM-r2, alongside all four Timestral sizes.
All models are evaluated zero-shot, without fine-tuning, using the official IND-Eval context–target windows and a context capped at 4,096 time steps.
We report
nmase
(
nmase
) and
ncrps
(
ncrps
) relative to Seasonal Naive. Each task score divides the model’s error by the corresponding error of Seasonal Naive; values below one indicate lower error.
We first take the geometric mean of task scores within each dataset, then the geometric mean of the resulting dataset scores.
This gives each dataset equal weight in the aggregate.
Aggregate results.
Figure
10
compares aggregate errors for all four Timestral sizes and the eleven competitors evaluated here.
Timestral-209M  ranks first among the models compared, with aggregate
nmase
of 0.646 and
ncrps
of 0.435. Relative to t0-gamma, the strongest model outside the Timestral family on both metrics (0.697 and 0.469), this is about 7% lower error.
Accuracy improves at every increase in Timestral model size.
Timestral-123M  obtains 0.663
nmase
and 0.441
ncrps
, and Timestral-28M  obtains 0.692 and 0.464, respectively; both remain ahead of every model outside the family on the two aggregates.

Pairwise Win Rates
Aggregate errors summarise overall forecasting accuracy, while pairwise win rates measure how often one model outperforms another across tasks.

Each cell reports the row model’s win rate against the column model across the benchmark’s tasks, with lower error counting as a win and exact ties as half a win, following the fev definition

Errors are compared before rounding, and all tasks receive equal weight.
We follow the official evaluation protocols for each benchmark; IND-Eval task errors come from our own evaluation runs described in

For fev-bench, win rates use task errors rather than aggregate skill scores.
Timestral-209M  wins on a majority of tasks against every selected competitor on both metrics of each benchmark.

article.headline: Timestral：解耦预测 token 与上下文
article.lede: Mistral 发布 5M 到 209M 四个时间序列基础模型，在 GIFT-Eval、TIME、fev-bench 上
article.problem: 现有因果解码器式时序基础模型多用 cpm 训练多步预测：把输入中的连续 patch 整块掩掉，模型才能学到向前多步的预测。但被掩掉的观测同时也不可作为同一训练序列中后续预测的上下文，于是预测视界分布与上下文掩码被绑死。另一个难点是已知未来协变量：它的未来取值必须能被预测读到，而目标变量的未来值必须隐藏，这在纯因果架构里并不自然。
article.method: 论文提出 Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF)：上下文 token 与预测 token 分成两条流，预测 token 只注意其所在预测块之前的上下文和块内更早的预测 token，上下文 token 从不在意预测 token，因此每个观测值既是预测目标又是后续预测的上下文，视界采样与缺失掩码相互独立。协变量按角色（目标变量、仅历史协变量、已知未来协变量）通过非对称注意力掩码进入模型，已知未来协变量可覆盖整个窗口但只与其他已知未来协变量交互，以免泄漏目标未来值。训练分两阶段：先在纯合成语料上以 8,192 步上下文预训练，再在真实与合成混合数据上以 32,768 步上下文后训练。
article.results: Timestral-209M 在 GIFT-Eval 上 MASE 0.6575、CRPS 0.4460，在 TIME 上 MASE 0.6262、CRPS 0.5223，在 fev-bench 上 MASE skill score 39.49%、sql skill score 50.39%，六项指标均为对比模型第一；Timestral-123M 六项全部第二。Timestral-28M 在全部六项指标上超过 Chronos-2（GIFT-Eval MASE 0.6978）和 Toto-2.0-2.5B（0.6956），后两者参数量分别约为它的 4 倍和 90 倍；Timestral-5M 在 fev-bench 上超过所有 Toto-2.0 模型，而 Toto-2.0-2.5B 参数量约为它的 480 倍。推理侧，预测 96 步、上下文 2,048 步时，单次预测在 8 线程 CPU 上耗时 17 至 113 毫秒，单核吞吐 3.5 至 106 条序列每秒，单张 H100 为 3,650 至 18,770 条每秒。最长 1,024 步的预测可在一次前向中完成；超过该长度则要按块滚动预测，并以前一块的预测中位数作为条件。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“长视界训练不该以牺牲上下文为代价”做成架构层面的解耦，并给出了一套从 5M 到 209M 都能落在精度—参数量帕累托前沿上的配方，说明时序基础模型的收益未必只来自堆参数。小模型可在 CPU 上毫秒级出预测，适合嵌入现有监控管线或作为 agent 工作流中的预测组件。
article.limitations: 这是一份技术报告而非同行评审论文，IND-Eval 上的对比（209M 的 nmase 0.646、ncrps 0.435，比最强的非 Timestral 模型 t0-gamma 低约 7% 误差）由作者自行复现，基准对比也截止到 2026 年 10 月 15 日。DHF 的代价是训练时因预测块铺满整条序列而 token 数约翻倍；超过 1,024 步的视界需按块自回归滚动，依赖前块预测中位数，误差累积风险论文未量化。

Within the Transformer, context and prediction tokens form two separate streams ( {sec:timestral:dhf}): $ _i$, $ _i$, and $ _i$ denote the context tokens of patch $i$ of a target variate, a past-only covariate, and a known-future covariate, respectively, and $ _i$ denotes the prediction token at the temporal position of patch $i$. page_papers.title: From History to State: Constant-Context Skill Learning for LLM Agents
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to operate browsers, files, code and tools, making personal assistants a natural deployment target. Yet personal agents face a privacy-cost-capability tension: cloud models execute multi-step workflows well but expose sensitive intermediate context to external APIs, while local models preserve privacy but remain less reliable. Both settings also pay repeatedly for long skill prompts and growing histories. We propose constant-context skill learning, a context-to-weights framework for recurring agent workflows: reusable procedures are learned in lightweight task-family modules, while inference conditions only on the current observation and a compact state block. A deterministic tracker renders this state block from task progress and supplies aligned subgoal rewards, so each module can be trained with step-level SFT and refined through online RL. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld, our agents achieve strong performance across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. With Qwen3-8B, SFT+RL reaches 89.6\% unseen success on ALFWorld, 76.8\% success on WebShop, and 66.4\% unseen success on SciWorld. They match or exceed strong published agent-training results while reducing prompt tokens per turn by 2--7$\times$ relative to controlled ReAct prompting baselines, showing that procedural context can be moved from prompts into weights.

From History to State: Constant-Context Skill Learning for LLM Agents
Haoyang Xie
Xinyuan Wang
Yancheng Wang
Puda Zhao
Feng Ju
†
†

Corresponding author
Affiliation:
School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence, Arizona State University
Affiliation:
{hxie40, xwang735, ywan1053, pzhao34, fengju}@asu.edu
Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to operate browsers, files, code and tools, making personal assistants a natural deployment target. Yet personal agents face a privacy-cost-capability tension: cloud models execute multi-step workflows well but expose sensitive intermediate context to external APIs, while local models preserve privacy but remain less reliable. Both settings also pay repeatedly for long skill prompts and growing histories. We propose constant-context skill learning, a context-to-weights framework for recurring agent workflows: reusable procedures are learned in lightweight task-family modules, while inference conditions only on the current observation and a compact state block. A deterministic tracker renders this state block from task progress and supplies aligned subgoal rewards, so each module can be trained with step-level SFT and refined through online RL. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld, our agents achieve strong performance across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. With Qwen3-8B, SFT+RL reaches 89.6% unseen success on ALFWorld, 76.8% success on WebShop, and 66.4% unseen success on SciWorld. They match or exceed strong published agent-training results while reducing prompt tokens per turn by 2–7
×
\times
relative to controlled ReAct prompting baselines, showing that procedural context can be moved from prompts into weights.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are moving from conversational assistants toward systems that execute real multi-turn tasks across browsers, files, code, GUIs, and other tools
[
12
,
39
,
40
,
25
,
24
,
38
]
. As agents become capable of operating tools and files, a natural next step is to deploy them as personal assistants. Systems such as OpenClaw illustrate this direction, where agents interact with personal devices, local tools, and user feedback during normal use
[
23
]
. Such local and user-specific deployment makes privacy and cost first-order concerns. Today, the strongest agent models are often accessed through external APIs
[
22
,
2
]
, while models that can run locally are typically less reliable on long-horizon interactive tasks
[
33
]
. As a result, personal agents face an uncomfortable trade-off. Cloud models provide stronger execution, but personal agents may handle sensitive data such as emails, calendars, code, documents, and tool outputs, making it undesirable to send every intermediate state to an external service. At the same time, token costs grow quickly with daily use when every step must process long skill descriptions and accumulated execution histories.
Current approaches still treat agent behavior largely as a context-management problem. ReAct-style agents preserve task progress by replaying prior actions, observations, and reasoning traces in the prompt
[
40
]
. Memory-augmented agents reduce this burden by storing, organizing, or retrieving past interactions
[
44
,
37
,
30
,
3
]
. Recent agent-training methods improve the policy through expert trajectories, self-generated experience, or multi-turn preference and reinforcement-learning objectives
[
27
,
5
,
31
,
4
,
42
,
19
]
. These directions substantially improve long-horizon behavior, but they largely preserve the same inference-time interface: before each action, the agent is still prompted with task instructions, skill descriptions, retrieved memories, demonstrations, or accumulated histories. For recurring personal workflows, this is inefficient, the agent repeatedly re-reads procedures it has already practiced, instead of using that experience as part of the policy itself.
A recurring workflow should not require the agent to reread the same procedure, instructions, and examples at every execution. In personal settings, successful executions naturally accumulate as users repeat the same workflow, and even tens of expert trajectories provide many state-action decisions for supervision. This makes the task family a natural unit of learning. Rather than treating repeated executions as isolated episodes, we group variants of the same skill when they share a tool environment, action space, and procedural subgoals. Learning at this level encourages the module to capture the shared procedure across variants, rather than replaying a fixed action sequence from the training trajectories. The prompt only needs the information that changes from step to step, including the current observation and a compact state block describing progress, relevant entities, and remaining subgoals. Inference is therefore shorter but still well specified. The agent need not reread long skill descriptions or replayed histories, yet it has enough state to choose the next action. We keep the base model fixed and learn a separate lightweight skill module for each task family, first from expert demonstrations and then through interaction. Adding a new workflow only requires training a new module. At inference time, running a workflow loads its corresponding module, keeping computation modest and avoiding catastrophic forgetting across unrelated skills.
Our solution
: We instantiate this idea as a context-to-weights training pipeline. For each task family, we train a lightweight skill module with step-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and then refine it with interaction-based reinforcement learning (RL). A deterministic task tracker provides the interface between raw interaction and learning. It summarizes control-relevant progress into a compact state block, such as acquired objects, completed subgoals, and remaining requirements, and also supplies shaped subgoal rewards during RL. The tracker is a deterministic algorithm, not an LLM reasoner. It converts observations and actions into task progress through simple environment-specific rules. At inference time, the agent loads the corresponding module and conditions on the current observation and state block, rather than the full execution history or long skill prompt. We evaluate this design on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld
[
29
,
39
,
35
]
, which provide representative recurring workflows analogous to personal-agent use cases, including household manipulation, web interaction and procedural tool use.
Our experiments show that this context-to-weights design improves both task performance and context efficiency. With Qwen3-8B, SFT+RL reaches 83.6% / 89.6% success on ALFWorld seen/unseen, 76.8% success on WebShop, and 62.9% / 66.4% success on SciWorld seen/unseen. At the same time, it substantially reduces inference context. Compared with full-history ReAct, our method reduces prompt tokens per turn from 1.3k to 0.18k on ALFWorld, from 3.1k to 0.49k on WebShop, and from about 2.0k to 0.49k on SciWorld. It also reduces total tokens per episode from 34k to about 3k on ALFWorld, from 47k to 3.4k on WebShop, and from 42k to 18k on SciWorld. Building on these findings,
we summarize our main contributions as follows:
•
We formulate recurring personal-agent workflows as
constant-context skill learning
, where reusable procedures are moved from prompts and growing histories into lightweight skill-module weights, while step-specific progress remains explicit in a compact state block.
•
We introduce a modular SFT+RL training pipeline that learns lightweight skill modules from expert trajectories and refines them through interaction, pairing deterministic state-block construction with subgoal rewards aligned to the same tracker fields.
•
We conduct controlled evaluations, ablations, and context-efficiency analyses across ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld using Qwen and Llama backbones, showing that bounded-context skill modules can match strong agent-training baselines while reducing prompt-token cost by 2–7
×

4
Experiments and Results
We evaluate the proposed context-to-weights pipeline on three representative agent benchmarks, using Qwen and Llama backbones at different model scales. Our experiments are organized around four research questions. (
RQ1
) Does task-family skill learning improve agent performance across benchmarks and backbones, and how much does interaction-based RL refinement add over SFT-only skill modules? (
RQ2
) How much inference context does the bounded-context interface save compared with ReAct-style prompting, a representative history-based agent interface that repeatedly conditions on long instructions and growing execution histories? (
RQ3
) Which components of the pipeline, including the state block, one-step context, SFT training, and subgoal-guided reward shaping, are responsible for the gains? (
RQ4
) How does the method compare with prior agent methods across memory-based prompting, learned memory and RL-based agent training?
4.1
Experimental Setup
Benchmarks.
We evaluate on three text-mode agent benchmarks that approximate recurring personal-agent workflows in different fixed environments.
ALFWorld
[
29
]
represents household assistance: the agent navigates simulated rooms, finds target objects, applies transformations such as cleaning, heating, or cooling and places objects in target receptacles. We evaluate on 140 seen and 134 unseen games.
WebShop
[
39
]
represents shopping assistance: the agent searches for products, opens item pages, selects required options, and purchases the target item. We use the 1,000-product text setting and evaluate on 500 test goals.
SciWorld
[
35
]
represents procedural tool use: the agent manipulates objects, uses instruments, performs experiments, and reports answers in science-lab environments. We evaluate on 194 seen and 211 unseen variants following the ETO split structure
[

4.2
Main Task Performance
Table
1
shows that moving recurring procedures from context into task-family modules is effective across benchmarks. SFT already gives strong performance, indicating that expert trajectories provide enough step-level supervision for the model to act from compact per-step inputs rather than long skill prompts or full histories. On WebShop, for example, the untrained prompt variant with a state block reaches only 23.6% success in Table
3
, while SFT raises success to 62.2% with Qwen3-8B. RL refinement further improves the trained modules. With Qwen3-8B, SFT+RL reaches 83.6% / 89.6% success on ALFWorld seen/unseen, 76.8% success on WebShop, and 62.9% / 66.4% success on SciWorld seen/unseen. Across the three backbones, RL improves over SFT by roughly 13–28 percentage points on ALFWorld, 15–17 points on WebShop, and 5–15 points on SciWorld. The improvements are also not tied to a single backbone. Qwen3-8B gives the strongest ALFWorld performance and the best SciWorld unseen results, while Llama-3.1-8B is strongest on WebShop score and SciWorld seen performance. Qwen3-4B also benefits from the same training recipe despite its smaller size. This pattern suggests that the gains come from the task-family training setup, not from a particular pretrained model. As a modularity check, we also train a single unified Qwen3-8B module across all ALFWorld families, which reaches 74.3% / 70.9% seen/unseen success after SFT and 86.4% / 88.1% after RL. This shows that a unified module is viable, but we use task-family modules for realistic deployment because they reduce interference among different skills, especially for smaller local models, and avoid training bias from imbalanced task-family data. We analyze the individual contributions of the state block, SFT, and RL in Section
4.4
.

Table
2

Many prompt- and memory-based agents keep more history, retrieved memories, or both. Our method still uses 2.1–3.0
×

The episode-level totals show the same pattern. On ALFWorld and WebShop, failed executions often continue producing unproductive actions until the step limit, so better execution also reduces average steps. SciWorld behaves differently, invalid actions can terminate an episode early with negative score, while successful procedures can be long, with task-specific limits up to 100 steps. Thus, stronger SciWorld agents may take more steps because they survive and complete more procedures. Even there, our method substantially reduces total token use. Relative to ReAct-full, total token use drops by about 10–12

Conclusion and Limitations
We presented constant-context skill learning, a context-to-weights framework for recurring LLM-agent workflows. Instead of repeatedly prompting an agent with long skill descriptions and growing histories, we train lightweight task-family modules that internalize reusable procedure while conditioning on the current observation and a compact tracker-rendered state block. Across ALFWorld, WebShop and SciWorld, the resulting agents achieve competitive task performance while substantially reducing inference context compared with ReAct-style prompting. The results suggest that recurring agent behavior can be made both more capable and more context-efficient by moving procedural context from prompts into weights.
The main limitations concern automation, modality, and transfer. First, the state tracker and reward rules are specified at the task-family level. We use a strong reasoning model offline to draft deterministic subgoal rewards from the task description and state-block schema, but the rules still require validation before RL. This manual design may become easier to automate as agent systems expose
SKILL.md
-style specifications of procedures, tool constraints, and success conditions
[
1
]
. Compiling such specifications with execution logs into state-block schemas and subgoal rewards is a promising future direction. Second, our evaluation is limited to text-mode environments. Extending the interface to GUI and multimodal agents is a natural next step. Third, per-family modules do not zero-shot transfer to new skills. Adding a workflow requires training a new adapter, although the base model remains fixed and existing skills are preserved. Moreover, each adapter is only

GB on disk and only the active one loads at inference, making the storage cost modest in practice.

7
Technical appendices and supplementary material
7.1
Training Details and Hyperparameters
All three benchmarks provide expert trajectories, which we use directly to construct the SFT data after benchmark-specific filtering. Each successful trajectory is converted into step-level bounded-context inputs paired with the expert action, so the number of SFT samples is larger than the number of trajectories. Table
5
reports the resulting data scale and training settings for the main Qwen3-8B experiments. The Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B runs use the same recipe unless otherwise specified. Because Qwen3-8B supports a chat-template thinking mode, we disable it during both training and evaluation (
enable_thinking=False
) and use the model as a standard instruction-following language model. Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B do not have a thinking mode and are used with their default chat templates.
ALFWorld contains five base task families in our training setup: Pick, Clean, Heat, Cool, and Examine. Pick2 is not trained as a separate module because it does not introduce a new procedure: it consists of two sequential executions of the same Pick-and-Place skill. At evaluation time, we therefore reuse the Pick module twice rather than learning an additional Pick2-specific module.
WebShop is treated as a single task family because all examples share the same shopping workflow. To align with standard WebShop evaluation, we use the 1K-product text environment and evaluate on 500 held-out goals.
For SciWorld, we follow the ETO evaluation protocol, which is the common setup used by recent ScienceWorld agent-training work, including the task-family grouping, official train/dev/test splits, and per-task step limits
[
31
]
. We keep the family definitions fixed rather than regrouping tasks manually. We train nine task-family modules: find_X, lifespan, conductivity, measurement, growth, state_change, power, chemistry, and life_stages. The first five families have more expert data, with 480, 254, 256, 348, and 145 training variants respectively. Their SFT policies are already near-saturated, so we do not apply RL refinement to them. The remaining four families are lower-data: state_change has 56 training variants, power has 16, chemistry has 52, and life_stages has 10. We apply RL refinement to these four families in the main SciWorld setting. Evaluation is performed over the full ETO dev/test sets used in our experiments, containing 194 seen and 211 unseen variants across the nine families.

7.3
Data Efficiency of Expert Trajectories
To study how many expert trajectories are needed to learn a recurring workflow, we run a data-efficiency sweep on WebShop with Qwen3-8B. We focus on the SFT stage only, because adding RL would introduce additional interaction budget and make the effect of demonstration count harder to isolate. For each setting, we train the same WebShop skill module with the same hyperparameters as the main experiment, varying only the number of expert trajectories used for SFT. Evaluation is performed on a fixed 100-goal test subset, so these numbers are intended to show trends rather than replace the full 500-goal results in Table
1
.
Figure 4
:
WebShop SFT performance versus expert trajectory count.
Figure
4
shows a clear scaling trend. With only 5 trajectories, the model fails to learn a usable shopping policy. Performance improves steadily from 25 to 1,000 trajectories, with success rate increasing from 16.0% to 57.0%. Using all available WebShop trajectories gives similar performance to the 1,000-trajectory setting, suggesting that SFT begins to saturate at this scale for the fixed 100-goal subset.

article.headline: 恒定上下文技能学习：把过程写进LoRA
article.lede: 论文提出将可复用流程从提示词迁入任务族LoRA，让Agent每步只看当前观测和紧凑状态块。
article.problem: ReAct式Agent靠回放历史、技能说明和检索记忆维持进度，重复工作流每步都要重读相同过程，上下文随回合增长；云端API还会暴露中间敏感上下文，本地模型则不够可靠。个人Agent因此同时受隐私、成本和能力约束。
article.method: 作者为每个任务族冻结基座模型、训练一个LoRA技能模块。确定性tracker把交互压缩成状态块，成功轨迹转成逐步SFT样本，再用与状态块字段对齐的子goal奖励做GRPO式在线RL。推理时只输入任务指令、当前观测、一步上下文和状态块。
article.results: 在Qwen3-8B上，SFT+RL取得ALFWorld seen/unseen 83.6%/89.6%、WebShop 76.8%成功率、SciWorld 62.9%/66.4%；WebShop得分84.0，SciWorld得分79.7。每轮提示token在ALFWorld为183.8（ReAct-full为1310.5），WebShop为488.0（ReAct-full为3092.7），论文称相对ReAct-1step少2.1–3.0×、相对full少4–7×。ALFWorld每episode总token从ReAct-full的34,199降至3,251。
article.why_it_matters: 这提供了一条把重复流程从提示词搬到权重、以固定小上下文运行个人Agent的路径，有望降低推理token成本，并减少每步向外部API发送长历史的必要。
article.limitations: 状态tracker和奖励规则仍需按任务族设计并人工校验，论文虽用GPT-5.5离线起草规则，但rollout时不调用LLM judge；评测仅限文本环境，新技能必须训练新适配器，不能零样本迁移。与已发表结果的比较并非完全受控，训练目标、数据构造和实现细节不同。

page_papers.title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
page_papers.abstract: Agentic services alternate between model inference on clustered GPUs and external tools on distributed CPUs. In this scenario, existing systems (1) overlook tool-return readiness in service evaluation, wasting limited resources, and (2) use heuristic strategies to decide admission and placement on GPUs, resulting in suboptimal scheduling decisions. To bridge this gap, we present TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. Its value interface combines near-term tool readiness, node-specific cache credit with time-aware decay, and token footprint; a dynamic program jointly selects and places waiting sessions under capacity constraints. Across the 12 reported model-workload-concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the best evaluated state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.

Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract
Agentic services alternate between model inference on clustered GPUs and external tools on distributed CPUs. In this scenario, existing systems (1) overlook tool-return readiness in service evaluation, wasting limited resources, and (2) use heuristic strategies to decide admission and placement on GPUs, resulting in suboptimal scheduling decisions. To bridge this gap, we present TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. Its value interface combines near-term tool readiness, node-specific cache credit with time-aware decay, and token footprint; a dynamic program jointly selects and places waiting sessions under capacity constraints. Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the best evaluated state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in language models have expanded their use beyond basic chatbots to complex agents, making CPU-based tool execution a substantial source of latency alongside GPU-based inference
(
Qiao et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
. Specifically, an agent operates through an
agent session
that alternates between LLM inference and external tools, such as compilers and retrievers, to complete multi-step tasks
(
Anthropic, 2026b
;
OpenAI, 2026
)
. When tools run outside the inference service, a session’s demand for GPU computation becomes interruptible. We call this serving scenario
C
lustered-
G
PUs with
D
istributed-
C
PUs (CGDC), illustrated in Figure
1
(Left): clustered GPUs, i.e., nodes, provide shared inference capacity, while external tool calls introduce delays between LLM requests
1
1
1
One agent session consists of multiple LLM inference requests (i.e., steps) after tool calls.
. Hence, efficient agentic serving must account for both inference demand and tool timing to sustain throughput and session responsiveness.
We find that existing serving systems generally follow an
evaluate-then-decide
scheduling pattern
(
Guy et al., 2025
;
SGLang Team, n.d.
;
vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.
)
. They evaluate node features at the session level and then decide where and when to serve each session. This separates the problem into two related challenges: (1) how to value a session’s next model turn, and (2) how to select and place sessions under shared capacity constraints.
For
session evaluation
, existing systems in CGDC scenarios generally overlook tool-call latency when evaluating established workload features.
Cache-aware systems reuse KV prefixes and balance inference load
(
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Srivatsa et al., 2025
;
Qin et al., 2025
;
NVIDIA, 2025
)
; workflow-aware systems anticipate future calls
(
Wadlom et al., 2026
;
Pan et al., 2026
)
; and latency-aware schedulers prioritize sessions using latency or remaining-work estimates
(
Choi et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Tool timing provides another useful signal, yet timing is utilized only as a surrogate for KV reuse or token count:
Li et al. (2025)
predicts tool duration to choose KV-cache retention times, while
Kang et al. (2026)
discounts the token footprint of sessions executing tools as time elapses. Such features commonly enter fixed scoring rules or manually chosen thresholds.
For
decision making
, existing systems usually apply heuristic scheduling strategies to each session, leading to myopic and suboptimal placements.
In llm-d and SGLang
(
Guy et al., 2025
;
SGLang Team, n.d.
)
, per-session scoring and routing rules assign inference opportunities
individually
. Yet sessions compete for the same node capacity. In particular, assigning one session can prevent a more valuable combination of other sessions from being served. Furthermore, the heuristic selection and placement rules can also lead to suboptimal choices
(
Peng et al., 2026
;
Yuan et al., 2026
)
. As shown in Figure
1
(Right), they fail to formulate scheduling jointly across multiple sessions.
Figure 1:
Left: In the CGDC serving scenario, external tool calls create intervals between LLM requests and opportunities to reallocate inference capacity. Right: Two scheduling challenges motivate TAO, including (1) overlooking tool-return readiness and using heuristic merging for evaluation, and (2) making myopic and suboptimal decisions about session admission and placement.
To address these challenges, we propose TAO, a
T
ool-
A
ware j
O
int scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving.
To incorporate
tool latency
into
session evaluation
, we propose tool-return readiness and explicitly integrate it with established features such as KV-cache reuse. Following
Kang et al. (2026)
, we interrupt sessions during tool calls and put them into a
waiting pool
. Tool-return readiness estimates which sessions will need inference within the next scheduling window. For each session–node pair, we form a value triplet from readiness, time-decayed
KV-cache reuse
, and token footprint.
Given these evaluation triplets, we design a
joint scheduling
algorithm in the
decision making
stage that considers all sessions in the waiting pool. Across deployments in different scenarios, joint optimization considers how the admission of each session affects the placements available to others. The optimizer maximizes the additive evaluation triplets using dynamic programming. Their coordinates evolve with cache age and tool progress, allowing distinct signals to guide decisions over time without a weighted sum. Separating the optimization procedure from session evaluation makes the framework extensible.
We summarize our contributions as follows:
•
We identify the Clustered GPUs with Distributed CPUs (CGDC) serving scenario in the era of LLM-based agents, which shifts the key bottleneck of latency to tool calls.
•
We propose TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. It improves the evaluate-then-decide paradigm through session evaluation with explicit tool-return readiness and decision making with joint modeling and optimization.
•
TAO can be generalized and extended to different workloads such as multi-agent orchestration and Looped Agents. Moreover, it is also compatible with non-agent chatbot scenarios.
•
Across the 12 reported model–workload–concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.
2
Background and Problem Description
2.1
Agent Session and distributed resources
An agent session is a persistent interaction that alternates between model requests and external tool calls. During a model request, it uses a serving node; during tool execution, it awaits a result outside the inference service. A scheduler records each session’s state and controls session admission, while the serving engine manages physical KV-cache residency and eviction.
A later model request can reuse the KV prefix produced by earlier turns and avoid prefill computation
(
Kwon et al., 2023
)
. Because an agent session carries its instructions, history, and tool observations across turns, reuse depends on both the agent session history and the node selected for its next request. SGLang and Preble exploit related prefix structure in model programs and distributed scheduling
(
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Srivatsa et al., 2025
)
.
Our CGDC separates clustered GPU inference from distributed tool execution. Client or remote tools introduce variable delays between model requests, while their CPU and RAM are managed
outside
the GPU admission budget
(
Anthropic, 2026b
;
OpenAI, 2026
;
Chang et al., 2026
)
. Tool latency therefore determines when an agent session may need GPU resources for inference again.
2.2
session interruption and session restart
During tool execution, a session can release its GPU resources safely, although its cached prefix may subsequently be evicted. In contrast, preempting an active inference session requires recomputation. Repeated recomputation and reconstruction cause
KV-cache thrashing
, wasting capacity on state that must be rebuilt. This phenomenon motivates cache-aware engine and scheduling work
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Srivatsa et al., 2025
;
NVIDIA, 2025
)
, as well as policies that weigh retaining state against serving other work
(
Li et al., 2025
;
Abhyankar et al., 2024
)
.
Therefore, at a tool boundary, the scheduler can apply
session interruption
. Specifically, a scheduler can interrupt the agent session’s model admission and release its node resources while the external tool continues. When inference service is needed again,
session restarting
restores admission on an eligible node and resumes the existing interaction. Session interruption and session restarting describe session state transitions. They are decoupled from the underlying inference engine.
We find that the decisions made for these two operations can be based on the same session evaluation. Thus, we optimize toward a unified goal for maximizing the evaluation.
Session interruption can be decided by ordering sessions according to their values. Interrupted sessions join new arrivals in a waiting pool. We focus on
unified session evaluation
and
restarting decisions
from this pool.
3
Method
3.1
Framework overview
We present TAO, which combines agentic session evaluation with decision making, i.e. dynamic programming for joint selection and placement. The detailed formulation appears in Section
3.2
.
Figure
2
illustrates the pipeline of our method. First, session evaluation maps agent session and node observations to assignment values (Section
3.2
), including KV cache with time-aware decay (Section
3.3
) and tool-return readiness (Section
3.4
). Second, an exact dynamic program jointly selects waiting agent sessions and assigns them to nodes under residual capacity constraints (Sections
3.2
and
3.5
). Separating session evaluation from decision making lets the evaluation interface evolve while preserving the scheduling procedure.
Figure 2:
The TAO evaluate-then-decide framework in CGDC.
External tools on distributed CPUs provide historical tool-call durations, while the serving engines on clustered GPUs provide cache observations.
Then, the session evaluation component constructs triplets
(decayed KV-cache credit, binary readiness, token count)
.
The decision making component jointly selects and places waiting agent sessions. The executor validates the plan against live state before applying it.
The resulting assignments schedule sessions to eligible nodes.

Experiment Setup
Models and workloads.
We evaluate DeepSeek-V4 Flash, Qwen3-32B, and GLM-4.7
(
DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2025
)
on the SWE-bench Lite workload (SWE-Lite) using the mini-SWE-agent harness (MiniSWE)
(
mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026
;
Jimenez et al., 2024
)
. For DeepSeek, we also use Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.0
(
Merrill et al., 2026
)
for challenging tasks. For Qwen, we test with SWE-verified to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. We further evaluate GLM-4.7 on SWE-Lite to test single-node performance. Appendix
F
reports an InferenceX trace-replay evaluation.
Deployment.
DeepSeek runs on 2 nodes with
4
×
4\times
H100 per node; Qwen runs on 4 nodes with
2
×
2\times

8
×

E.1
reports a lower-concurrency DeepSeek check on the same single-node topology.
Baselines.
vLLM Scheduler w/ RR and vLLM Scheduler w/ CA denote the vLLM schedulers with round-robin and cache-aware policies, respectively
(
vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.
)
, which align with the policy in SGLang
(
Zheng et al., 2024
)
. These baselines cover load spreading and prefix-locality scheduling. Dynamo is a KV-aware scheduler
(
NVIDIA, 2025
)
. ThunderAgent uses token-count scheduling and best-fit-decreasing placement
(
Kang et al., 2026
)
. TAO combines predictive cache-aware session evaluation with joint dynamic-programming placement.
Metrics.
We report mean task end-to-end latency, mean time to first token (TTFT), and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS). Task latency includes both model inference and tool execution. Component analyses also measure prefix-cache hit rate, tool-end-to-first-token delay, and pause wait, which includes the tool call latency of an interrupted session.
4.2
Main Results
Table
1
compares five baselines across different levels of concurrency, models, and topologies. Taken together, these results make TAO the strongest overall choice: it combines consistently low latency and TTFT with high decode throughput more effectively than any single baseline, consistent with our focus on responsiveness after tool calls and improved KV reuse.
DeepSeek-V4 Flash.
We evaluate on challenging benchmarks with moderate concurrency. On SWE-Lite, , relative to the best competing method in each column, latency falls by 2.4–26.8%, TTFT by 7.4–36.3%, and decode throughput rises by 5.1–29.5%. On Terminal-Bench, TAO also leads on latency and TTFT at all three concurrency levels.
Qwen3-32B.
We use higher concurrency to exercise the serving capacity of its smaller model replicas. On SWE-Lite, TAO achieves the lowest TTFT at all three worker counts and the highest decode throughput at 96, 128 and 160 workers. On SWE-verified, TAO leads on TTFT and decode throughput throughout, with reductions of 12.9–29.9% in TTFT and gains of 4.0–7.8% in decode throughput. It also reduces latency by 8.3% and 9.0% at 96 and 160 workers; at 128 workers, latency is 2.5% higher than ThunderAgent.

Improvement Breakdown
As shown in Section
4.2
, the worker sweep exposes a latency–throughput tradeoff: the lowest latency and TTFT occur at the smallest worker count, while peak decode throughput occurs at 64 workers for DeepSeek SWE-Lite and Terminal-Bench, 128 workers for Qwen SWE-Lite, and 96 workers for SWE-verified. We use DeepSeek at 32 workers as a balanced operating point and examine how cache-aware valuation, tool readiness, and joint placement improve reuse, tool-return responsiveness, and admission decisions.
Cache-aware valuation.
In a fixed-workload replay of 218 tasks with DP placement held fixed for the ThunderAgent control and cache-aware variants, cache-token ordering raises prefix-cache hit rate by 0.19 percentage points and reduces mean pause wait by 4.5% relative to ThunderAgent. Adding cache-credit decay raises hit rate by 0.31 percentage points and decode throughput by 1.68% relative to ThunderAgent. Figure
5
summarizes these changes; bars are percentage points for cache hit and percentages for the other metrics, with positive values denoting improvement.
Figure 5:
Cache-aware valuation in the 32-worker replay, relative to the ThunderAgent control with DP placement.
Reductions in prefill, TTFT, and pause wait are shown as positive improvements.
Tool readiness.
Enabling readiness in the paired SWE-Lite runs increases decode throughput by 4.03% and reduces tool-end-to-first-token delay by 10.88%. Mean pause wait falls from 1.067 to 0.972 s. Figure
6
shows the return-delay distributions and prediction error. Across 10,967 completed tools, the final duration prediction has a mean absolute error of 0.410 s, with 82.9% of errors within 0.5 s.

Joint Scheduling.
Joint optimization improves the lexicographic
scheduling objective in six of the 23 replay snapshots with multiple
candidates (26.1%), matching the short-first heuristic in the remaining 17.
Across all 35 reconstructable snapshots, including single-candidate cases,
DP improves six (17.1%) and matches the heuristic in 29 (82.9%).

Conclusion
Tool execution makes agentic inference demand intermittent, while accumulated context makes the choice of node consequential. TAO brings these two properties into a common scheduling objective through cache credit, tool-return readiness, and token footprint. Joint dynamic-programming placement maximizes this objective under snapshot capacity constraints, and asynchronous revalidation connects the plan to live execution. Across the evaluated DeepSeek-V4 Flash and Qwen3-32B settings, this design delivers improvements of up to 26.8% in latency, 36.3% in mean TTFT, and 29.5% in decode throughput. The resulting architecture gives agentic serving an extensible way to translate workload knowledge into coordinated admission and placement.

B.2
Asynchronous execution
The scheduler solves a frozen snapshot in an isolated worker. Before applying the plan, it checks that selected agent sessions remain eligible and match their recorded state signatures, then applies the longest prefix permitted by current capacities. Changed selected-agent session signatures cause the plan to be discarded. Revalidation preserves feasibility under current admission constraints. We quantify the effect of stale values, discarded plans, and partial application through a loss bound relative to the fresh-snapshot optimum, and measure these execution outcomes alongside solve time and plan age.

E.2
KV-Cache Management Compatibility
TokenCake uses workflow dependencies and agent priorities to guide its Space Scheduler, and tool-stall events and timing prediction to guide offload and upload in its Time Scheduler
(
Bian et al., 2025
)
. Agentix prioritizes and preempts LLM calls using program-level service history to reduce request- and program-level blocking
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
. It operates at the request-scheduling layer, so integrating it with TAO would require coordinating the two admission policies. KVFlow represents a workflow as an Agent Step Graph and uses steps-to-execution to prioritize cache eviction and prefetching
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
. CacheScout learns execution transitions online to guide cache management without requiring a predefined graph
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. These mechanisms provide information about future cache use. In our formulation, such information can inform the program–node values supplied to session evaluation, while engine-local cache policies can operate beneath TAO’s admission and placement decisions. This is an architectural extension for KVFlow and CacheScout, while the implemented composition evaluated here uses TokenCake.
With TokenCake enabled, the combined system completes validated 300-task SWE-Lite runs on DeepSeek-V4 Flash TP4
×
\times
2 at 16 and 32 workers. Relative to the same engine behind consistent-hash routing, the combination increases decode throughput from 785.159 to 886.772 tok/s and from 1292.584 to 1347.373 tok/s, respectively (12.9% and 4.2%). These runs establish operational compatibility.

At 16 and 32 workers, TAO lowers mean task latency relative to consistent hashing by 3.1% and 2.0%, while increasing decode throughput by 12.9% and 4.2%. At 32 workers, client TTFT increases slightly from 0.220 to 0.223 s. Both combined runs record balanced request routing across the two replicas (5816/5393 and 5328/5683 requests) and tool-prediction updates (22085 and 21776). Neither records a program pause, resume, or migration, and their final offload series are absent. The evidence therefore establishes lifecycle and serving compatibility under these loads; attribution to DP selection or overlapping offload would require runs that activate those mechanisms. Separate transfer qualifications verify actual GPU–CPU movement.

Appendix J
Extended Related Work
Capacity-constrained optimization.
Dynamic programming and exact multiple-knapsack algorithms provide established tools for selecting items and assigning them to capacity-limited resources
(
Bellman, 1957
;
Kellerer et al., 2004
;
Pisinger, 1999
)
. Node-dependent assignment values place our formulation within the multiple-knapsack/generalized-assignment family. Approximation algorithms address the computational cost of this family
(
Chekuri and Khanna, 2005
;
Shmoys and Tardos, 1993
)
, while online resource-allocation algorithms analyze decisions under specified arrival models
(
Li et al., 2020
)
. TAO uses this classical optimization machinery to connect agentic session evaluation with joint admission and node placement. Its additive, lexicographic objective makes cache opportunity, tool readiness, and token footprint precedence explicit, and its asynchronous executor revalidates assignments against live state. Section
3.5
and Appendix
B.2
specify snapshot optimality and the bounds for asynchronous application.
KV locality and agent scheduling.
PagedAttention improves physical KV allocation and sharing, while SGLang’s RadixAttention reuses prefixes within the serving runtime
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
)
. Preble co-optimizes distributed prefix reuse and computation balance; Mooncake combines a distributed KV store with disaggregated serving
(
Srivatsa et al., 2025
;
Qin et al., 2025
)
. Dynamo and production gateways expose cache- and load-aware request scheduling
(
NVIDIA, 2025
;
vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.
;
SGLang Team, n.d.
)
, and llm-d provides pluggable scoring components
(
Guy et al., 2025
)
. SMetric exploits session structure by balancing first-turn requests and assigning later turns to nodes with reusable cache, using a global cache tier to limit the cost of redistribution
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
. TAO builds on these locality and load-balancing principles with joint optimization of assignments for waiting agent sessions under shared capacity. This joint view accounts for how one admission consumes capacity needed by other session–node assignments.
Program-level schedulers also preserve information across model calls. Autellix uses attained service and critical-path information to prioritize single-threaded and distributed programs
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
. ThunderAgent introduces the program abstraction, state-aware pausing, elapsed-time discounting of tool execution programs’ effective token demand, and a global waiting queue
(
Kang et al., 2026
)
. TAO adds node-specific cache values and readiness to the joint placement objective. Tool-gap cache management addresses a complementary decision: InferCept chooses among preservation, swapping, and recomputation by modeling resource waste
(
Abhyankar et al., 2024
)
; Continuum selects a cache-retention TTL using historical tool-duration distributions, reconstruction cost, and returning programs’ queueing cost, together with TTL-aware program ordering
(
Li et al., 2025
)
. These systems control physical KV retention. TAO coordinates scheduler-level admission opportunities, with predicted readiness distinguishing plans that have equal higher-precedence cache value. The serving engine controls the resulting cache residency.
Workflow, prediction, and tool execution.
Workflow structure provides information beyond an isolated request. Parrot exposes inter-request dependencies through Semantic Variables, and Helium compiles workflow query plans for proactive reuse and cache-aware execution
(
Lin et al., 2024
;
Wadlom et al., 2026
)
. KVFlow uses an Agent Step Graph and steps-to-execution to guide eviction and prefetching
(
Pan et al., 2025
)
; CacheScout learns execution transitions online without a predefined graph
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. Their predictions guide context residency and prefetching; readiness supplies a binary near-term admission-opportunity signal derived from tool timing. SAGA combines workflow graphs, session-affinity batching, and work stealing
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
. TOPAS also uses heuristic state searching: it scores prefix-residency and request-admission states using remaining workflow paths, movement costs, and downstream reuse, with bounded candidate search and greedy packing
(
Ni et al., 2026
)
. Its task-dependent utility and engine-level residency decisions differ from our fixed additive value contract and exact multi-node scheduling problem.
Prediction also supports latency-oriented scheduling. ELIS predicts response length, while Kairos combines workflow-aware priority with memory-aware dispatch
(
Choi et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
. Recent work separates already-ready turns from their release, using a mean–CVaR objective and an adaptive budget for committed inference work
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
. This addresses tail-aware release after dependencies complete; TAO additionally evaluates near-term return opportunities during external tool execution. Complementary mechanisms change the execution timeline itself: Conveyor exposes partial tool execution, Sutradhara overlaps tool work and prefill through orchestrator–engine cooperation, and PASTE speculates on future tools while coordinating tool execution with returning model agent sessions
(
Xu et al., 2024
;
Biswas et al., 2026
;
Sui et al., 2026
)
. SmoothAgent prepares transformed context on a lookahead stream, and Pie exposes programmable generation and KV handlers
(
Pan et al., 2026
;
Gim et al., 2025
)
. TAO operates in the scheduler, using timing evidence to coordinate admission and node placement.
Deployment and workloads.
AgentSysBench documents substantial non-LLM latency and deployment-dependent resource demands
(
Chang et al., 2026
)
. MARS explicitly coordinates GPU inference, CPU tool pressure, admission, and KV retention in heterogeneous serving
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
. In our CGDC scenario, distributed executors manage tool CPU and memory, and their resource pressure reaches the GPU scheduler through tool-return timing. TAO captures this interaction through readiness when allocating GPU admission capacity. OpenHands supports separate execution environments
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
. Coding and terminal workloads, together with InferenceX/AgentX trace replay, provide complementary evidence about task completion and serving behavior
(
mini-SWE-agent Contributors, 2026
;
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Merrill et al., 2026
;
SemiAnalysis, 2026b
;
SemiAnalysis, 2026a
)
, with workload-specific timing metrics defined in the evaluation.

article.headline: TAO：工具感知的智能体服务联合调度
article.lede: TAO在GPU集群与CPU工具分离的智能体服务中，联合评估工具就绪与KV缓存价值，并用动态规划做会话选择与放置。
article.problem: 在CGDC场景中，智能体会话在GPU推理与分布式CPU工具执行之间交替，外部工具调用使推理需求出现中断。现有系统评估会话时通常忽略工具调用延迟，只把工具时序当作KV复用或token数的替代信号；决策阶段又逐会话套用启发式打分与路由，难以考虑多个会话对同一节点容量的竞争。
article.method: TAO为每个会话–节点对构造三元组价值：带时间衰减的KV缓存信用、二值化的工具返回就绪信号和token占用，其中就绪预测结合工具进度暴露、解析的sleep命令与历史时长。随后，一个容量状态动态规划在冻结快照上联合选择等待会话并分配到节点，异步执行器在应用前复核实时状态。
article.results: 在12组模型–负载–并发设置中，相对各指标最佳基线，TAO最多降低26.8%延迟、36.3%平均TTFT，并提升29.5%解码吞吐；消融中完整配置解码1417.97 tok/s，去掉就绪降至1363.06 tok/s，用BFD替换DP降至1233.72 tok/s。
article.why_it_matters: 把工具返回时序纳入调度价值，并将会话级评估与联合放置解耦，为智能体服务提供可扩展的调度接口，也兼容非智能体聊天负载。
article.limitations: 局限在于DP只对冻结且离散化的问题精确，取整可能排除原本可行的方案，容量预算耗尽时回退到BFD（64个DeepSeek worker下回退率5.24%）；收益也非全覆盖，Qwen3-32B SWE-verified在128 workers时延迟比ThunderAgent高2.5%。此外，35个可重建快照中DP仅在6个（17.1%）改进启发式目标，说明联合优化的增益依赖快照中的竞争程度。
