page_papers.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
page_papers.content:
Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He,
Jun Lan, Renjie Gu, Linhan Cao,
Junkai Lin, Huijia Zhu,
Weiqiang Wang, Linghe Kong, Yue Wang,
Zhuosheng Zhang, Weiran Huang
School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University  Ant Group
Zhongguancun Academy  Shanghai Innovation Institute  Fudan University
Abstract
Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence.
In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly.
Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer.
Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves.
To strengthen this capability, we propose
EvidenceConnect
, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence.
To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions.
We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2).
Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning (shown in Figure
1
).
These results establish
EvidenceConnect
as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.

Introduction
Multimodal perception is the foundation of multimodal intelligence: before a multimodal model can reason or act, it must determine what is present in a scene. Recent progress on this front, such as multimodal Chain-of-Thought
(
Zhang et al., 2023
;
Xu et al., 2024
;
Li and Ma, 2026
)
and Thinking-with-Images
(
Zheng et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, has improved the ability of open-source vision-language models (VLMs) to perceive fine-grained visual content and use it in reasoning
(
Wei et al., 2026
;
Wei et al., 2025b
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
.
However, these advances do not reliably extend to tasks in which critical visual cues are dispersed across objects, relationships, frames, or dialogue turns. Two such tasks, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding, are particularly important because they underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents, respectively.
Spatial perception requires a model to recover how entities are arranged relative to one another and how several spatial relations compose
(
Gemini Robotics Team, 2025
;
Li et al., 2025a
)
. Embodied AI relies on it to ground navigation, manipulation, and viewpoint-dependent decisions in object locations and spatial relations
(
Brohan et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
. Multimodal long-context understanding requires a model to locate evidence across images and dialogue history, preserve entity identity, and bring that evidence to bear on the current question
(
Wu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2025d
;
Song et al., 2024
)
. Multimodal agents rely on it to retrieve relevant past observations, resolve references across interactions, and integrate earlier evidence into current decisions
(
He et al., 2024
;
Su et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2025b
)
.
Strengthening these capabilities, however, is constrained by the difficulty of building high-quality training data.
For spatial perception, existing efforts mainly scale up region-grounded relational data
(
Chen et al., 2024a
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, but reliable labels require precise localization and relational grounding across multiple objects. Such labels are expensive to annotate by hand, while automated generators often hallucinate relations.
For long-context understanding, existing multi-image and multi-turn instruction data
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2024
)
concentrate on a few formats and task types, because diverse questions that remain answerable over long sequences are hard to construct automatically.
Data for embodied spatial reasoning and multimodal agents are even harder to synthesize, since they additionally involve physical or interactive environments and multi-step trajectories. Consequently, neither these capabilities nor the applications built on them have a scalable and high-quality source of clean, verifiable supervision.
Our key insight is that these tasks build on a shared atomic capability of VLMs, which we call
connecting evidence
: identifying task-relevant visual facts, binding each fact to the correct entity, recovering the relations among them, and integrating the evidence into an answer.
These tasks instantiate this capability differently: spatial perception connects objects within a scene through spatial relations, whereas long-context understanding, on which multimodal agents rely, connects facts across images and dialogue turns through entity identity and reference.
Despite these differences in where the evidence resides and how it is linked, both tasks rely on the same underlying steps, so strengthening these steps can benefit both. Moreover, since the first step, identifying visual facts, is itself fine-grained perception, fine-grained perception benefits as well.
Crucially, training data that target this capability are far easier to construct and verify than data for the tasks themselves. To turn this insight into trainable supervision, we propose
EvidenceConnect
, an easy-to-implement, fully automated framework that synthesizes visual questions requiring the model to connect evidence across regions.
Specifically, we select a group of related regions within a single image and synthesize a compositional question over them from
privileged
zoomed views, which make small details visible but are used only during data construction.
Depending on the scene, we synthesize questions to compare, aggregate, or chain evidence across the regions.
Answering such questions thus exercises the same steps as the target tasks: relating regions spatially, including from a given viewpoint, parallels spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, whereas locating scattered regions, binding their facts to the right references, and integrating them parallels long-context understanding and multimodal agents.
To ensure data quality, we keep a question only if VLMs from different families agree on its answer, and we use region-ablation tests to discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions.
Finally, each verified question is converted into multiple-choice form for rule-based rewards and paired with the full image, where colored outlines typically mark the selected regions to avoid ambiguous references, so the model must still perceive and connect the evidence by itself.
To evaluate whether this supervision generalizes beyond the synthesized questions, we train Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Qwen3.6-27B
(
Qwen Team, 2026a
;
Qwen Team, 2026b
)
with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)
(
Lambert et al., 2024
;
DeepSeek-AI, 2025
)
using only our synthesized data, without supervised fine-tuning or benchmark-specific question formats.
The resulting models, ZwZ2-4B/9B/27B, achieve substantial improvements in fine-grained and spatial perception as well as multimodal long-context understanding, with gains that further extend to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning.
For example, ZwZ2-4B improves over its base model from 37.43 to 45.26 (+7.83) on ViewSpatial-Bench (spatial reasoning) and from 60.08 to 70.08 (+10.00) on MileBench (long-context understanding).
More broadly, its average over all 25 benchmarks increases from 49.41 to 54.79, and the corresponding averages improve from 51.63 to 56.59 for ZwZ2-9B and from 55.52 to 60.51 for ZwZ2-27B.
Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, it also improves on multi-image long-context benchmarks and multimodal agent tasks. These results demonstrate that connecting evidence is indeed a generalizable training target for multimodal perception.
To summarize, our key contributions are the following:
•
We identify connecting evidence as an important atomic capability of VLMs, underlying fine-grained perception, spatial perception, and multimodal long-context understanding.
•
We develop
EvidenceConnect
, a structured and audited synthesis pipeline for single-image, multi-region compositional questions, with privileged region views and independent checks for answer correctness and evidence dependence.
•
Experiments demonstrate that RLVR on the resulting synthetic data improves a broad range of perception benchmarks and further generalizes to many real-world tasks, including embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning.

To construct this supervision, we propose

, a data synthesis framework centered on coherent groups of image regions. Within this framework, high-resolution privileged crops render local details visible for question synthesis, while cross-model answer anchoring and region ablation check label reliability and evidence dependence.

Restricting the evidence to a single image keeps training inexpensive, while several related regions of one image already require a model to locate, bind, and compose dispersed evidence.
Importantly, the regions are selected to jointly support one question
q

Corresponding to these three kinds of roles,
q
q
connects the regions through one of three forms.
Aggregation
combines counts or other numeric facts from the regions, possibly through a short calculation.
Comparison and matching
treats the regions as the complete candidate set, so that an answer such as an outlier, an extremum, or a pairing can be identified only by considering all of them.
Dependency chains and compositions
build the answer in several steps, e.g., by using a clue to decide what to read next, fixing a viewpoint for interpreting the rest, or combining predicates from different regions.
In all three forms, the answer is determined only when the assigned roles are taken together.
These forms also tie our questions to the target tasks: spatial relations, including those in an agent’s or object’s own frame, parallel spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, while binding facts to regions referenced by outline colors and integrating them parallels how long-context understanding and multimodal agents handle facts tied to image or turn references.
To synthesize such questions, we first locate candidate regions, then group those that support one of the three forms, and finally compose questions over each selected group.
Grounded evidence discovery.
Since multi-region questions need detail-rich scenes, we start from high-resolution, visually complex images.
For each image, a strong VLM judges whether it can support such questions and, if so, is prompted to propose concrete, clearly localizable regions, each with a bounding box and a short description, prioritizing regions that can be related to one another over isolated salient ones.
We then discard proposals that are too small, too large, or heavily overlapping.
As these model-generated descriptions may be wrong, they only guide grouping and question writing, whereas reference answers are later derived from the image itself.
Task-conditioned evidence grouping.
An arbitrary collection of these proposals, however, does not necessarily support a valid compositional question.
We therefore prompt a strong model with the image caption and region descriptions to propose several groups per image, each labeled with a task family (a specific question type such as anomaly detection) and a necessity mode (how removing a region should affect the answer).
We then discard invalid or duplicated groups and closed sets of incomparable objects, and keep groups with distinct task families first.
The task family only guides question writing, whereas each region’s concrete role is fixed when a question is written.
Privileged evidence layout.
Since fine-grained details are difficult to inspect at full-image scale, we construct for each group a privileged evidence layout

In addition, each region is outlined in a distinct color that also marks it in the full image, allowing questions to refer to regions by color unambiguously.

4.2
Main Results
Table
1
shows that ZwZ2 improves over its base model on all 25 benchmarks at every scale, raising the overall average by 5.39, 4.96, and 4.99 points at 4B, 9B, and 27B, respectively.
In particular, fine-grained and spatial perception improve by 5.2–6.3 points on average, with gains of up to 11.1 points on MIMIC and 10.8 points on CountQA, and embodied spatial reasoning improves by 5.5–8.1 points, including 10.5 points on ERQA at 27B.
Qualitative examples are provided in Appendix
F
.
Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, its gains carry over to multi-image and interactive settings.
Long-context understanding improves at every scale, most markedly at 4B, where the domain average rises by 5.6 points, including a gain of 10.0 points on MileBench.
Likewise, the multimodal agent benchmark AgentVista improves by 4.8–6.2 points, and GUI grounding also improves consistently.
These results support our premise that connecting evidence within an image transfers to tasks whose evidence spans images, dialogue turns, or interaction steps.
ZwZ2 remains competitive with frontier models. ZwZ2-27B achieves the highest overall accuracy (60.51%), compared with 54.02%, 57.24%, and 55.47% for GPT-5.6-Luna, GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, and leads the fine-grained perception domain.

Table

compares
EvidenceConnect
with existing synthetic datasets on the same 4B base model.
These datasets target single-region fine-grained perception (ZwZ), grounded counting and spatial reasoning (TVG), dialogue-fragment retrieval (F

Training on TVG, F

In contrast,
EvidenceConnect
improves every benchmark over the base model and outperforms these four datasets on all 11 benchmarks, with a comparable amount of data (20.4K examples versus 19.4K–37K).
ZwZ-73K is the strongest baseline.
Since it also synthesizes questions from zoomed-in views but grounds each question in a single region, the comparison with ZwZ serves as an approximate ablation of connecting multiple regions.
Although ZwZ uses 3.6
×

raises the average accuracy from 49.86 to 53.86 and surpasses ZwZ on 10 of the 11 benchmarks, trailing it only on MileBench by 0.13 points.
The largest margin appears on MindCube-Tiny, where ZwZ reduces accuracy by 13.8 points whereas

Ablation study on drop-one verification.
To evaluate adaptive drop-one verification during data synthesis, we compare Qwen3.5-4B trained on 7K examples constructed with or without this verification step (Table
3
).
As described in Section
3.2
, this step masks one selected region at a time in the privileged layout and tests whether the reference answer remains recoverable.
When the verifier returns the reference answer or an unusable response, additional queries are used; a region is marked as empirically redundant only if most queries recover the reference answer.
A question is rejected only when more than one region is empirically redundant, allowing for noise from overlapping crop margins and variable verifier responses.
With drop-one verification, average accuracy rises from 51.03 to 52.65 (+1.63 points), with improvements on 10 of the 11 benchmarks.
The largest gains are on MindCube-Tiny (+5.15), O3-Bench (+4.64), and CountQA (+3.79), while ERQA decreases by 4.00 points.
These results support the usefulness of this synthesis-time verification step for downstream performance, although its gains are not uniform across tasks.
Ablation study on privileged views.
To examine the role of privileged views, we train Qwen3.5-4B on 7K examples synthesized from privileged views or original images, with all other settings fixed (Table
3
).
Synthesis from privileged views achieves a higher average accuracy than synthesis from original images (52.65 versus 51.38), with higher scores on 9 of the 11 benchmarks.
Original-image synthesis performs better on Chartography and ERQA, by 4.00 and 4.75 points, respectively.
Thus, privileged-view synthesis improves average accuracy by 1.27 points in this 7K comparison, although its gains are not uniform across benchmarks.

Context length.
Figure

ZwZ2 outperforms or matches its base model at every length and scale, and on MemLens its gains persist up to 256K tokens.
The gains, however, narrow at the longest contexts.
At 128K on the MMLongBench visual core, for example, ZwZ2-4B and ZwZ2-9B merely match their base models.

Conclusion
We presented
EvidenceConnect
, a fully automated framework that synthesizes multi-region visual questions and answers, requiring a model to connect evidence within an image.
Trained with RLVR on these data alone, ZwZ2 improves over its base models on all 25 benchmarks at 4B, 9B, and 27B.
Notably, although training uses only single images, the gains extend beyond fine-grained and spatial perception to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, and multimodal agent tasks.
These results suggest that connecting evidence is a transferable training target, and thus tasks whose training data are costly to build can benefit from data that are far easier to construct and verify.

Image source and pre-filtering.
We use SA-1B
(
Kirillov et al., 2023
)
as the sole image source.
Before any model call, we keep only images whose longer side has at least 1280 pixels, whose mean per-channel intensity entropy is at least 6.5 bits, whose Canny edge density is at least 0.04, and whose luminance standard deviation is at least 60.
Grounded evidence discovery.
For each image, a single call with the image and its caption (Prompt
B.1
) judges whether the image can support multi-region questions and returns up to 18 region proposals, whose box coordinates are converted to pixels and clamped to the image.
We then discard boxes that cover less than 0.04% or more than 18% of the image, as well as boxes whose IoU with an earlier kept box is at least 0.65.
Images judged unsuitable, or with fewer than four remaining regions, are skipped.
Task-conditioned evidence grouping.
A text-only call receives the caption together with the label and local description of each region, ranked by grounding confidence (Prompt
B.1
), and proposes up to six groups of 3–7 regions.
Each group is annotated with one of 22 task families, which map to four necessity modes that refine the three question forms of Section
3.1
.
Specifically,
answer_sensitive
covers aggregation (counting, numeric aggregation, and arithmetic),
set_complete
(filtering, anomaly, extremum, matching, and geometric, topological, or depth relations) and
pair_complete
(cross-region pairing) cover comparison and matching, and
chain_dependency
(OCR, spatial, viewpoint, conditional, Boolean, relational, and multi-hop chains) covers dependency chains and compositions.
We keep groups whose region identifiers are valid, whose size lies in the allowed range, and that do not repeat an earlier group.
In addition, the candidates of a filtering, anomaly, or extremum group must not mix coarse semantic classes, and groups with distinct task families are kept before groups that repeat a family.
Privileged evidence layout.
Each region is cropped at native resolution with a margin of 8% of its box size on every side.
The crops are placed on a white canvas through an order-preserving remapping of each image axis, which removes the rows and columns not covered by any crop, and the canvas is uniformly downscaled only when its longer side exceeds 4096 pixels.
Each region receives a distinct color from a seven-color palette, which bounds the group size at seven.
The same colors are used in the question text, in the privileged and ablated layouts, and for the outlines on the marked policy view.
Question realization.
For each group, the generator receives the privileged layout, the group metadata (labels, local descriptions, natural referents, box coordinates, and outline colors), four blueprints sampled from a library of 104 reasoning templates, and up to four additional free-form slots, and it returns up to eight candidates (Prompt
B.1
).
The first blueprint follows the proposed task family when possible, and the remaining ones diversify answer forms and question types.
Each candidate declares its question type, necessity mode, answer semantics (scalar, unordered set, or ordered pair), answer kind (outline color, number, Boolean pattern, semantic phrase, text, semantic set, or semantic pair), the contribution of every region, the predicted answer after removing each region, and a reasoning certificate.
Open-vocabulary answers must contain fewer than ten words.
Rule-based checks and candidate selection.
A certificate is valid only if every step reads from earlier steps alone, every selected region lies on a path to the output step, and no step is disconnected from it.
Aggregation, arithmetic, and Boolean questions must further use an executable certificate with a restricted operator set.
For aggregation questions, every region must receive a positive value, and the values must sum to the answer without all being one, since the answer would otherwise equal the number of outlined regions.
Similarly, arithmetic expressions must reference every region and evaluate to the answer.
We further reject candidates that expose region identifiers, do not refer to the marked regions, use conditional wording without explicit branches or outside conditional types, count vague background targets, request more than one output for a scalar answer, omit an explicit coordinate frame for spatial types, leak the answer through an outline color, use subjective phrasing, or declare an answer form that the answer does not match.
Candidates whose own predicted answer after removing some region equals their proposed answer are rejected as well.
The remaining candidates are ranked by the generator’s self-assessed naturalness, visual confidence, and multi-region scores, with bonuses for compositional types and non-numeric answers, and this ranking only determines which candidates proceed to verification.
Per group, we keep up to four top-ranked candidates, preferring distinct question types and allowing at most one numeric and two outline-color answers.
Per image, we keep up to eight candidates but always retain the best candidate of each question type.
Cross-model answer anchoring.
Each candidate is answered on the privileged layout by both anchoring families, with up to four samples per family and without the region descriptions or the generator’s answer (Prompt
B.2
).
For closed-form questions, the prompt also lists the allowed answer labels, and we first draw two samples per family.
Such a candidate is rejected early unless at least three of these four responses agree and each family contributes at least one of them.
Responses are clustered by normalized string matching with numeric equivalence, and if the largest cluster has fewer than six members, the text-only judge re-clusters all responses by semantic equivalence (Prompt
B.2
).
A candidate is accepted if the largest cluster is not an insufficiency response and contains at least three of the four responses from each family, and its answer then becomes
a
⋆
a^{\star}
.
Finally,
a
⋆
a^{\star}
is re-checked against the answer-form constraints above.
Adaptive drop-one testing.
For each selected region, its crop in the privileged layout is replaced by a gray block with a red cross, while all other crops stay in place.
The first anchoring family answers each ablated view once, with a mode-specific addendum to the answering prompt (Prompt
B.2
).
If the response matches
a
⋆
a^{\star}
or cannot be parsed, the same view is queried twice more, and the region is redundant if at least two of its three responses match
a
⋆
a^{\star}
.
A candidate is rejected if two or more of its regions are redundant.
Policy view.
Unmarked rewriting is attempted only for aggregate question types (object counts, attribute counts, and sums of visible numbers), whose answers do not depend on the outlines, whereas the answers of selection and pairing questions are often outline colors themselves.
The first anchoring family rewrites the question for the unmarked image and proposes distractors (Prompt
B.3
), and rewrites that still mention boxes or outlines are discarded.
Two audits from each family (Prompt
B.3
) must then all report unique references, task preservation, identifiable targets, multi-region dependence, and necessity of every evidence area.
Each audit must also recover
a
⋆
a^{\star}
and ground exactly one box per intended region, and the grounded boxes must match the intended regions one-to-one, where a grounded box matches a region if its center lies inside the region’s box enlarged by 15%.
Otherwise, the example keeps the marked policy view, on which the box of each selected region is outlined in its assigned color.
Multiple-choice conversion.
For marked examples, the first anchoring family proposes three distractors given the marked image, the question, and
a
⋆
a^{\star}
(Prompt
B.3
), whereas unmarked examples reuse the distractors from the rewrite step.
We remove empty distractors, distractors that match
a
⋆
a^{\star}
after normalization, duplicates, and, for closed-form answers, options outside the label vocabulary.
If fewer than three distractors remain, we fill the missing options deterministically, for example with alternative subsets of set-valued answers, unused vocabulary labels, or neighboring integers for count answers.
The four options are then shuffled, and the prompt asks for the option letter.
Difficulty filtering.
The screening model answers each example four times on its policy view (Prompt
B.3
).
Examples with four correct responses or any unparseable response are discarded, and the remaining ones are labeled easy, medium, hard, or very hard when three, two, one, or none of the responses are correct.
Finally, we keep at most four examples per source image, and each training example consists of the policy view and the multiple-choice question.

Prompt Templates for
EvidenceConnect
This section lists the prompt templates used by
EvidenceConnect
.
We replace instance-specific values with angle-bracketed placeholders and condense long templates for readability.
Specifically, we keep their task definitions, key constraints, and main output fields, and omit examples, formatting reminders, repeated instructions, and fields unused in our setting.

Prompt B.1: Grounded region inventory
[IMAGE]
You are a precise visual grounding annotator and data-quality gate.

Task: Decide whether this image can support natural questions whose
answer genuinely depends on 3--7 distinct regions, then propose up to
<MAX_REGIONS> useful evidence regions.

Image caption, if available: <IMAGE_CAPTION>

Return regions that are:
- visually concrete and clearly localizable;
- useful for multi-region reasoning, including people, animals, objects,
signs, screens, text regions, fine details, and distinctive parts;
- preferably small or medium-sized, spatially diverse, and not overly
overlapping;
- suitable for coherent tasks such as positive-contribution counting,
closed-set filtering, anomaly/extremum detection, candidate matching,
pairing, OCR--visual verification, or a short dependent spatial chain.

Prioritize groups of related regions over isolated interesting objects.
The image is suitable only if at least one coherent all-region task is
possible. Avoid vague regions such as "background," "scene," "sky,"
"room," or the whole image.

For each region, return:
- label: short name;
- bbox: [x1,y1,x2,y2] in pixels, or normalized 0--1000 coordinates;
- caption: one concise visible description;
- natural_referent: an identifying phrase without coordinates or IDs;
- role: candidate | reference | comparator | text_region |
      count_target | fine_part | distractor;
- confidence: grounding confidence.

"richness_reason": "...",

],

Prompt B.2: Task-conditioned region-group proposal
You are an expert VQA data curator. Below are <N> candidate evidence
regions detected in one image.

Image caption: <IMAGE_CAPTION>
Regions:
- <REGION_ID>: label=<LABEL>; caption=<LOCAL_CAPTION>
- ...

Propose up to <MAX_GROUPS> combinations that are good for natural
questions requiring many regions. A good combination is a coherent
candidate/evidence set, not a bag of unrelated boxes. Prefer the
largest valid set, but every selected region must have a real role.

Allowed task families and necessity modes:
- answer_sensitive: aggregate_count, aggregate_attribute_count,
aggregate_numeric, arithmetic_composition;
- set_complete: set_filtering, anomaly_detection, extremum,
candidate_matching, geometric_line_relation, topological_relation,
depth_ordering;
- pair_complete: cross_region_pairing;
- chain_dependency: ocr_visual_verification, spatial_chain,
dependent_chain, viewpoint_transform, agent_relative_direction,
spatial_transitivity, conditional_composition, boolean_composition,

- Preferred task family: <TASK_FAMILY>.
- Preferred necessity mode: <NECESSITY_MODE>.

- Ask for one final answer.

- Use outline colors only as reference anchors, never as leaked object
attributes.

Appendix F
Case Study
To complement the quantitative evaluation, we examine three selected examples in which ZwZ2-4B answers correctly while its base model, Qwen3.5-4B, fails.
Figure
8
presents examples from MIMIC, ZoomBench, and CountQA, covering cross-image category identification, spatially specified text recognition, and object counting.
We analyze the models’ visible responses to identify how their answers differ in the use of visual evidence and the satisfaction of question constraints.
Cross-image consistency.
In Figure
8
(a), the MIMIC question asks for a category that appears in all five images.
The base model selects
wine glass
, even though its response explicitly acknowledges that this object is absent from some images.
It justifies the answer by referring to the most prominent shared item across the majority of the set, effectively replacing the requirement of universal presence with majority overlap.
ZwZ2 checks candidate categories against the full set of images.
Its response rules out
wine glass
because it is absent from Images 4 and 5, and identifies
person
as the category shared by all five images.
This example illustrates the importance of preserving the question’s scope when integrating evidence across images: an object shared by several images does not necessarily satisfy a constraint over the entire set.
Question-conditioned text localization.
Figure
8
(b) asks for the black text above the lower archway.
The base model recognizes the word
SEGATORI
on the adjacent building, but associates the question with inscriptions on the fountain and ultimately selects
FONTE
.
Its response therefore reveals a mismatch between the recognized text and the region specified by the question.
ZwZ2 identifies the entrance of the yellow building as the relevant lower archway and reads the sign immediately above it, yielding the correct answer,
SEGATORI
.
The case highlights the role of spatial reference resolution in visual text understanding: recognizing a visible word must be accompanied by establishing whether it belongs to the queried location.
Structured visual counting.
In Figure
8
(c), the CountQA question asks for the number of tablets in a blister pack.
The base model divides the image into regions above and below the yellow rubber band, reports two and four tablets, respectively, and returns
2
+
4
=
6
2+4=6
.
Its arithmetic is consistent with these counts, so the error lies in enumerating the tablets.
ZwZ2 describes the pack as two columns and five rows, counts five tablets in each column, and obtains the correct total of
5
+
5
=
10
5+5=10
.
Here, the response uses the regular spatial arrangement to account for the complete set of tablets.
Together, these cases reflect the steps of connecting evidence: integrating facts over the full set of images in (a), binding recognized text to the queried location in (b), and accounting for every instance before aggregating in (c).
Figure 8:
Qualitative comparisons between Qwen3.5-4B and ZwZ2-4B.
Three selected examples show correct predictions by ZwZ2-4B where the base model fails:
(a) identifying a category present in every image;
(b) associating recognized text with the queried location;
and (c) counting all instances in a structured arrangement.
Responses are excerpted from the original outputs, with omissions marked by
[...]
and answer fields reformatted.
The enlarged image region in (b) is provided for visualization only.
Appendix G
Limitations and Future Work
Our work has two main limitations.
First, although our single-image supervision transfers to multi-image and agent tasks, it does not directly model temporal or cross-frame dependencies, so extending the synthesis to evidence spread across video frames is a natural next step.
Second, we apply RLVR to models of up to 27B parameters, and whether the same supervision benefits larger models or earlier training stages, such as pre-training, remains to be studied.

article.headline: 从看清细节到串联证据：多区域合成数据训练 VLM
article.lede: 上海交大与蚂蚁等提出数据合成框架 EvidenceConnect，用单图多区域问题训练 VLM，25 个基准全线提升。
article.problem: 空间感知与多模态长上下文理解分别支撑具身智能和多模态智能体，但两者都缺少可规模化的高质量监督：空间关系标注需要精确定位与多物体关系 grounding，人工昂贵、自动生成器又常幻觉关系；长序列上仍然可回答的多样问题也难以自动构造。作者认为这些任务共享同一底层原子能力——「连接证据」，即找出相关视觉事实、绑定到正确实体、恢复关系并整合成答案。
article.method: EvidenceConnect 从单张高分辨率图像中选出 3–7 个相关区域，用只在数据构造阶段可见的「特权」放大裁剪视图生成需要比较、聚合或链式推理的组合式问题。候选答案只有在来自不同模型家族的两个 VLM 多数一致时才保留为参考答案，再通过逐一遮罩所选区域的 drop-one 测试剔除答案并不真正依赖证据的问题。最终每条样本配上带彩色区域轮廓的原始整图，转为四选项选择题并做难度过滤，仅用 GRPO/RLVR 训练，不做监督微调。
article.results: 以 Qwen3.5-4B/9B 和 Qwen3.6-27B 为基座，ZwZ2 在全部 25 个基准上都优于基座，总体平均分分别从 49.41 升至 54.79、51.63 升至 56.59、55.52 升至 60.51。4B 上 ViewSpatial-Bench 从 37.43 升至 45.26（+7.83），MileBench 从 60.08 升至 70.08（+10.00）；细粒度与空间感知平均提升 5.2–6.3 分，其中 MIMIC 最多 +11.1、CountQA 最多 +10.8，27B 上 ERQA +10.5。仅用 20.4K 合成样本时，11 个基准平均 53.86，高于用 73K 样本的 ZwZ（49.86）和基座（47.16）。ZwZ2-27B 总体 60.51%，高于论文报告的 GPT-5.6-Luna（54.02%）、GLM-5.3-Flash（57.24%）与 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash（55.47%）。
article.why_it_matters: 如果「连接证据」确实是一项可迁移的原子能力，那么训练数据昂贵甚至难以构造的任务（具身空间推理、多模态智能体、长上下文理解）都可以借助更易合成、更易校验的替代数据获得提升。论文显示只用单图数据训练，增益也能外溢到多图、对话与交互场景。
article.limitations: 单图监督并不直接建模跨帧或时序依赖，扩展到视频证据仍是未来工作，且 RLVR 只验证到 27B 参数，更大模型或预训练阶段是否受益未知。增益也不均匀：MMLongBench 视觉核心在 128K 上下文上 4B/9B 仅与基座持平，消融中 drop-one 验证令 ERQA 反降 4.00 分，用原图而非特权视图合成时 Chartography 和 ERQA 反而分别高 4.00 和 4.75 分。
article.figure_caption_zh: EvidenceConnect 流程：从单张图像选出相关区域并构造特权裁剪视图生成组合式问题，经跨模型答案锚定与逐一去区域检验后，转为多项选择题并做难度过滤；训练时策略模型只看到带区域轮廓的完整图像。

page_papers.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
page_papers.abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.

Abstract
We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.
1
Introduction
Embedding models map data to fixed-length vector representations, placing semantically similar data near each other in the embedding space. Text embedding models have become a popular choice for tasks like information retrieval, semantic similarity, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation. However, to work with audio and visual data, these require additional tools like automatic speech recognition (ASR) and image captioners which both add computational cost and fail to capture signals like fine-grained visual details and non-verbal or environmental sounds.
Multimodal embedding models like CLIP
[
1
]
, ALIGN
[
2
]
, and SigLIP
[
3
]
add a modality tower for vision, and so achieve strong cross-modal quality, but they are unable to natively process mixed-modal input to capture interactions between input modalities. Recent efforts have adapted Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into embedding models that allow interleaved mixed-modal input and support more complex tasks such as visual question answering and visual grounding
[
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
]
; subsequent work has built on more capable MLLMs to incorporate video and audio modalities
[
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
]
. However, as MLLMs have grown in size, so have embedding models adapted from them. These models typically contain several billion parameters, making them prohibitively expensive for applications that are latency-sensitive, high-throughput, or require on-device deployment for privacy or offline access.
In this paper, we introduce EmbeddingGemma 2,
1
1
1
Our model is available at
https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/embeddinggemma
.
a 744M-parameter general-purpose multimodal embedding model that maps text, images, video, and audio—as well as arbitrary interleaved combinations thereof—into a single unified embedding space (
Figure
1
). EmbeddingGemma 2 combines a 271M-parameter bidirectional transformer backbone (embedder included) with a 167M-parameter vision encoder and a 305M-parameter audio encoder. The modality encoders independently convert media into sequences of soft token embeddings that enter the shared transformer backbone, which means these parameters are modular: EmbeddingGemma 2 can alternatively be run with 271M parameters as a text-only model, with 439M as a vision-language model, or with 577M as an audio-language model.

The model builds on the architecture and weights from the capable Gemma 4 model family
[
13
]
and learns from the powerful Gemini Embedding 2 model
[
8
]
. Our training regime consists of three stages spanning various tasks, modalities, and domains, which results in a broadly capable model, excelling at problems like code search, visual question answering, video moment retrieval, audio classification, and much more. We separate text-only and multimodal training as a form of curriculum learning, and separate distillation from contrastive and regularization objectives in order to effectively learn an embedding space tailored to the model. For extreme resource-constrained settings, the model offers high-quality truncated embeddings and separate checkpoints adapted with quantization-aware training.
We present ablation studies explaining our architectural and training choices. We find that simplifying per-layer embeddings to omit the dedicated lookup table not only reduces cost but improves performance; we present the effects of using different vision token budgets during training and inference, observing it only significantly affects tasks like document retrieval which require fine-grained visual understanding; we demonstrate the importance of co-training the vision encoder; we show the impact of finetuning with contrastive learning rather than distillation; and we confirm the value of native audio understanding over ASR.

Recipe
Initialization
EmbeddingGemma 2 builds directly on Gemma 4’s extensive world knowledge and capabilities. The backbone is adapted from a pretrained Gemma 4 decoder-only model, switching the causal attention mask to bidirectional attention to enable fully contextual token representations
[
34
,
35
,
36
,
8
]
. We omit explicit adaptation stages for bidirectional attention
[
23
,
37
]
, which can be costly and have been shown to be unnecessary for learning expressive representations
[
23
,
38
]
. We also remove the PLE-specific token lookup table (detailed in
Table
2
), and add mean pooling
[
39
,
23
]
, a linear projection, and
ℓ
2
\ell_{2}
-normalization after the transformer. The vision encoder is initialized with the smaller Gemma 4 vision encoder and further trained in the two multimodal stages, which we show in
Section
3
to be critical for quality. The audio encoder is bit-identical to that in the Gemma 4 E2B and E4B models
[
13
]
and kept frozen during training.
We then train EmbeddingGemma 2 on a mixture of embedding tasks spanning various modalities and task types. In total, the model sees approximately 2.9T tokens, of which
∼
\sim
300B are seen during text pre-finetuning,
∼
\sim
2T during multimodal pre-finetuning, and
∼
\sim
600B during multimodal finetuning.
Text Pre-finetuning
We begin with a pre-finetuning stage like the one in
Schechter Vera et al. [23]
. This entails a large-scale unsupervised data mixture of query-target pairs from question answering, sentence similarity, code retrieval, and web search tasks using various languages. As before, we opt for a larger batch size both to stabilize the gradient and to provide more (in-batch) negatives for each input example. In this stage we almost exclusively employ distillation loss, with only an additional contrastive loss using a small weight. Here, as with subsequent stages, tasks are sampled at pre-determined, empirically defined rates. We found the inclusion of a text-only stage important for the model’s final text quality. This stage can be seen as a form of curriculum learning, or as an implicit warm-up for the bidirectional attention, similar to
BehnamGhader et al. [37]
; it has also been shown to enhance the discriminability of both text and non-text embeddings
[
10
]
.
Multimodal Pre-finetuning
We then continue with pre-finetuning, but with a new mixture which also includes inputs with images, audio, video, and documents across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal tasks, most with additional hard negatives. The text tasks in this stage and the next include those described in the finetuning stage of
Schechter Vera et al. [23]
, which aim to cover task diversity, language diversity, and coding capability. In this stage, we exclusively employ distillation loss, to inherit the teacher’s ability to map diverse and mixed modalities into a shared semantic space. We continue training with larger batch sizes and larger learning rates, but train for twice as many steps as in text pre-finetuning to cover the expanded multimodal training set.
Multimodal Finetuning
In the finetuning stage, we completely replace distillation with contrastive loss. This allows the model to learn a tailored embedding space independent of its teacher, as the teacher’s embedding space is not optimized for the student’s architecture, size, and MRL sub-dimensions. We also add other losses which aim to shape the final embedding space to have desirable properties: spread-out regularizer and MRL losses. As in
Schechter Vera et al. [23]
, we transition to smaller learning rates and batch sizes, and shift towards higher-quality, task-specific datasets, such as tool retrieval, audio captioning, video ranking, medical imaging, visual product search, cropped-object retrieval, and academic question-answering.
Model Merging
Finally, we combine checkpoints from our finetuning run by averaging their weights, to improve our final model’s quality and robustness. Rather than running multiple finetuning jobs, either with different data mixture rates
[
23
]
or with different hyperparameters
[
40
]
, we merge checkpoints along a single finetuning trajectory
[
41
]
. Specifically, we compute an unweighted average between the final checkpoint from the finetuning run and a significantly earlier checkpoint from the same run. Like
Wortsman et al. [42]
, which similarly merges pretrained and finetuned checkpoints, we found that this helps mitigate degradation on tasks that overfit during finetuning, while also further improving performance on tasks that already benefited from finetuning.

We additionally provide quantized versions of EmbeddingGemma 2 in different quantization configurations. We provide checkpoints with two types of weight representations for the backbone: int4 per-block (Q4_0) and int4 per-channel (Q4_C). For the modality encoders, we follow the quantization schemes used in Gemma 4: the vision encoder uses 8-bit precision for both weights and activations (W8A8), and the audio encoder uses 8-bit activation precision and {2, 4, 8}-bit weight precision varying by layer cluster.
We apply quantization-aware training
[
43
, QAT,]
to both the backbone and vision encoder to minimize quality degradation (the audio encoder is taken directly from Gemma 4). However, instead of applying QAT directly in the finetuning stage as in
Schechter Vera et al. [23]
, we introduce a separate post-merging tail-patch stage in which we distill (and initialize) our QAT checkpoint from the frozen float checkpoint
[
44
]
. This allows for a more resource-efficient QAT stage and narrows the gap in quality between the float and quantized checkpoints for some evaluations, notably MTEB(English, v2).

1
shows the quality is comparable between our quantized checkpoints and our raw checkpoint (evaluated at half-precision bfloat16 weights). With Q4_C quantization, the peak on-device memory footprint during inference (including runtime compilation overhead) on a Google Pixel 11 Pro is reduced to 191 MB for text-only, 447 MB for text and vision, and 567 MB for the full multimodal model.

We train EmbeddingGemma 2 with a budget of 280 vision tokens for images and 140 tokens per frame for videos, but the underlying Gemma 4 vision encoder supports budgets from 70 to 1120 tokens. In
Table
5
(top), we show the effect of using different vision token budgets at inference time using an intermediate checkpoint trained with 280 tokens per image and 140 per frame. Overall performance scales monotonically, with some distinct modality-specific behaviors. Visual document tasks are highly sensitive to fine-grained details and continue to improve greatly past the training budget; image quality in aggregate begins to saturate at the 280-token budget (despite continued gains on several individual tasks); and video performance actually degrades between 280 tokens and 560, likely because the excessive sequence lengths dilute attention and mean-pooled representations.
Additionally, we compare models trained with 70 vs. 140 per-frame video tokens (
Table
5
, bottom) to see whether training with a smaller vision budget could improve quality when using smaller vision budgets at inference time, for resource-constrained deployment. When evaluated with 70 tokens, training with 70 video tokens improves performance on video tasks, as the model is directly exposed to 70-token frames during training. But this advantage does not hold for image or visual document tasks, which drop in quality. This is likely because a) single-image tasks, which continue to be trained with 280 tokens, are treated as a separate modality and do not benefit from seeing 70-token video frames; and b) coarser video representations discard spatial details that otherwise transfer to stronger general visual representations. The latter is further supported when evaluating with 140 tokens, where training with 70 video tokens degrades performance even more, and across modalities—this makes the 140-token video budget preferable across both evaluation regimes. More gains are likely possible by increasing train-time budgets, but with seemingly diminishing returns and at a significant computational cost.

For MTEB, MAEB, and MIEB(lite), we compare against models under 1B parameters; for MMEB-v2, we include models under 2B parameters, as small models are scarce. Text
The MTEB suite consists of a massive collection of individual, quality-controlled evaluation tasks. Together, the 162 tasks cover 250+ natural languages and 14+ programming languages, 20 domains (e.g. legal, medical, news, programming, web), and 10 task types: bitext mining, classification, clustering, instruction retrieval, multilabel classification, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic text similarity (STS), and summarization.
Despite having fewer text parameters and sharing its representation space with vision and audio, EmbeddingGemma 2 improves over its predecessor on multilingual text (driven by gains in bitext mining and classification). On English, the model sees a modest regression. Only two smaller models surpass it on multilingual text, and one on English, but they are all trained as specialist text models (
Appendix
B

On code (

×
\times

Vision
MMEB-v2 spans 78 tasks across image, video, and visual document modalities, the latter of which includes PDFs, slides, and charts. These include retrieval, classification, question answering, visual grounding, and moment retrieval. MIEB(lite) complements this with linear-probe classification, clustering, multiple choice, compositionality, and visual semantic text similarity. They both implicitly evaluate countless visual skills like object detection, counting, optical character recognition, and temporal reasoning. They also cover various permutations of cross-modal and mixed-modal situations.
EmbeddingGemma 2 is the smallest model on the MMEB-v2 leaderboard (
Table
8
). It excels especially at classification and retrieval, but provides strong scores across the board—its overall score is exceeded only by models around 2B parameters. It also outperforms various recent models including vision-language specialists with more than 8B parameters. On MIEB(lite), only two models beat EmbeddingGemma 2, and they have well over 4B parameters. Compared to top models under 1B parameters (
Table
9
), EmbeddingGemma 2 sets the state of the art on both aggregate metrics by a wide margin (+7.9 Task, +12.2 Type). It also offers remarkable improvements in nearly all task types, notably multilingual visual STS (+22.8) and multilingual retrieval (+12.5). Even at 128 dimensions, the model outperforms every other sub-1B model at full dimensionality.

MAEB includes 30 tasks encompassing five acoustic domains: speech, music, environmental, bioacoustics, and emotion. These are spread across unimodal and cross-modal tasks within retrieval, reranking, clustering, and multiple types of classification. MSEB(Retrieval) contributes a focus on multilingual speech understanding. It evaluates the model’s ability to retrieve a text passage from a spoken query, both in the same language and across languages, with a total of 26 languages and regional locales.
On MAEB, EmbeddingGemma 2 again sets a new frontier for efficiency. Notably, among sub-1B models, it achieves state-of-the-art scores on any-to-any retrieval and audio classification (
Table
10
), as well as on about a third of all individual tasks. It is also state-of-the-art among models of all sizes for classification of audio pairs and a sixth of all individual tasks. Its mean task score is only about 0.2 points away from the best model under 1B parameters, and about 3.5 points away from the highest-scoring model overall. Even its 128-dimensional embeddings beat every other sub-1B model.
On average, the model surpasses various audio-text specialists, but there is an interesting specialization divide between them. While EmbeddingGemma 2 does beat specialists like CLAP at non-speech tasks like clustering vehicle sounds (
VehicleSoundClustering
), these models still outperform in tasks like audio captioning (
ClothoT2ARetrieval
). In speech tasks, EmbeddingGemma 2 sets the state of the art even in tasks with multiple languages (
FleursT2ARetrieval
) and singing (
JamAltLyricA2TRetrieval
). But it sometimes struggles at zero-shot tasks with a paralinguistic focus, despite understanding the acoustics deep down. For example, it struggles tremendously at clustering speakers by gender (
VoxPopuliGenderClustering
: 0.40), but recovers quickly when doing the same task with a linear probe (
IEMOCAPGender
: 66.40). This indicates the model’s speech representations are dominated by semantics, desirably avoiding biases such as speaker demographic while retaining paralinguistic and acoustic attributes for extraction when needed.
The model’s excellence on spoken language is further underscored on MSEB. Even when using ASR and text embeddings, EmbeddingGemma 2 greatly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1, indicating the strength persists throughout modalities (
Table
11
). Encoding audio natively yields another even larger improvement. Instead of suffering from transcription errors from accents, homophones, or artifacts, native audio inputs preserve these signals and let the model take them into account. As a result, even the 256-dimensional embeddings greatly outperform the full-dimension ASR embeddings.

5
Future Work
Our work points to several concrete directions for future research. EmbeddingGemma 2 supports long sequences and variable vision token budgets, but further extending context length, for example via content-aware methods, could enable direct indexing of full-length media, improve performance on long-horizon tasks, and support novel agentic memory systems. Innovations such as encoder-free architectures could enable both quality improvements and further reductions in memory footprint and latency. Changes in training paradigms like the introduction of end-to-end RAG training present another opportunity to further optimize embedding models for downstream use. As interleaved all-to-all multimodal search becomes more prevalent, evaluation frameworks that represent novel use cases will become more important.
At the same time, EmbeddingGemma 2’s utility extends far beyond single-vector retrieval, serving as a general-purpose multimodal encoder. Operating on its final embeddings or unpooled token representations, the model can be adapted into (or may even excel zero-shot as) a general decision model

6
Conclusion
EmbeddingGemma 2 builds on its predecessor with a smaller, stronger backbone and native multimodal capabilities. Our approach introduces improvements like simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with both modality and objective progression. This enables EmbeddingGemma 2 to set a new Pareto frontier across text, vision, and audio benchmarks, often surpassing specialist and general-purpose models several times larger. With native support for weight quantization, embedding truncation, and modular encoder loading, EmbeddingGemma 2 makes high-quality multimodal embeddings practical in resource-constrained and on-device settings. We release EmbeddingGemma 2 checkpoints to the community to accelerate research and development, for both off-the-shelf use and as a foundational multimodal encoder.

article.headline: 744M开源嵌入模型统一文本图像音频视频
article.lede: 谷歌发布744M参数开源多模态嵌入模型EmbeddingGemma 2，将文本、图像、音频、视频及交错组合映射到同一向量
article.problem: 现有多模态嵌入模型分两类：CLIP、SigLIP一类的双塔模型虽然跨模态检索强，但无法原生处理图文音交错输入的模态交互；另一类由多模态大模型改造而来，参数量动辄数十亿，对延迟敏感、高吞吐或需端侧部署的场景代价过高。依赖ASR和图像描述器把音视频转成文本的做法，还会丢失细粒度视觉细节与非语言、环境声音信息。
article.method: 模型以Gemma 4为起点：271M参数的双向注意力Transformer主干，加167M参数的ViT视觉编码器和305M参数的USM式Conformer音频编码器，各模态软token拼接进同一序列后做均值池化与ℓ2归一化。相比Gemma 3n/4，它去掉了PLE专用的查找表，只用主嵌入投影生成逐层输入；训练分三阶段课程，先约300B token纯文本预微调，再约2T token多模态预微调（仅用蒸馏），最后约600B token多模态微调（换成对比损失、spread-out正则和MRL）。
article.results: 在MTEB(Code)上Mean(Task)为78.68，高于前代EmbeddingGemma 1的68.76，并接近榜单领先者2分以内；MTEB(Multilingual, v2)为61.36（前代61.15），但MTEB(English, v2)从69.67退到68.46。多模态侧MMEB-v2 Mean(Task)为59.01，MIEB(lite)为60.17，MAEB为49.87，MSEB(Retrieval)用原生音频达69.54，而前代用ASR仅50.95。经int4 per-channel量化后，在Pixel 11 Pro上的推理峰值内存为纯文本191MB、文本加视觉447MB、全模态567MB。
article.why_it_matters: 它把多模态嵌入压到1B参数以下，并支持按模态选择性加载编码器（纯文本271M、视觉语言439M、音频语言577M）、70至1120的可调视觉token预算、768到128维的MRL截断和量化权重，使端侧与高吞吐检索场景可以实际部署。
article.limitations: 英语文本检索相比前代出现小幅回退，MAEB上与部分更大模型仍有差距（如986M的jina-embeddings-v5-omni-nano为50.14），按说话人性别等副语言零样本任务表现很差（VoxPopuliGenderClustering仅0.40）；此外不少基线分数取自公开榜单而非统一复现，量化与浮点评测所用的harness也不完全一致。
article.figure_caption_zh: EmbeddingGemma 2原生将文本、图像、视频、音频及其组合映射到一个语义对齐的统一向量空间。

figure.caption: EmbeddingGemma 2 natively maps text, images, video, audio, and combinations thereof into a unified, semantically-aligned vector space.

page_papers.title: DTCA: Denoising Token Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Language Models
page_papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance. However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA), a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training. DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

Abstract
Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance. However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose
Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA)
, a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training. DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

Introduction
Diffusion language models (DLMs) have recently attracted increasing attention as an emerging paradigm for language modeling due to their ability to model bidirectional context and perform parallel token refinement
(
Labs et al., 2025
;
Google DeepMind, 2025
;
Song et al., 2025
)
, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation
(
Nie et al., 2025
;
Sahoo et al., 2024
;
Ye et al., 2025a
;
Yu et al., 2025
)
. Recent studies have explored reinforcement learning for DLMs by leveraging the generation process, mainly constructing learning signals from denoising trajectories or intermediate states during training
(
He et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Oba et al., 2026
;
Monsefi et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2025
)
. However, DLMs generate sequences through multiple denoising steps, where tokens are gradually committed and each commitment can affect the refinement of
remaining masked positions
(
Ou et al., 2025
)
. Therefore, RL optimization in DLMs requires finer-grained credit assignment that considers how different tokens affect subsequent refinement.
Figure 1:
Preliminary analysis of POS-level differences in DLM denoising using rollouts
generated from the GSM8K
(
Cobbe et al., 2021
)
training set.
(a) Commitment timing of different POS categories across denoising steps.
(b) Improvement in the prediction confidence of remaining masked
positions after individual token commitment, averaged within each POS category.
POS tags denote NOUN (noun), NUM (numeral), PUNCT (punctuation), PROPN (proper
noun), VERB (verb), ADP (adposition), DET (determiner), and ADJ (adjective).
Achieving finer grained credit assignment requires estimating the contribution
of individual tokens during DLM denoising. Specifically, we measure token
contribution by how much a committed token improves the model’s prediction
confidence on the remaining masked positions. However, directly estimating such
token-level confidence improvements during RL training is challenging because
multiple tokens are committed at the same denoising step and interact through
the shared denoising process, making their individual effects difficult to
isolate. Moreover, the estimated contribution can vary substantially across
different rollout samples. To obtain more reliable estimates, we categorize
tokens by part-of-speech (POS) categories and aggregate their refinement
effects within each category. POS categories provide a natural grouping criterion because they capture
different linguistic functions, with nouns and verbs typically carrying lexical
information while determiners and adpositions mainly providing grammatical
structure
(
de Marneffe et al., 2021
)
.
The denoising behaviors of different POS categories are further analyzed using
rollouts generated from the GSM8K
(
Cobbe et al., 2021
)
dataset. As shown in Figure
1
(a), different POS categories exhibit distinct commitment trajectories across denoising steps. NOUN maintains a relatively high commitment ratio, whereas VERB has a high ratio at the beginning that declines substantially over the denoising process. Other categories, such as ADP, DET, and ADJ, exhibit relatively lower commitment ratios with more stable variations. Figure
1
(b) further shows the confidence gain associated with different POS categories. Clear differences emerge across categories: VERB achieves the largest confidence gain, followed by NOUN and PROPN, whereas categories such as DET and ADP show relatively smaller gains. These observations indicate that POS
categories capture different denoising behaviors and refinement effects, making
them a useful basis for grouping tokens and estimating contribution weights.
Based on these observations, we propose
Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA)
, a token-level credit assignment framework for reinforcement learning in diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions from denoising refinement signals and aggregates them into POS-level contribution weights to obtain more stable and interpretable learning signals. These contribution signals are then used to select informative denoising timesteps and derive token-level learning signals during RL optimization. DTCA further incorporates an entropy-based credit calibration module inspired by OPEFO
(
Xu et al., 2026
)

Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with improvements of up to 9.0 percentage points on MATH500

The main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We analyze different denoising behaviors across POS categories in
diffusion language models and use POS categories to estimate the effect of
token commitments on subsequent refinement.
•
We propose
DTCA
, a token-level credit assignment framework that aggregates denoising refinement signals by POS categories and uses the resulting contribution weights for denoising timestep selection and token credit assignment. DTCA further adapts entropy-based credit calibration from OPEFO
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
to the diffusion language model setting for improved RL optimization.
•
Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DTCA on
mathematical reasoning benchmarks and validate the benefits of its key
components.

5
Experiments
5.1
Experimental Setup
Model and data.
We initialize RL training from LLaDA-8B-Instruct
(
Nie et al., 2025
)
without additional
SFT. Following RLDF
(
He et al., 2026
)
, we use the MATH
(
Hendrycks et al., 2021
)
training split with the same data processing pipeline for RL optimization.
To construct the fixed POS contribution table, DTCA collects offline denoising
rollouts from the training data of MATH and GSM8K and builds a shared POS
contribution table without updating model parameters.
Training.
We train LLaDA-8B-Instruct with reinforcement learning without an intermediate
SFT stage. For each rollout, DTCA selects denoising states with the highest POS-weighted
uncertainty scores until covering 70% of the total score mass, with the number of selected states constrained
between 2 and 32. We perform policy optimization using group-relative
advantages and regularize the policy against a frozen reference model with the
k3 KL estimator
(
Schulman, 2020
)
. Rollouts are generated using block-wise decoding with KV cache, following Fast-dLLM
(
Wu et al., 2026b
)
. Full implementation details and
hyperparameters are provided in Appendix
C
.
Evaluation and baselines.
We evaluate mathematical reasoning performance on MATH500
(
Lightman et al., 2024
)
and GSM8K
(
Cobbe et al., 2021
)
using final-answer accuracy. Following prior
work, we evaluate all models under generation budgets of 128, 256, and 512,
with denoising steps matched to the corresponding maximum generation lengths.
We compare DTCA with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Uniform SFT, LLaDA-1.5, and
representative reinforcement learning methods for diffusion language models,
including d1
(
Zhao et al., 2025
)
, ESPO
(
Ou et al., 2026
)
, TraceRL
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
,
Coupled-GRPO
(
Gong et al., 2026
)
, and RLDF
(
He et al., 2026
)
. Additional details on
training configurations and baseline evaluation settings are provided in
Appendix
C.2
and Appendix
C.4
.
5.2
Main Results
Table
1
compares DTCA with supervised and reinforcement
learning baselines on MATH500 and GSM8K. DTCA consistently improves over
LLaDA-8B-Instruct across both benchmarks and all evaluated generation budgets.
On MATH500, DTCA improves the base model by 9.0, 6.8, and 4.8 percentage points
at budgets of 128, 256, and 512, respectively. On GSM8K, the corresponding
improvements are 5.3, 2.1, and 2.5 percentage points. These results show that
DTCA provides consistent gains under different denoising budgets rather than
relying on a specific inference setting. Compared with supervised optimization
and existing diffusion language model reinforcement learning methods, DTCA
achieves competitive performance across the reported settings, demonstrating
the effectiveness of the proposed token-level credit assignment framework.
The largest improvements on both benchmarks occur at the smallest evaluated
generation budget of 128, while gains remain positive at budgets of 256 and
512. Although the relative improvements become smaller at larger generation
budgets, DTCA consistently improves over the base model, highlighting its
stronger gains under limited denoising computation.

5.3
Ablation Study
Table
1
reports ablation results for different DTCA
components.
DTCA w/o Contribution Credit
replaces the
contribution-based token credits with uniform credits while keeping the same
timestep selection strategy.
DTCA w/o Entropy Calibration
removes the
entropy-based credit calibration module while preserving contribution-based
credit assignment and timestep selection.
Removing either component decreases performance compared with the full DTCA
model across both benchmarks and different generation budgets. At the 256
generation budget, removing Contribution Credit leads to decreases of 3.8 and
2.4 percentage points on MATH500 and GSM8K, respectively, while removing
Entropy Calibration results in smaller drops of 1.4 and 1.4 points. At the 512
generation budget, removing Entropy Calibration causes larger performance
decreases, with drops of 4.2 and 3.5 points on MATH500 and GSM8K. These results
show that both components contribute to the overall performance of DTCA.
5.4
Analysis of Optimization Dynamics
To understand how different DTCA components influence RL optimization, we
analyze training dynamics in terms of reward, gradient norm, and KL divergence.
Figure
3
compares DTCA with variants without
Contribution Credit and Entropy Calibration during training.
Removing Contribution Credit results in similar reward trajectories to DTCA,
but leads to substantially different update behaviors. In particular, the
variant with uniform credit assignment consistently exhibits larger gradient
norms throughout training while achieving comparable reward improvements. This
suggests that contribution-based credit assignment mainly affects the quality
of token-level learning signals, allowing the model to optimize with different
update dynamics rather than simply changing the final reward trend. By
considering token-level contribution differences, DTCA provides a more
structured learning signal than uniform credit assignment.
Removing Entropy Calibration mainly affects the stability of later-stage policy
updates. Although its reward trajectory initially follows a similar trend, the
variant without entropy calibration shows a faster increase in KL divergence
and lower reward in later training stages. This indicates that entropy
calibration helps control policy changes by adjusting learning signals
according to entropy changes, leading to more stable optimization during RL
training.

Analysis of commitment dynamics on MATH500.
DTCA is compared with the base model across three denoising stages. Each cell
shows the difference in (a) token commitment ratio, (b) confidence at
commitment, and (c) entropy at commitment.
5.5
Analysis of Token Commitment Dynamics
To understand whether contribution-based credit assignment changes the denoising
behavior of diffusion language models, we analyze token commitment patterns after
RL training. Token commitment reflects when tokens become fixed during
denoising, while the commitment distribution and prediction states provide
insights into the learned denoising behavior. Figure
4
compares DTCA with the base model on MATH500 across early, middle, and late
denoising stages. Each cell reports the difference between DTCA and the base
model in token commitment ratio, prediction confidence at commitment, and target
entropy at commitment.
DTCA changes the commitment distribution across token categories rather than
uniformly shifting all commitments. For example, DTCA consistently reduces the
commitment ratio of NUM tokens while increasing the commitment ratio of PUNCT
tokens across different denoising stages. These changes suggest that DTCA
learns different commitment patterns across token categories instead of simply
accelerating or delaying all token predictions. Notably, changes in commitment
frequency do not always correspond to changes in commitment states. For
example, VERB shows limited changes in commitment ratio but substantial
increases in confidence and reductions in entropy at commitment. This indicates
that DTCA influences not only which tokens are committed, but also the model
states when commitments occur. The observed changes are consistent with
leveraging denoising refinement signals to improve token-level credit assignment
during reinforcement learning.
5.6
Analysis of Entropy-Based Credit Calibration
We study how entropy calibration changes token credits and prediction entropy
across POS categories. We compare DTCA with a variant that keeps the same
contribution-based credit assignment and timestep selection but removes
entropy calibration. Figure
5
shows the
entropy changes during training. Positive values mean increased entropy, and
negative values mean decreased entropy. Values in parentheses show the
relative change in assigned credit after calibration. We compare these credit
changes with the entropy curves for each category.
In Figure
5
, the two variants show similar
entropy changes early in training and gradually diverge later. For most of
the shown POS categories, DTCA has a lower curve late in training. Each curve
shows changes relative to that run’s early training average. For example,
without calibration, the NUM curve rises above zero after about 200 updates
and stays positive for most of the remaining steps. DTCA stays near or below
zero for most of this period. For SYM, the curve without calibration returns
toward zero late in training, while DTCA remains negative. AUX shows the
opposite pattern. Its curve without calibration drops sharply below zero near
the end, while the DTCA curve stays close to zero. The differences between
the two variants therefore vary across POS categories, rather than following
the same direction for all categories.
Credit changes and entropy changes do not always follow the same direction.
For example, SYM receives more credit but stays below its early entropy
average late in training. AUX receives less credit but ends above its early
average. Credit changes the strength of the existing policy update. Whether
entropy rises or falls also depends on the advantage signal, the current
prediction distribution, and the target token. Compared with
OPEFO
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, DTCA applies entropy flow balancing after assigning
POS-based credits. Within each response, updates in the same entropy-change
set share a scaling factor. This factor and the final normalization preserve
the credit ratios within that set. Thus, entropy flow balancing still leaves
different credits for tokens with different POS contribution weights. The
two runs also see different denoising states and different mixes of target
tokens as training progresses. The curves therefore show overall training
trends, rather than measuring the same tokens immediately before and after a
single policy update.

6
Conclusion
We presented
Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA)
, a framework for
fine-grained token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for
diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions from the
confidence improvement of remaining masked positions after token commitment,
aggregates these signals by POS categories, and uses the resulting contribution
weights for denoising timestep selection and token-level credit assignment.
DTCA further calibrates contribution credits according to entropy changes
induced by policy updates, balancing entropy-increasing and entropy-decreasing
updates. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, DTCA improves the reproduced base model by 6.8
percentage points on MATH500 and 2.1 points on GSM8K under the 256-step
evaluation setting. Training dynamics and component ablations show that
contribution-based credit assignment improves token-level learning signals,
while entropy-based calibration helps maintain more stable policy updates.
These results demonstrate that denoising dynamics provide useful information
for fine-grained credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion
language models.
