Appendix A
Related Work
A.1
Diffusion Language Models
Building on the denoising paradigm of diffusion models
(
Ho et al., 2020
)
, diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising
(
Hoogeboom et al., 2021
;
Dieleman et al., 2022
;
Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023
)
rather than autoregressive next-token prediction
(
Lou et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2022
;
Ye et al., 2024
)
.
Early discrete diffusion language models explore masked generation objectives and iterative refinement for language modeling
(
Austin et al., 2021
;
Sahoo et al., 2024
;
Shi et al., 2024
)
.
LLaDA scales this paradigm to large language models with a masked diffusion objective and demonstrates competitive language generation performance
(
Nie et al., 2025
)
.
Subsequent works further study improved training objectives, generation strategies
(
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Xie et al., 2025
)
, scaling behaviors
(
Ye et al., 2025b
;
Gong et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026b
)
, and data efficiency under limited-data and multi-epoch training settings
(
Prabhudesai et al., 2025
;
Ni et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2025
)
.
When applying reinforcement learning to these models, their iterative generation process requires particular consideration.
Unlike autoregressive models, DLMs maintain multiple intermediate denoising states, where tokens are progressively committed and remaining masked positions are refined.
This generation process introduces new challenges and opportunities for reinforcement learning in diffusion models.
A.2
Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
Reinforcement learning for diffusion language models requires optimization
methods that account for the iterative denoising process
(
Raajesh et al., 2026
;
He et al., 2025
)
. Existing approaches
mainly adapt RL objectives
(
Schulman et al., 2017
;
Shao et al., 2024
;
Zekri and Boulle, 2025
;
Ni et al., 2026
)
or exploit intermediate denoising information
(
Xie et al., 2026
)
to
construct effective learning signals
(
Tang et al., 2026
;
Rojas et al., 2026
;
Zhu et al., 2026
)
. d1 introduces diffu-GRPO
(
Zhao et al., 2025
)
, Coupled-GRPO reduces likelihood
estimation variance through complementary masks
(
Gong et al., 2026
)
, and ESPO
uses evidence lower bound as a proxy for sequence likelihood during RL
optimization
(
Ou et al., 2026
)
. Other methods leverage denoising trajectories
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
and
intermediate states to improve RL training, including TraceRL, RLDF, and
DiSPO
(
Wang et al., 2025b
;
He et al., 2026
;
Oba et al., 2026
)
. These methods demonstrate how diffusion
generation characteristics can be incorporated into RL optimization
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. However,
they mainly focus on optimization objectives
(
Zhong et al., 2026
;
Jiang et al., 2026
)
, likelihood estimation
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
, or
denoising trajectories, while how to assign fine-grained credit to individual
tokens during the denoising process remains underexplored.
A.3
Fine-grained Credit Assignment
Sequence-level rewards in language model reinforcement learning
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
;
Guo et al., 2025
)
provide limited
information about which tokens or reasoning steps contribute to the final
outcome, motivating recent studies on fine-grained credit assignment
(
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Cheng et al., 2026
)
. Existing
approaches improve reward granularity through process supervision
(
Uesato et al., 2022
)
, step-level
feedback, and token-level reward redistribution
(
Tan et al., 2026
)
or importance estimation
(
Lightman et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2025
;
Kazemnejad et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
.
However, these methods are mainly developed for autoregressive language models,
where tokens are generated sequentially. For diffusion language models,
DACA-GRPO provides an initial exploration of token-level credit assignment by
weighting committed tokens according to denoising progress and changes in the
predicted probabilities of remaining masked positions
(
Monsefi et al., 2026
)
.
Different from DACA-GRPO, DTCA estimates token contributions from confidence
improvements after token commitment, aggregates these signals according to POS
categories, and uses the resulting contribution structure for denoising
timestep selection and token-level credit assignment.

Appendix C
Experimental Setup and Implementation Details
C.1
Base Models and Datasets
The policy and frozen reference model both start from LLaDA-8B-Instruct,
without an intermediate SFT stage. RL training uses the MATH training set
processed for RLDF. Offline POS contribution
estimates are constructed from denoising rollouts over the MATH and GSM8K
training splits without parameter updates to build a shared fixed POS
contribution table. We evaluate on MATH500 and the GSM8K test split; neither
evaluation split is used for RL training or POS table construction.
C.2
Training Configuration
We reproduce the compared methods under a unified experimental setup wherever
applicable. RL methods start from LLaDA-8B-Instruct and use the same
RLDF-processed MATH training split and mathematical correctness reward. All
methods are evaluated using the common protocol in
Appendix
C.4
. Each method retains its own objective
and method-specific settings: we follow its original paper first, and use its
released open-source code for details not specified in the paper.
For DTCA and the locally reproduced RLDF baseline, we use full-parameter
bfloat16 training with AdamW, a constant learning rate of
10
−
6
10^{-6}
, and zero
weight decay. Each prompt produces four responses, whose rewards are
standardized within the group to form response advantages. Both methods use the same low-probability threshold of 0.2 for training-target
filtering, token-level loss normalization, and a frozen-reference

penalty with coefficient
0.01
0.01
.
Their training rollouts use a maximum response length of 256 tokens and 256
denoising steps. Decoding uses a block size of 32 and a dynamic confidence
threshold of

from the

We evaluate each checkpoint at maximum response lengths of 128, 256, and

Appendix E
Limitations
While DTCA provides an effective approach for fine-grained credit assignment in
diffusion language model reinforcement learning, several aspects remain open
for future exploration. DTCA uses POS categories to aggregate token-level
confidence improvements and obtain stable contribution estimates. This design
relies on the quality of POS alignment and annotation, and more accurate
token-level labeling strategies may further improve the estimation process.
Moreover, DTCA currently defines token contribution based on the confidence
improvement of remaining masked positions after token commitment. Developing
more principled theoretical formulations for contribution estimation in
diffusion language models remains an interesting direction. Finally, our
experiments focus on mathematical reasoning with LLaDA-8B-Instruct. Applying
DTCA to other tasks, such as code generation, may require adapting the token
grouping strategy to different token distributions and generation patterns.
Further evaluation on diverse diffusion language model architectures is also
needed to understand the general applicability of DTCA.

article.headline: 扩散语言模型RL的token级信用分配
article.lede: 用去噪过程中掩码位置置信度的提升来估计token贡献，按词性分组后在RL中做时间步选择与token级信用分配。
article.problem: 扩散语言模型通过多步迭代去噪生成文本，token逐步被提交，每次提交都会影响剩余掩码位置的细化。现有的RL方法主要依赖序列级结果奖励，难以判断哪些token的提交真正帮助了后续去噪，因此信用分配过于粗糙。作者先用GSM8K rollout做了初步分析，发现不同词性类别在提交时机和对剩余位置置信度的提升上存在明显差异。
article.method: DTCA用「提交某个token后，剩余掩码位置的最大预测概率之和提升了多少」来估计该token的细化贡献，并在RL训练前用离线去噪rollout逐token额外前向计算这些量，再按词性（POS）类别取平均，归一化成[0.8, 1.2]范围内的类别权重。训练时，这些权重一方面用于给每个去噪时间步打分（分数为各类别权重与(1-p)乘积之和），按累计分数覆盖70%、步数限制在2到32的方式选出信息量高的时间步；另一方面在每个时间步内对token信用做归一化加权，使各时间步平均信用保持为1。此外还借用OPEFO的一阶熵变估计，在扩散设定下按token级熵增或熵减对学习信号做缩放，并恢复每个响应的总信用。
article.results: 在LLaDA-8B-Instruct上，DTCA在MATH500的128/256/512生成预算下分别比基座模型提升9.0、6.8、4.8个百分点（39.8/43.2/44.0 对 30.8/36.4/39.2），在GSM8K上分别提升5.3、2.1、2.5个百分点（80.6/85.3/85.4 对 75.3/83.2/82.9）。消融显示，在256预算下去掉「贡献信用」会使MATH500和GSM8K分别下降3.8和2.4个百分点，去掉「熵校准」各下降1.4个百分点；在512预算下去掉熵校准则分别下降4.2和3.5个百分点。训练动态方面，401–500步区间DTCA平均奖励0.537、策略熵2.00 nats、平均KL 0.36，而RLDF为0.482、1.78 nats、0.89。
article.why_it_matters: 它把扩散语言模型RL中的信用分配从序列级推进到去噪步与token级，并且贡献信号来自去噪动力学本身而非额外的奖励模型，思路可以迁移到其他掩码扩散模型的RL后训练。
article.limitations: 贡献估计依赖spaCy的POS标注与词跨度对齐质量，且「置信度提升」这一贡献定义本身缺少更严格的理论刻画；POS权重在训练前离线固定，不随策略更新而调整。实验只覆盖LLaDA-8B-Instruct上的数学推理，代码生成等其他任务、以及其他扩散架构上的适用性尚未验证，熵变相关分析也只是基于训练信号的一阶估计而非参数更新后的实测。

page_papers.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
page_papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.

Abstract
Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
Project page:
https://sinnnj.github.io/qcp
1
Introduction
Robot foundation models have shown strong generalization across tasks, environments, and objects
(
Black et al., 2025
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
.
These policies are usually trained with behavior cloning (BC) on successful demonstrations, which treats every successful trajectory as equally desirable regardless of how the task was executed.
As a result, the learned policy reproduces the mixture of execution behaviors in the data, whether fast or slow, smooth or jerky, and offers no way to steer toward the behavior a deployment actually requires.
In practice, however, the desired behavior of a robot is not defined by task success alone
(
Wang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Mao et al., 2026
)
and different tasks call for different
quality attributes
.
For example, a robot deployed on a conveyor line should prioritize execution speed, whereas a robot carrying wine glasses on a tray must prioritize transport stability.
To address this, prior work has proposed quality-controllable policies whose execution behavior can be adjusted along a chosen quality axis at inference time
(
Zhan et al., 2020
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Petitbois et al., 2026
)
.
However, such policies are trained on static demonstration datasets, which typically cover only a bounded quality range and lack the high-performance regimes needed in deployment (e.g., maximum speed or ideal smoothness).
Our goal is therefore not only to learn a quality-controllable policy, but also to continuously expand its controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations through online data collection and policy updates.
Figure 1:
Overview of QCP and iterative hindsight relabeling.
Left:
QCP controls execution quality at inference time through conditioning on quantized quality tokens.
Right:
Iterative hindsight relabeling shifts the quality distribution of successful rollouts toward higher quality, expanding the controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations.
In this paper, we introduce
Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP)
, which addresses this limitation of BC by making execution quality an explicit conditioning input (Figure
1
).
For each demonstration, we measure the target quality attributes with rule-based score functions and quantize the scores into discrete quality labels.
The policy is then trained to generate actions conditioned on both the observation history and these labels.
Rather than averaging over execution behaviors, QCP learns task completion from all successful trajectories while distinguishing how each one was executed.
At inference time, the user specifies a target label to steer execution behavior, for example, requesting the highest speed label for conveyor operations.
To extend the controllable quality range beyond the demonstrations, we pair QCP with
iterative hindsight relabeling
.
At each iteration, we collect rollouts conditioned on the highest quality label, keep the successful ones, relabel them by the quality they actually achieved, and add them to the dataset.
We then recompute the quality labels of all trajectories and retrain the policy.
As higher-quality rollouts accumulate, the highest label comes to represent progressively higher quality, allowing the policy to reach operating regimes absent from the initial demonstrations.
Because quality is measured by rule-based score functions, this loop requires no manual quality annotation.
Experiments on Robomimic
(
Mandlekar et al., 2022
)
and RoboEval
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
show that QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling improves both target quality and task success across iterations, outperforming quality-filtered BC and RL baselines
(
Mao et al., 2024
;
Petitbois et al., 2026
;
Wagenmaker et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2026
)
.
Iterative relabeling pushes the quality distribution well beyond the range of the initial demonstrations, reaching an IQR-normalized Wasserstein distance above 1.5.
Beyond single-attribute control, QCP controls multiple attributes jointly, improving six quality attributes simultaneously in RoboEval.
Finally, in real-world experiments, controlling execution speed substantially increases throughput in conveyor operations, and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses on a tray.
2
Related Work
Policy learning with quality control.
Prior work studies how to learn different ways of executing a task, representing behavioral styles through learned trajectory representations or explicit labels
(
Petitbois et al., 2025
;
Zhan et al., 2020
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Learning a requested style, however, can conflict with task performance. SORL addresses this tension by combining trajectory clustering with task advantage weighting
(
Mao et al., 2024
)
, while SCIQL combines task and style advantages to account for both task performance and style alignment
(
Petitbois et al., 2026
)
. QCP combines quantized quality conditioning with iterative hindsight relabeling. Our experiments show simultaneous gains in execution quality and task success, demonstrating that this trade-off can be overcome.
Online improvement of behavioral quality.
Freeform Preference Learning (FPL) learns a reward model for the desired quality axes from human comparisons of robot trajectories and trains policies conditioned on the predicted rewards
(
Torne et al., 2026
)
. This supports online improvement through repeated rollout collection and policy training, but requires additional human comparisons at each round. In text generation, Quark repeatedly samples under the highest reward token, relabels accumulated samples by reward quantiles, and retrains the language model conditioned on the assigned labels
(
Lu et al., 2022
)
. QCP applies a similar loop to robot execution quality, using automatically computed quality labels and accumulated successful trajectories to extend the controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations without additional human annotation.
3
Method
In real-world deployment, users often care about quality metrics beyond binary task success, such as execution speed or motion smoothness.
To account for these, we propose Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), which adjusts its execution behavior along user-specified quality axes by conditioning on quantized quality levels (Section
3.1
).
Because demonstration data typically covers only a limited range of quality, we extend QCP’s controllable quality range through iterative hindsight relabeling, alternating between collecting online rollouts, relabeling trajectories by their achieved quality, and updating the policy (Section
3.2
).

4.5
Quality control for real robot tasks
We evaluate whether controlling execution quality leads to practical gains in real-world robot tasks. We consider two tasks with distinct quality requirements: execution speed for the conveyor task, measured by end-effector speed, and transport stability for the wine-glass task, measured by the tray’s tilt angle from horizontal (Appendix
A
).
Serving wine.
The robot must carry a tray holding wine glasses from one table to another without dropping any glass. This task is challenging even for human operators: only 50 of 382 teleoperated attempts (13.1%) succeeded during data collection, as keeping the tray level while moving proved difficult. Conditioning QCP on the highest stability bin reduces the mean tilt angle from 0.0660 rad for BC to 0.0482 rad, a 27.0% reduction, while the success rate improves from 30.7% to 42.0% over iterations (Figure
7
a). In contrast,
BC
filter
{}_{\text{filter}}
improves tilt angle and success rate through iteration 1 but degrades at iteration 2, suggesting that retaining lower quality data provides broader coverage needed to sustain task success. Notably, even the initial QCP policy, trained only on demonstrations, already achieves a higher success rate than BC. We attribute this to the quality label, which separates stable from unstable executions in the demonstrations so that the policy does not average over them. The final policy succeeds far more often than teleoperation did during data collection.
Conveyor belt work.
Twenty cans are placed on a conveyor belt moving at a fixed speed, one every three seconds, and throughput is defined as the number of cans successfully grasped per minute. Achieving high throughput under this fixed schedule requires both fast execution and a high success rate. Relative to BC, QCP increases mean end-effector speed from 188.6 to 257.6 mm/s and throughput from 8.2 to 13.0 cans per minute, improvements of 36.6% and 59.3% (Figure
7
b). In contrast,
BC
filter
{}_{\text{filter}}
falls behind QCP in end-effector speed after iteration 0 (217.7 mm/s at iteration 2), and its throughput drops from 8.3 to 6.3 cans per minute, below BC, consistent with the loss of coverage observed in wine serving. The initial QCP policy again already exceeds the throughput of BC, while the final QCP policy surpasses the 173.5 mm/s of human teleoperation, where high-speed control is challenging.

5.1
Effect of quality conditioning on rollout distributions
We examine whether the distribution shift in Figure
4
comes from the iterative hindsight relabeling loop or from quality conditioning alone, since a conditioned policy might reach rare behaviors simply by sampling more. To separate the two, we spend the same rollout budget in two ways under the best quality bin
q
⋆

3
q^{\star}=3
: 1,800 rollouts from the QCP policy frozen at iteration 0, or 300 rollouts at each of iterations 0 to 5 with retraining in between (Figure
9
). The fixed policy reproduces its iteration-0 distribution regardless of sample count, and none of its successful rollouts reaches the median smoothness of the final iteration. The improvement thus comes from policy updates on the relabeled data, which move the best bin to a quality level the previous policy could not produce.
5.2
Continuous quality scores versus quantized quality labels
We examine why QCP uses quantized quality labels rather than continuous scores. With four quantile bins, roughly the best quarter of the training trajectories share the best label, giving the policy multiple examples of the requested behavior. Learning from multiple trajectories with the same label can provide a more stable training signal than conditioning on a score represented by only a few examples. The importance of training support is also evident in return conditioning, where Decision Transformer
(
Chen et al., 2021
)
and RvS
(
Emmons et al., 2022
)
can be unreliable for requests outside the training distribution
(
Brandfonbrener et al., 2022
)
. On Square, quantized quality labels execute faster than a fixed continuous target at every iteration, and four bins also reach higher task success from iteration 1 onward; increasing the number of bins beyond four buys a small gain in speed at a growing cost in task success (Figure
9
). These results support simple quantization as an effective representation for quality control. Experimental details are provided in Appendix
F
.
6
Conclusion
We presented QCP, a robot policy that uses quantized quality labels to control individual execution attributes and their combinations at inference time. Iterative hindsight relabeling extends the controllable quality range beyond the initial demonstrations through online rollout collection and policy updates, without additional human annotation. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval show that QCP can improve execution quality and task success while retaining quality control across iterations. Real robot experiments further demonstrate that QCP can be directed to pursue the execution quality desired for a given task.

\textsc{BC}_{\text{filter}}
additionally ranks the successful trajectories of the accumulated set (demonstrations included) by the target score at every iteration and keeps the best 10%. At every iteration the filter is applied again to the whole accumulated set, not to the previously filtered set, so the filtered training set grows with the accumulated data rather than shrinking over iterations; the setting does not force the dataset to become smaller. On Robomimic at least 20 trajectories are kept, and on RoboEval the filter is implemented as a sampling weight of 0 or 1 without a floor. In the real robot experiments the filter keeps the best 20%, because the initial datasets are small (50 episodes for wine serving) and a 10% filter would leave too few trajectories to train on.

Appendix F
Analysis Experiment Details
Rollout collection comparison (Section
5.1
).
The comparison uses the Square smoothness attribute with 30k training steps per iteration, an 800-step episode limit, and three seeds. The frozen variant draws 1,800 rollouts per seed from the checkpoint trained at iteration 0, conditioned on the best bin
q
⋆
=
3
q^{\star}=3
, with the dataset normalization that checkpoint was trained under, and without any further training. The iterative variant is the loop itself, which draws 300 rollouts per seed at each of iterations 0 to 5 under the same best-bin request, so both variants spend 1,800 rollouts per seed. The purpose of this comparison is to separate the effect of the quality-conditioned architecture from the effect of the iterative hindsight relabeling loop. The frozen variant has the architecture but no further loop iterations, so any additional shift of the iterative variant comes from the loop rather than from conditioning or sampling alone. Statistics are computed over successful rollouts pooled across seeds; per-seed medians agree with the pooled values to within 0.002. The frozen policy has a success rate of 54.5% and a median action jerk of 0.0335 (interquartile range 0.028 to 0.043) over 2,943 successful rollouts, against 57.0% and 0.0324 at iteration 0 of the loop. By iteration 5 the loop reaches 73.9% and a median of 0.0098 (interquartile range 0.0088 to 0.0109). The smoothest frozen rollout has a jerk of 0.0171, above the 75th percentile of the iteration-5 distribution. The later iterations therefore produce behavior that the iteration-0 policy does not generate at all, not merely behavior that it generates rarely: the quality-conditioned architecture alone does not reach this range, and the additional shift comes from the iterative hindsight relabeling loop.
Quality representation (Section
5.2
).
This experiment examines how the quality condition should be represented: as a quantized label, and if so with how many bins, or as a continuous score. Figure
9
compares six variants on the Square speed attribute, all run with the same loop (30k training steps and 300 rollouts per iteration, seven policies, three seeds). Four variants use quantized labels with
B
=
4
B=4
, 8, 16, or 32 equal-frequency bins, recomputed at every iteration, and always request the best bin; with more bins the requested bin covers a smaller share (
1
/
B
1/B
) of the training data. Two variants use a continuous score instead of a label: the score is normalized so that the best and worst initial demonstrations map to 0 and 1, this normalization is fixed for the whole loop, and the requested value is set once to the 25th or the 12.5th percentile of the initial demonstrations. Curves are means over seeds and bands are one standard deviation. At iteration 6, the four-, eight-, sixteen-, and thirty-two-bin variants reach 70.3%, 63.2%, 57.7%, and 28.1% success with 139, 120, 116, and 112 steps; the two continuous variants reach 55.0% and 67.0% success with 246 and 209 steps.
More bins make executions slightly faster but cost success, sharply so beyond sixteen bins, and neither continuous target matches the bins in speed at any iteration; in success, four bins exceed both continuous targets from iteration 1 onward. Because the continuous variants also use a different way of selecting the requested value, this experiment supports quartile labels with per-iteration recomputation as a reliable default rather than ruling out continuous conditioning in general.
Appendix G
Quality Labels for Shorter Segments
This experiment tests whether a quality label assigned to shorter segments of a trajectory is a better training signal than one label for the complete trajectory. We compare three labeling options.
Trajectory
is QCP as used in the main experiments: one label per trajectory.
Segment
assigns a label to every decision step from the score measured in a window of
±
8
\pm 8
steps around it.
Hybrid
conditions on both the trajectory label and the segment label through two embeddings. A segment score depends strongly on the stage of the task (for example, approaching versus inserting), so for the segment labels the quartile boundaries are computed separately within each of ten intervals of normalized trajectory time, and the best quartile is requested at every step. All options run the same loop otherwise.
Figure
10
shows the comparison on the end-effector speed attribute for Square and Transport, with 10% filtered BC as a reference, over ten iterations with 100k training steps and 300 rollouts per iteration and one seed. At iteration 9 on Square, the trajectory label reaches 84.3% success at 6.08 mm per step, the segment label 48.0% at 4.80, and the hybrid 71.0% at 5.07; on Transport, the trajectory label reaches 13.3% success against 3.7% and 4.0% for the segment and hybrid labels, at similar speeds (5.2 to 5.7 mm per step). The trajectory label therefore gives the largest gains in both success and speed on Square and the highest success on Transport. A segment label provides a more local signal, but the signal reflects the stage of the task as much as the quality of execution even after the stage-wise normalization, and the policy can improve a local score without making progress toward completion. These results support labeling complete trajectories; using finer quality signals may require methods that separate quality from task progress, which we leave to future work.

article.headline: 机器人策略可用质量标签调节执行质量
article.lede: 研究者提出 QCP：把执行速度、平滑度等质量分数量化为标签作为条件输入，并用迭代事后重标注把可控范围推出示教数据之外。
article.problem: 机器人策略通常只以任务是否成功作为训练信号，行为克隆会把示教中快慢、平滑或抖动的执行方式平均在一起，部署时无法按需调节。已有质量可控策略受限于静态示教数据，覆盖的质量范围有限，缺少最高速度、理想平滑度这类部署真正需要的高性能区间。
article.method: QCP 用规则化分数函数测量每条成功轨迹的质量属性，按经验分位数将其量化为 B 个等频标签，训练以观测历史和标签为条件的流匹配策略；推理时用户指定标签即可调节执行行为。为突破示教范围，作者提出迭代事后重标注：每轮在最高标签下收集 rollout，保留成功样本，按实际测得质量重新标注并与原示教一起重新分箱，再从头训练策略。
article.results: 在 Robomimic Square 上，仅用示教训练的初始策略已能响应标签：请求最高 bin 时平均 193.7 步完成任务，请求最低 bin 时为 308.1 步。迭代 5 轮后，Square+Speed 的成功率达 82.2%、平均 120.3 步。作者用 IQR 归一化的 Wasserstein-1 距离衡量分布偏移，平滑度和关节路径长度均超过 1.5，说明 rollout 质量分布已超出初始示教范围。真实机器人上，传送带任务把末端速度从 188.6 mm/s 提到 257.6 mm/s（+36.6%），吞吐从 8.2 提到 13.0 罐/分钟（+59.3%）；端酒任务把托盘倾斜角从 0.0660 rad 降到 0.0482 rad（−27.0%），成功率从 30.7% 升到 42.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「怎样执行」变成推理时可调的输入，并证明在线收集加自动重标注能在无需人工质量标注的情况下持续抬高可控质量上限，对传送带、端酒这类对速度或稳定性有硬性要求的部署有直接意义。
article.limitations: 质量轴与分数函数仍需人工设计，每个任务都要单独训练并每轮从头重训；真实实验仅两个任务、初始数据很小（端酒只有 50 条成功示教），结论的统计支撑有限。此外分箱数增加会明显牺牲成功率（32 个 bin 时成功率降至 28.1%），作者也承认连续分数条件化的对比因请求值选取方式不同，尚不能排除连续条件化本身。
article.figure_caption_zh: QCP 概览：左为推理时以量化质量标签为条件控制执行质量，右为迭代事后重标注把成功 rollout 的质量分布推向更高，从而扩展可控范围。

figure.caption: {Overview of QCP and iterative hindsight relabeling.} {Left:} QCP controls execution quality at inference time through conditioning on quantized quality tokens. {Right:} Iterative hindsight relabeling shifts the quality distribution of successful rollouts toward higher quality, expanding the controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations.

Abstract
The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g.,
FlashInfer
).
We introduce
Evolving Agent Teams
, a multi-agent framework that
escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses
each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with
accumulated experience.
Under a matched token budget,
Evolving Agent Teams
consistently
outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget,
Evolving Agent Teams

1.2
×

Introduction
The rapid progress of coding agents on software engineering tasks
[
15
,
42
,
38
]
has driven interest in applying them to open-ended discovery tasks such as GPU kernel optimization. Here, the goal is not just to produce a correct
kernel but to search a large, hardware-dependent design space for high performance. Expert-written kernels such as
FlashInfer
[
46
]
and
FlashAttention
[
31
]
navigate this space across two levels: low-level primitive use (e.g., WGMMA tensor cores, swizzled shared-memory layouts) and high-level architectural design (e.g., dispatch strategies, warp specialization, dataflow). While low-level primitive use can substantially improve performance within a chosen design, high-level architectural choices often determine which hardware bottlenecks remain and thus largely shape the attainable performance ceiling.
Unfortunately, even strong coding agents struggle to write challenging GPU kernels. They often make rapid initial progress, but then converge to local optima far below expert-written baselines. A common failure mode is that agents select design directions that are initially easier to implement but architecturally limited, spend most of their budget tuning within those directions, and fail to revisit harder alternatives that require substantial debugging or architectural rethinking.
For example, when writing the MLA decode kernel used in DeepSeek-V3 inference
[

These designs plateaued far below expert-written baselines: Codex 5.5 xHigh reaches only 28% of expert performance despite a $1K budget and multiple days of effort. The process moves through distinct phases, from establishing correctness to debugging hardware primitives, profiling bottlenecks, and redesigning the kernel architecture. Each phase requires different expertise, tools, and coordination patterns, causing fixed agent organizations to become mismatched to the current stage.
We introduce
Evolving Agent Teams
, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima by evolving the agent team’s organization alongside the optimization process. This evolution is driven by a central supervisor agent, grounded in a persistent file system with accumulated experience. Concretely, the supervisor monitors team progress, reflects on the agent behavior, diagnoses the cause of plateau (e.g., a knowledge gap or an exhausted search), and adapts the team accordingly: spawning specialists for high-effort tasks, introducing profiling roles to get more insights, or running parallel roles for different directions (Section
3.2
). The file system contains a learning document of empirical observations, per-team artifacts, and an evolution history.
On the MLA decode kernel,
Evolving Agent Teams
explores over 100 team configurations. The supervisor repeatedly reconfigures the team around the current failure mode, which improves token efficiency and enables successive architectural advances, including performant WGMMA-based matrix multiplication, a PV accumulation strategy, and L2 prefetching. Together, these improvements allow

to substantially outperform prior single-agent and static-team approaches (Figure

5
Conclusion
Strong coding agents make rapid initial progress on GPU kernel optimization but converge to local optima well below expert-written baselines.
Evolving Agent Teams
escapes these local optima by evolving the team’s organization alongside the search: a central supervisor diagnoses each plateau and restructures the team’s roles, grounded in a persistent file system. Across four CUDA kernel optimization tasks on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, it consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines under a matched token budget, and with additional budget it surpasses the production
FlashInfer
MLA decode kernel at
1.21
×
1.21\times
mean speedup across 47 workloads. It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs, MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon, and robot manipulation.
Limitations.
We run each main setting twice and each setting in Section
4.7
once, which limits statistical comparisons; a cost-vs-performance Pareto analysis and a controlled study of noisier domains remain future work.

Appendix B
Case Study: Why the Fixed Four-Role Baseline Starts Slowly
Figure
6
shows the fixed four-role baseline (Planner, Hardware Researcher, Implementer, and Profiler; all Claude Opus 4.7, coordinating through a shared filesystem and a SendMessage primitive) reaching its first correctness-passing commit substantially later than the single agent on MLA decode.
Most of this delay is traceable to a single class of bug: a low-level SMEM-layout mismatch in which WGMMA on SM90 requires
8
×
64
8\times 64
atom-tiled shared memory, but the Implementer wrote row-major tiles, silently corrupting the QK output.
The information needed to identify the bug is present in the team but partitioned across agents: the Hardware Researcher holds the layout requirement, the Implementer holds the actual SMEM declaration, and both agree on the descriptor numerics, leading them to localize the bug elsewhere.
The team iterates through incorrect hypotheses without any agent reading the Implementer’s source to inspect the layout, despite all having Read access.
A single agent holding both specification and code in its context would identify the discrepancy on direct inspection.
The failure is structural rather than capability-driven.
Each role’s charter implicitly scopes its outputs (the Hardware Researcher operates as a recipe expert, not an auditor); spawn prompts specify reactive behavior, locking roles into question-and-answer loops that preclude proactive code inspection; and the SendMessage primitive carries prose, encouraging abstract agreement (“
LBO=16
, confirm?”) over byte-level cross-checking.
Fixed-role multi-agent systems can therefore stall on debugging tasks that cross role boundaries.
Evolving Agent Teams
addresses this class of failure: the supervisor diagnoses the stall as a
knowledge gap
and introduces a Knowledge Integrator (Section
3.3
) that mandates cross-agent artifact reads.

article.headline: 智能体团队边优化边重组，反超生产级内核
article.lede: 让监督智能体在停滞时重组角色与协作，MLA 解码内核以 1.21× 平均超越 FlashInfer。
article.problem: 在 GPU 内核优化这类开放式问题上，代码智能体往往开局进展很快，随后陷入局部最优：为了好实现而选架构受限的设计路线，把预算耗在局部调参上，不再回头啃需要大量调试的难方案。论文举的例子是 DeepSeek-V3 的 MLA 解码内核，单智能体反复失败后放弃 WGMMA 路线，退回到更简单但效率更低的 WMMA 实现；固定角色的多智能体团队同样受困，因为优化过程会经历正确性、硬件原语调试、瓶颈剖析、架构重设计等性质不同的阶段，静态组织很快与当前阶段错配。
article.method: 作者提出 Evolving Agent Teams，分两层循环：团队执行层由若干带 shell、可读写文件、能调用编译器和 profiler 的 Claude Code 智能体按当前配置干活；团队进化层由一个监督智能体在团队跑完或定时触发时，检查进展、反思失败模式（如滑向简单路径、跨团队知识丢失、卡在调试、过度微优化），并重新设计角色、协作协议和知识管理三要素。两层之间用一个持久文件系统连接，其中包含累积经验的学习文档、每个团队的产物以及监督者的进化历史，使每次重组都能继承此前的成功与失败记录。
article.results: 在 MLA 分页解码上，预算对齐时系统达到 0.74×（相对生产 FlashInfer），Claude Code 为 0.51×、K-Search 为 0.61×；追加预算后达到 1.21× 平均加速，47 个生产负载中 36 个胜出，其余 11 个为 0.86–0.99×。消融显示固定四角色团队为 0.31×、Codex（GPT-5.5 xhigh）为 0.28×，作者据此把 0.31×→0.74× 的差距归因于团队进化本身。其他任务上，GDN prefill 从 2.2× 提升到 4.06×（21 个团队版本），GEMM+AllReduce 达到 1.56×（ThunderKittens 为 1.54×），Flash-KMeans 的 CUDA 重写默认负载为 1.71×；在 KDA prefill 上，AMD MI350X 比 vLLM 手写 HIP 内核快 3.01×，B200 比 FlashKDA 快 3.44×；Apple M4 Pro 上的 MoE offload 解码为 30.3 tokens/s（单智能体方案 28.2，起点 26.7）；RoboDojo 42 个任务在留出种子上得分 62.1，高于榜单最佳的 55.3。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「搜索过程本身」当作优化对象，而不是只优化候选程序，为长周期、阶段性质会变化的开放式工程任务提供了一个可复用的多智能体元优化范式。
article.limitations: 论文自述每个主实验设置只跑两次、第 4.7 节的额外设置各只跑一次，统计结论有限，成本-性能 Pareto 分析和更嘈杂领域的受控研究都留作未来工作；此外 MLA 上仍有一个负载的最佳内核不及 Claude Code，且部分结论依赖作者自建的评测与按公开定价折算的成本口径。
article.figure_caption_zh: Evolving Agent Teams 框架：团队执行层通过工具调用与执行反馈让编码智能体推进任务，团队进化层充当元优化器，分析此前的成败模式并针对当前发现阶段调整团队构成、角色分工、协作协议与知识管理。

figure.caption: The {Evolving Agent Teams} framework. Team execution runs coding agents on the task through tool use and execution feedback. Team evolution acts as a meta-optimizer: it analyzes the past success and failure patterns, and adapts the team composition, role specialization, coordination protocol, and knowledge management for the current stage of discovery.

ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
Chaehyun Kim
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Affiliation:
KAIST
Chi-Pin Huang
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Jisoo Kim
Affiliation:
KAIST
Min-Hung Chen, 
Yu-Chiang Frank Wang
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Seungryong Kim
Affiliation:
KAIST
Fu-En Yang
Corresponding author:
X
Affiliation:
NVIDIA
Abstract
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce
ThinkWorld
, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
Links:
Project Page
Figure 1
:
We introduce
ThinkWorld
, a vision-language-action framework that learns transferable Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) reasoning from diverse human and robot experiences. CoD captures action-induced dynamics across embodiments and is reinforced through future imagination, enabling robust generalization in the real world and skill composition guided by human videos.
\abscontent
1
Introduction
Building general-purpose action models that transfer across tasks, objects, environments, and embodiments is a central goal of robot learning. Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs)
(
Brohan et al., 2023
;
O’Neill et al., 2024
;
Team et al., 2024
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2024a
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
)
have made substantial progress by transferring pretrained vision-language knowledge and scaling across heterogeneous robot demonstrations. Nevertheless, their policy learning and behavioral coverage remain largely tied to action-labeled robot trajectories, whose collection requires physical platforms, embodiment-specific interfaces, and substantial human effort. Human videos offer a complementary source of experience with far greater behavioral and environmental diversity, but do not provide directly executable robot actions.
Existing approaches seek to extract actionable supervision from human videos along two main directions. Latent action models
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Bu et al., 2025
;
Dai et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2026a
)
infer transition variables from pairs or sequences of frames and use them for representation or policy learning. While naturally scalable to action-unlabeled videos, these inferred variables are underconstrained and may capture appearance changes or camera motion rather than controllable behavior. In contrast, fully supervised approaches recover hand poses, object interactions, or retargeted trajectories to provide explicit motion supervision
(
Kareer et al., 2025
;
Zheng et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026c
)
. Such supervision provides direct physical grounding, but relies on accurate pose estimation and human-to-robot correspondence. Human-video learning therefore yields a trade-off between stronger action grounding from explicit supervision and broader behavioral coverage from unlabeled videos.
Future observations provide a natural supervisory signal to bridge this gap as every video records the consequences that follow a behavior, regardless of embodiment. Predictive world models
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Assran et al., 2025
)
and foresight-based VLAs
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2026a
;
Cai et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026c
)
exploit this signal by forecasting future pixels, visual features, or trajectories, providing a direct account of
what changes
in the world. However, inferring the intermediate dynamics that result in these changes remains challenging, particularly from large-scale human videos without action annotations. Recent reasoning-augmented VLAs offer a useful perspective by introducing intermediate tokens, such as textual plans
(
Zawalski et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2026b
)
, visual guidance
(
Lee et al., 2025
;
Fang et al., 2026
)
, continuous latents
(
Huang et al., 2026a
)
, or coarse action trajectories
(
Zhong et al., 2026
)
, to structure action generation. This raises a natural question of whether such intermediate representations can instead be grounded in the dynamics they induce in the world, providing a shared action interface across embodiments.
Motivated by this perspective, we introduce
ThinkWorld
, a VLA learning framework that formulates action thoughts as Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) and reinforces them through world imagination. CoD represents an action as a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures how the world evolves over time, providing a common reasoning interface across human and robot behaviors. We first initialize this space with action-labeled demonstrations, grounding CoD in physically meaningful behavior. ThinkWorld then predicts the future world representation induced by each CoD and compares it with the future observation, using their alignment to reinforce action reasoning. As a result, videos even without motion annotations provide a learning signal, allowing large-scale human videos and robot trajectories to jointly refine the same CoD space. This training objective propagates through the shared VLM, enriching the representations for action prediction with knowledge of how motion transforms the world. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, we demonstrate that ThinkWorld enables human-to-robot skill composition and generalization to unseen scenarios.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce
ThinkWorld
, a VLA learning framework that couples a common VLM-native action-reasoning interface for both human and robot with internal world imagination.
•
We propose consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, which rewards CoD according to its consistency with observed future consequences and thereby enables action reasoning to improve from videos without action labels.
•
We show that ThinkWorld benefits from scaling action-unlabeled human video and enables human-to-robot skill transfer, allowing robots to execute complete tasks demonstrated in human videos while receiving robot supervision only for the constituent atomic skills.
2
Related Works
Generalist Robot Policies.
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models
(
Kim et al., 2024
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Black et al., 2024a
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Team et al., 2025
)
build upon advances in vision-language models (VLMs)
(
Bai et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026a
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2026a
)
to learn generalist manipulation policies that map visual observations and language instructions to executable actions..
Despite acquiring broad capabilities from large-scale robot demonstrations, end-to-end imitation remains bounded by the behaviors observed during training.
Recent embodied reasoning methods introduce intermediate reasoning between perception and control
(
Zawalski et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2026b
;
Lee et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026a
;
Fang et al., 2026
;
Zhong et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026a
)
.
ThinkAct
(
Huang et al., 2026b
)
reinforces textual and visual plans with action-aligned rewards, MolmoAct
(
Lee et al., 2025
)
reasons through spatial traces, Fast-ThinkAct
(
Huang et al., 2026a
)
compresses reasoning into latent thoughts, and ACoT-VLA
(
Zhong et al., 2026
)
predicts coarse reference actions to guide policy generation.
However, these methods largely augment robot demonstrations with intermediate reasoning, without explicitly grounding the learned thoughts in the task-relevant changes they induce in the world.
Their generalization to novel scenes and skills therefore remains constrained by the behavioral coverage of the underlying robot data.
Learning Robot Policies from Human Videos.
Improving generalization also requires expanding the behavioral coverage of the training data.
Human videos capture substantially greater diversity in scenes, objects, and skills than robot demonstrations, motivating their use for scaling robot learning
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Zheng et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026a
;
Li et al., 2026a
)
.
Supervised methods convert human interactions into robot-compatible representations, as in EgoScale
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
and EgoWAM
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
, but require costly cross-embodiment supervision.
Latent action models instead infer action-like variables from visual transitions without explicit control labels
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025c
;
Routray et al., 2026
)
, with LAPA
(
Ye et al., 2025
)
learning discrete latent actions before grounding them into robot control.
Such representations may capture appearance or embodiment cues rather than task-relevant dynamics. ThinkWorld grounds shared motion tokens and refines them by matching predicted and observed futures in videos.
World Models and Visual Foresight for Embodied Control.
Recent advances in generative video models
(
Wan et al., 2025
;
Agarwal et al., 2025
)
have enabled their application to a wide range of tasks
(
Xu et al., 2023
;
Tosi et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2025
)
. World models learn action-conditioned dynamics to support planning and policy optimization. Dreamer-style agents optimize policies through imagined rollouts
(
Hafner et al., 2023
;
Hafner et al., 2025
)
, while recent large-scale models acquire broad physical priors from diverse video data
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
. In robotics, visual-foresight methods generate video plans or image subgoals to guide control
(
Du et al., 2023
;
Black et al., 2024b
;
Bharadhwaj et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2025
)
, while predictive VLAs forecast future pixels or latent features for planning and representation learning
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Sun et al., 2026a
;
Cai et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026c
;
Kim et al., 2026b
)
. More recent world-action models jointly model future-world evolution and robot actions
(
Ye et al., 2026b
;
Pai et al., 2025
;
Cen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026c
)
. In contrast, ThinkWorld does not use future prediction as the control output or an imagined rollout for policy optimization. Instead, it treats agreement between predicted and observed futures as a training-time signal to reinforce action-grounded Chain-of-Dynamics within the VLM. This directly turns observed world changes, including those in action-unlabeled videos, into supervision for action reasoning, while future prediction is discarded at deployment.
3
Method
Figure 2
:
ThinkWorld architecture and training stages.
In stage (a), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) tokenizes robot actions and annotated human hand motions into a unified discrete motion space to ground Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) reasoning, while CoD-conditioned imagination predicts the future visual feature. In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

4.2
Real-World Generalization under Distribution Shifts
We evaluate real-world generalization under matched in-domain (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings across three manipulation tasks: placing cups on a hanger, color matching, and object sorting. OOD settings introduce changes in object color or category and, in some cases, require trajectories not observed during task-specific training. For each task, we collect demonstrations across at least six object configurations and evaluate multiple settings under both ID and OOD conditions, with five trials per setting. These tasks require the policy to identify task-relevant object attributes, such as color and category, and adapt its motion accordingly.
As shown in Fig.
3
, we compare ThinkWorld-YAM with Diffusion Policy
(
Chi et al., 2023
)
, MolmoAct2
(
Fang et al., 2026
)
, a VLA with explicit action reasoning, and LaWAM
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
, which conditions action generation on predicted latent visual subgoals. While the methods perform similarly in-domain, their differences become more pronounced under OOD shifts. ThinkWorld maintains higher success rates when object appearances change or unseen trajectories are required, outperforming both MolmoAct2 and LaWAM. This suggests that grounding CoD reasoning in action-induced world changes helps the policy adapt to task-relevant changes rather than relying on appearance cues or memorized trajectories.
4.3
Acquiring Skill Composition from Human Experience
We further evaluate whether human demonstrations can transfer compositional knowledge to robot control. We construct an oven manipulation task from reusable atomic robot skills and provide robot demonstrations only for the individual skills
1) open, 2) close, 3) put the left object in the oven
, and
4) put the right object in the oven

Successful execution requires the robot to identify the relevant skills, preserve their temporal order, and transition between them without observing the complete robot trajectory during training. These results demonstrate that the shared CoD reasoning space enables compositional knowledge to transfer from human demonstrations to robot execution, allowing the robot to perform a complete skill sequence never demonstrated in robot data. 4.5
Analysis
Cross-Embodiment Structure of CoD.
We first examine whether CoD induces a shared motion-centric structure across human and robot embodiments. For each sample, we extract the VLM hidden state of the final
</think>
token, which summarizes the generated CoD, and visualize these features with t-SNE in Fig.
6

Despite substantial differences in embodiment and visual appearance, samples with similar motion directions form coherent clusters that contain examples from multiple datasets, while samples from the same dataset separate according to their motions. This suggests that CoD features are organized primarily around action-relevant motion rather than embodiment identity, revealing a shared action-level structure shared across human and robot behaviors.
Effectiveness of Human Data.
We investigate the contribution of human egocentric video through a controlled pretraining study, keeping the amount of robot data fixed while increasing the human video fraction to 10%, 25%, and 50% of the total training data. We compare these variants against a robot-only baseline and an additional robot-only control that matches the training scale and number of training iterations of the 50% human-data variant by using additional robot data. This control helps distinguish the benefits of human video from those of increased training scale alone. These experimental configurations are designed to assess the contribution of heterogeneous human video to robustness and differ from our final model configuration. After SFT, each variant undergoes embodiment-specific post-training on LIBERO and is evaluated on LIBERO-PRO to assess generalization. As shown in Fig.
6
, overall success increases monotonically with the proportion of human video, from 45.4% for the robot-only baseline to 47.8% for the 50% human-data variant. The latter also outperforms the matched robot-only control by approximately 1.2 percentage points. These results suggest that the diversity provided by human egocentric video improves generalization beyond the gains attributable to increased training scale alone.

Role of CoD in Future Prediction.
We further examine how CoD contributes to future prediction. As shown in Fig.
7
, predictions conditioned on the generated CoD better capture the action-induced transition toward the ground-truth future, whereas shuffled, empty, or no-CoD variants tend to preserve the current-state structure or predict incorrect transitions. Tab.
3
quantitatively supports this observation: CoD achieves a cosine similarity of 0.74 across all patches, compared with 0.71–0.72 for the other conditions. The difference is more pronounced in the top 25% most dynamic target patches, where CoD reaches 0.62 compared with 0.54–0.55, indicating that CoD is particularly effective at predicting action-induced changes.
We further examine what information CoD captures through attention visualization in Fig.
8
. Across both human and robot examples, CoD consistently attends to action-relevant dynamic regions, including human hands or robot arms and the manipulated objects, rather than static background regions. This pattern indicates that CoD focuses on the parts of the scene most involved in the ongoing motion and links these motion cues to the resulting changes in object state and configuration. Together with the future-prediction results, these visualizations suggest that CoD captures action-centric dynamics that ground future prediction in the state transitions induced by an action.
Effect of Training Components.
To assess the effectiveness of each training component, we start from a baseline consisting of the Qwen3-VL backbone with the MolmoAct2 action expert, and progressively add visual history, future prediction, CoD, and world-imagination RL. As shown in Tab.
3
, history provides temporal context and slightly improves the average success rate from 40.1% to 40.7%. Future prediction brings a much larger gain to 50.4%, indicating the benefit of explicitly modeling how the scene evolves. Adding CoD further raises performance to 54.4%, with consistent improvements across all distribution shifts, showing the value of grounding future prediction in action-relevant dynamics. Finally, world-imagination RL improves the average to 55.6%, with further gains under position, task, and environment shifts, demonstrating its role in refining CoD reasoning beyond supervised training. Overall, these ablations support the design of ThinkWorld, showing that each component contributes to more robust and generalizable action reasoning.
5
Conclusion
We present
ThinkWorld
, a VLA learning framework that learns transferable Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) through reinforcement learning with world imagination. By grounding action thoughts in the world changes they induce, ThinkWorld learns a common representation across human and robot embodiments and extends action reasoning to videos without explicit action annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments, validating the effectiveness of learning transferable action reasoning from observed world dynamics and its potential for scaling robot learning with diverse human and robot experience.

Input and Output Configuration
Input prompt.
All media precede the textual metadata in a single user turn. When temporal context is available, the order is main-view history, current main view, and the remaining current views in their dataset-defined order. History contains at most 16 main-view frames sampled at 2 Hz and ordered from oldest to newest. The current main image is not repeated in the history.
The complete VLA input/output template is shown below. Bracketed lines are optional, and the textual portion is rendered as one normalized string rather than as separate lines.

USER MEDIA:
[main-camera history video: 0--16 frames]
<current_main_image>
[<current_wrist_image_1><current_wrist_image_2>]

USER TEXT:
The task is to {task}. The setup is {embodiment}
[ with {native_control} control].
[The current state of the robot is {state}.]
[A {N}-frame history video is followed by the current observation image.
| The current observation frame is provided.]
The future visual target is the main-view observation exactly one second
after the current observation. Given these, produce a future motion plan
and then predict the future state one second in the future.

ASSISTANT:
Proprioceptive state encoding.
Following MolmoAct2
(
Fang et al., 2026
)
, we encode proprioceptive state as discrete tokens. Each dataset-native state dimension is normalized using training-split statistics, clipped to
[
−
1
,
1
]
[-1,1]
, uniformly quantized into 256 bins, and serialized between dedicated state-boundary tokens. The native state width is preserved, so no common padded state vector is exposed in the prompt.
Media processing.
Dataset-side resizing is disabled. Qwen retains the source aspect ratio, with a pixel-area range of 4,096–200,704 for each current image and 4,096–50,176 for each history frame. State conditioning is dropped with probability 0.10 and wrist views with probability 0.20 during supervised training. The maximum multimodal sequence length is 2,048 tokens; over-length examples are removed rather than silently truncating their supervision.

Motion Tokenizer Training.
We train a motion tokenizer following the FAST architecture
(
Pertsch et al., 2025
)
on one-second windows of consecutive wrist-motion deltas from robot and human trajectories. Each time step contains a 6D motion vector for one hand or a 12D vector for two hands: translation in meters and rotation as a rotation vector in radians, with gripper state excluded. We normalize translation and rotation using fixed scales of 0.3448 m and 0.9119 rad, respectively, and encode the sequences with a vocabulary of 2,048 tokens. Robot poses are expressed in the robot base frame, whereas human poses are expressed in an actor-centered frame whose
+
z
+z
axis is gravity-aligned and whose
+
x
+x
axis follows the actor’s current yaw. Training on both domains yields a shared token space for intended wrist motion. The tokens are not executed as native robot actions; a separate continuous action expert predicts executable actions.

Appendix B
Evaluation Details
B.1
Simulation Benchmarks and Baselines
We fine-tune our policy only on standard LIBERO
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
and use its unmodified tasks as the in-distribution reference. We then evaluate the trained policy on LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Plus without further adaptation to either benchmark. We select LIBERO-PRO as the primary benchmark because its controlled changes to objects, object positions, task specifications, and environments directly test whether the policy can adapt its behavior to new manipulation settings. LIBERO-Plus additionally covers camera, lighting, background, and sensor-noise perturbations, which probe perceptual robustness beyond our main methodological focus. We report a supplementary LIBERO-Plus evaluation in Appendix
C.4
.
B.2
Real-Robot Setup
We use the BimanualYAM robot system to collect our in-lab dataset and evaluate trained policies. As shown in Fig.
9
, the system comprises two YAM arms and three RealSense D405 cameras: one providing a top view and one mounted on each wrist. Policies use RGB observations only.
Policy inference runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090. To account for differences in inference latency, we query each policy and execute its actions at the same 15 Hz control rate, while the remaining system components run at 30 Hz. For each predicted action chunk, we execute the first half and then replan using the latest observation.

Real-Robot Evaluation

For the real-robot experiments, we evaluate three tasks on the bimanual YAM platform: color matching (60 robot demonstrations), cup hanging (45), and object sorting (100). The tasks are designed to test whether the policy can infer task-level regularities and adapt its actions to the current scene rather than memorize a single trajectory. Separately, we study skill composition on the oven task using 100 robot episodes of atomic-action trajectories and 90 human-video episodes of full task sequences. Appendix D
Limitations and Reproducibility
Training results are obtained from a single training seed; accordingly, the reported episode-level confidence intervals characterize evaluation variability rather than variation across independently trained checkpoints. For real-robot experiments, we report the number of physical trials and task-level results to make the evaluation scope explicit. Inference latency should be interpreted under the stated deployment setup, as it varies with hardware and input configuration. To support reproducibility, we provide trial denominators, model initialization details, training configurations, and hardware specifications alongside the aggregate results.

article.headline: 用世界想象强化动作推理，VLA 泛化提升
article.lede: ThinkWorld 用跨具身共享的离散运动 token 表示动作，以想象未来与观测未来的对齐作为奖励，让人类视频无需动
article.problem: 视觉-语言-动作（VLA）模型的泛化能力受限于带动作标注的机器人演示的多样性与覆盖范围。人类视频的行为与环境多样性远高于机器人数据，但缺少可直接执行的动作。潜在动作模型虽可扩展到无标注视频，推断出的变量约束不足，可能只捕捉外观变化或相机运动；全监督方法依赖精确的姿态估计与人类到机器人的对应关系，因此学习人类视频时存在「动作接地强度」与「行为覆盖广度」之间的权衡。
article.method: 作者提出 Chain-of-Dynamics（CoD），把机器人动作与标注的人手运动统一映射为归一化 delta 末端执行器表示，再用 FAST 式运动 tokenizer 离散化为共享词表上的运动 token 序列，作为跨具身的动作推理接口。模型在 CoD 之后追加可学习 future query，在冻结的 DINOv3 特征空间中预测 1 秒后的未来视觉表示，先以动作标注数据做监督初始化。随后用 GRPO 做强化学习，奖励来自想象未来与观测未来在运动加权 patch 上的相似度，因此无动作标注的人类与机器人视频都能提供监督；部署时不生成 CoD，也不做未来预测。
article.results: 在 LIBERO 上平均成功率为 97.3%，在 LIBERO-PRO 上为 55.6%；其中任务偏移 31.9%、环境偏移 60.9%，分别比 VLA-JEPA 高 11.1 和 19.9 个百分点。真实双臂 YAM 平台上，ID 条件 60 次试验全部成功，OOD 条件 52/60 成功，宏平均与微平均成功率分别为 94.4% 和 93.3%，最强基线 MolmoAct2 为 62.2% 和 60.0%。控制机器人数据量不变、把人类自我中心视频比例增至 50% 时，LIBERO-PRO 成功率从纯机器人基线的 45.4% 升至 47.8%，比同等训练规模的纯机器人对照组高约 1.2 个百分点。在包含历史帧、未来预测、CoD 和 RL 的累积消融中，平均成功率依次为 40.1%、40.7%、50.4%、54.4%、55.6%。在固定 CoD 开/关的对比中，未来特征余弦相似度为 0.74 对 0.71–0.72，在运动量前 25% 的 patch 上为 0.62 对 0.54–0.55。论文给出训练使用 128 张 H100 做 SFT、64 张做 RL。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「预测未来」从控制输出改成训练时的奖励信号，使没有动作标注的人类视频能直接监督动作推理，并在部署时丢弃推理开销，为扩展机器人学习的数据来源提供可行路径。
article.limitations: 作者在附录中承认结果来自单一训练种子，报告的置信区间只反映评估波动，而非独立训练间的差异。LIBERO-Plus 上相机与噪声扰动明显弱于 DreamVLA（46.9% 对 65.0%、62.7% 对 84.9%），真实机器人评测也仅限三个任务与少量组合任务，规模仍小。
article.figure_caption_zh: ThinkWorld 的两阶段训练：阶段（a）把机器人动作与标注人手动作 tokenize 成统一离散运动空间以接地 CoD 推理，并由 CoD 条件的想象预测未来视觉特征；阶段（b）用想象与观测未来的对齐作为可扩展奖励，在无动作标注的人类与机器人视频上强化 CoD 推理。

figure.caption: {ThinkWorld architecture and training stages.} In stage (a), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) tokenizes robot actions and annotated human hand motions into a unified discrete motion space to ground Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) reasoning, while CoD-conditioned imagination predicts the future visual feature. In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

page_papers.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
page_papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.
page_papers.content:
GEPA-Curator:
Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
Zack Yu
1*
, Nicholas Lee

, Minjae Lee

, Luca Manolache

UC Berkeley
