3
LBNL
4
Furiosa AI
5
KAIST
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments.
Existing reflective prompt optimizers
such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges.
We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance.
We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization.
In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components:
task curation
, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and
prior success retrieval
, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer.
We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and
τ
\tau
-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models.
GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.
†
†
footnotetext:
∗
Equal contribution.
†
Equal Advising.
Correspondence to: Amir Gholami (amirgh@berkeley.edu).
1
Introduction
As interest in recursive self-improvement (RSI) grows, a central question is how agents can reliably learn from their own experience to improve future behavior
(
Favaro and Clark, 2026
)
.
Reflective prompt optimization, where an agent acts with tools in an environment and a Reflector uses the resulting trajectory or end state to identify lessons and revise the agent’s prompt, offers one practical mechanism for this form of self-improvement
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
.
The revised prompt is then used on subsequent tasks, creating a feedback loop in which experience can progressively improve agent behavior.
In agentic settings, this approach rests on the assumption that experience from previously attempted tasks contains signal and information that generalize to future tasks.
However, it is often difficult for the Reflector to correctly attribute the cause of a failure to the prompt.
In agentic tasks, execution is mediated by a harness interacting with an external environment, and success is often assessed by LLM-as-a-judge
(
Zheng et al., 2023
)
.
A failed rollout may therefore reveal a genuine prompt weakness, but it may also arise from external factors such as unavailability of needed tools, harness limitations, or even noise from execution or evaluation environments.
This problem is further exacerbated in real-world settings, where tasks themselves may be ambiguous or infeasible, introducing additional noisy signals to the Reflector.
When revising the prompt, the Reflector may nevertheless treat these potentially noisy observations as valid learning signals for
prompt
optimization
(
Kirichenko et al., 2025
)
, causing it to misattribute the associated failures to prompt deficiencies, thereby producing unnecessary or harmful updates.
As an example, consider an agent asked to purchase an item from a shopping website.
If the agent fails because it overlooks a required option before adding the item to the cart, the Reflector can usefully revise the prompt to encourage checking required fields before proceeding.
In contrast, if the same task fails because it runs in a broken environment where the purchase button in the webpage is temporarily malfunctioning, treating this failure as evidence about the prompt may lead the Reflector to introduce unnecessary or even harmful changes.
For example, it may conclude that
the agent needs to seek alternative ways to complete the purchase, while the button can become functional for future tasks.
To mitigate such issues, recent work
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
uses a held-out validation set in order to guard against these changes.
If the prompt does poorly on the validation set after mutation, the change can be rejected.
GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
goes a step further and evaluates the mutated prompt on the minibatch again to make sure that the model performance does not degrade after such a mutation.
However, such validation-based gating mechanisms alone may not be sufficient to prevent noisy signals, for two reasons.
First, bad mutations may be accepted and good ones rejected, e.g., because the gating decision relies on
aggregated
evaluation scores, which can be noisy due to stochasticity in execution or evaluation.
Second, such validation-based gating acts only
after
a mutation has been generated, and therefore cannot fundamentally improve the quality of the reflection or mutation itself.
This motivates us to maintain and provide additional contextual information in order to improve the capabilities of the Reflector.
Based on these insights, we present GEPA-Curator, an agentic data Curator which runs as a harness on top of existing prompt optimizers.
GEPA-Curator has two roles.
The first is
task curation
, where instead of randomly selecting tasks for the minibatch, the agent will curate a minibatch which is likely to provide clean signal and discard tasks which seem to be noisy or faulty.
The second is a
prior success retrieval
, where the Curator can selectively retrieve past successful trajectories for a task and provide them as context to the prompt optimizer to improve the quality of the mutation.
Providing the Reflector agent with successful exemplars is essential to give the model the proper context to see why the prompt is failing now, and when it succeeded in the past.
Overall, our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce GEPA-Curator, an agentic harness for prompt optimization that improves mutation quality through adaptive task curation (Section
3.1
) and selective retrieval (Section
3.2
) of prior successful trajectories.
•
We evaluate GEPA-Curator on four WebArena websites
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and
τ
\tau
-bench. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of the evaluated baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
and 21.2% over ACE
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. These results suggest that the benefits of curation extend across optimizer models.
2
Related Work
LLM Agents.
As LLMs become ubiquitous, LLM-powered agents have been equipped with tools and harnesses in order to interact and execute in external environments.
React
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
interwove reasoning with tool execution to improve performance.
Later work
(
Patil et al., 2024
;
Erdogan et al., 2024
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Shen et al., 2023
;
Xu et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
)
used tool calling, where the model generates a structured output which is parsed and used to execute functions to affect the environment.
This has led to LLM agents being used to control and interact with different environments; and
this has led to a variety of different benchmarks
(
Trivedi et al., 2024
;
Shridhar et al., 2021
;
Yao et al., 2024
;
Patil et al., 2024
;
Patil et al., 2025
)
to evaluate LLMs at tool calling.
One example is using LLMs as webagents in order to explore and act in web environments
(
Qi et al., 2025
;
Erdogan et al., 2025
;
Gür et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
.
This has led to the development of various browser and computer use benchmarks and environments in this area
(
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Gandhi and Neubig, 2026
;
He et al., 2024
;
Xue et al., 2025
;
Xie et al., 2024
;
Yuan et al., 2026
;
Rawles et al., 2023
)
.
Webarena
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
was one of the first web environments and benchmarks to cover realistic websites such as GitLab, Reddit, Shopping portals, etc.
Prompt Optimization.
Reflective optimizers use natural language feedback in place of numerical gradients to revise textual components of an AI system
(
Yuksekgonul et al., 2024
;
Agrawal et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Zhou et al., 2023b
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Pryzant et al., 2023
;
Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024
)
.
In particular, GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
applies reflection to system-level trajectories, using evaluator feedback to diagnose failures and propose prompt mutations within an evolutionary search.
ACE
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
introduced a framework for agentic context adaptation to create structured playbooks to organize and accumulate strategies at runtime.
SkillOpt
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
similarly treats an agent’s skill document as trainable external state; a separate optimizer analyzes scored rollouts and proposes bounded add, delete, or replace edits.
Meta-Harness
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
extended this idea further by having an outer optimization loop on the harness code which runs the agent instead of just the prompt.
These methods demonstrate that execution traces can provide substantially richer optimization signals than scalar rewards alone.
GEPA-Curator addresses a complementary question:
which agentic trajectories provide a valid signal for reflection, and what historical evidence should accompany them?
Curriculum Learning.
Curriculum Learning
(
Bengio et al., 2009
;
Fan et al., 2018
)
studies how the selection and ordering of training data can improve optimization and model training.
Recent work
(
Zhou et al., 2023a
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lee et al., 2024
;
Diao et al., 2024
)
has looked into how this can affect LLM training and alignment.
LIMA
(
Zhou et al., 2023a
)
established how having poorer quality data can negatively affect LLM alignment, and showed that a small amount of high-quality data can be as effective as a large scale training set.
3
GEPA-Curator Methodology
In this section, we describe how GEPA-Curator integrates with existing prompt optimizers.
To do so, we first formulate a prompt optimizer by its input-output interface.
At each step, a prompt optimizer receives a prompt, a minibatch of tasks, and optionally some input metadata. It executes the tasks using an actor agent conditioned on the prompt and returns an updated prompt, task-level agent trajectories, and evaluation results (See Figure
1
).
Ordinary prompt optimizers randomly permute and iterate through the tasks in the training dataset at each step.
We identify a few points in existing prompt optimizers where noisy optimization signals can arise.
When selecting tasks to execute, some tasks may yield noisy or unhelpful trajectories.
Furthermore, when reflecting on execution results, some failures may be difficult to attribute correctly from the failed trajectory alone.
In Section
5.1
, we present motivating experiments showing how such noisy signals can propagate through the optimization process and ultimately degrade training.
GEPA-Curator runs as a harness on top of the optimizer,
maintaining a per-task history, including agent trajectories and evaluation outcomes from previous optimization steps.
The Curator uses this history to address these sources of noise through two corresponding roles:
(i)
task curation
(Section
3.1
), which selects tasks likely to provide useful signal for prompt optimization to construct the next minibatch;
and
(ii)
prior success retrieval
(Section
3.2
), which retrieves relevant past successful trajectories for tasks in the current minibatch to provide the Reflector with concrete contextual references for failure diagnosis.
Note that these trajectories are provided to the prompt optimizer only as additional input metadata, leaving the optimizer itself unchanged.
The full workflow is depicted in Figure
1
.
We have found that both of these methods are critical for performance (Section
4.3
).
Figure 1:
GEPA-Curator system diagram.
The prompt optimizer takes in a minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories.
The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer.
The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal (Section
3.1
).
The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as a trusted reference example (Section
3.2
).
Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization.
The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds.
3.1
Task Curation
The Curator examines the training tasks and selects which tasks to run at each optimization step.
Underexplored tasks are initially prioritized to build sufficient per-task history.
As this history accumulates, the Curator may skip a task when there is strong evidence that further rollouts are unlikely to yield useful reflection signal for prompt optimization.
Such cases include repeated stable success, repeated failures caused by factors outside the prompt (e.g., harness or environment limitations), and inconsistent evaluations of similar outcomes, which can be judged based on the accumulated per-task history.
Importantly, skipping is a temporary decision rather than a permanent decision, and thus skipped tasks are reconsidered by the Curator at each training epoch.
This is necessary because tasks that were previously solved may regress as the prompt is updated for other tasks, e.g., through prompt compression or the addition of potentially conflicting rules.
Conversely, tasks that were initially too difficult, and therefore skipped after repeated failures, may become solvable as the prompt improves and can be reintroduced into training.
3.2
Prior Success Retrieval
Normally, prompt optimizers reflect on failure examples in the current minibatch and mutate the prompt based only on the failed trajectories and their evaluations.
Therefore, pairing a current failed execution with prior successful executions of the same task allows the Reflector to perform
contrastive learning
of the failed behavior against a known and trusted reference.
This provides the Reflector with a concrete basis for correcting the behavior, rather than forcing it to diagnose the failure by guessing.
The Curator is instructed to reason over the task history to select one successful trajectory that provides the most reliable reference for the current task.
In particular, it favors successes supported by consistent evaluation evidence and avoids using outcomes whose apparent success is ambiguous or inconsistent with other observations in the history.
When no appropriate success is available, the Curator abstains and does not provide this metadata to the Reflector.
This approach prevents noisy success trajectories from providing misleading positive examples, in the same way that removing noisy failure trajectories prevents misleading optimization signals.
The prompt for task curation and prior success retrieval is provided at Appendix
B.2
.
Note that because task curation and prior-success retrieval are performed jointly in a single Curator call, the latter requires no additional LLM invocation.
In summary, these two components of GEPA-Curator (task curation and prior success retrieval) work in unison to ensure that the prompt optimizer gets cleaner and curated data to train on.
By curating the tasks in each minibatch, we maximize the amount of signal provided at each step of the optimization loop through removing noisy or redundant tasks.
By providing reliable past successful trajectories to the Reflector, we enable the Reflector to create better mutations with grounded understanding instead of guessing the fix.
4
Empirical Evaluation
4.1
Experimental Setup
We compare GEPA-Curator against GEPA
(
Agrawal et al., 2026
)
and ACE
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
.
GEPA-Curator builds on a simplified, greedy variant of GEPA that removes Pareto-based candidate selection.
Rather than evolving a candidate pool and sampling from the Pareto frontier on validation set, GEPA-Curator maintains a single lineage in which each mutation becomes the next checkpoint.
We evaluate the prompt every 16 iterations unless specified on a held-out validation set and select the final model based on the best validation score at the end.
Because our ablation showed little difference between GEPA with and without Pareto selection, we adopt this greedy variant for simplicity.
The prompt-optimization experiments use gpt-oss-120b
(
Agarwal et al., 2025
)
as the actor agent.
We evaluate two optimizer models, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview
(
DeepMind, 2026
)
and Claude Opus 5
(
Anthropic, 2026
)
, using the selected model for all optimizer-side agents, including the Reflector and Curator, within each run. The minibatch size is 16.
The actor’s maximum context length is set to gpt-oss-120B’s native maximum context length (131072) so we constrain the optimized prompt to fit within this limit.
All seed prompts used for optimization are manually written.
The evaluation numbers are averaged over 5 repeated runs.
For evaluation of optimization on noisy data, we experimented with tasks from GoBrowse
(

5.3
Meta-Harness-Curator
Recently, Meta-Harness
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
introduced an optimization loop which acts on the harness code of agents in a similar manner to how GEPA optimizes prompts.
In this section, we extend the curation approach of GEPA-Curator to Meta-Harness, which we call Meta-Harness-Curator, to explore whether curation offers additional benefits when the optimizer itself has greater autonomy.
Although the coding agent used in the default Meta-Harness can inspect the full execution history, it must decide which failures to investigate while also reasoning about and modifying the harness. Curation may help by directing this investigation toward a focused set of tasks and relevant prior successes, providing concrete evidence to guide code changes. We hypothesize that this division of work becomes more useful as the pool of training tasks and execution histories grows.
Implementation.
We augment Meta-Harness with a Curator that inspects candidate code, training histories, and aggregate development scores to select a parent harness and a subset of training tasks, together with a rationale. The parent is freshly executed on these tasks, and the optimizer revises it using the resulting feedback and the Curator’s rationale. Each child is evaluated on the same tasks as its parent and on the full development set, regardless of whether its training score improves. Both agents can inspect prior training histories, including earlier modifications and their outcomes. The Curator may also select historical successful executions of the chosen tasks as references, which are passed to the optimizer only when the corresponding fresh parent executions fail. These references link to the original trajectories and the harnesses that produced them. Training and development executions count toward the search budget, and the candidate with the highest development score is selected for final test evaluation.
Experimental setup.
We evaluate on the Math-RAG and online text classification settings studied by Meta-Harness, with separate development sets for candidate selection. Math-RAG uses 150 training, 100 development, and 200 test tasks, with a budget of 15,000 training and development solver calls. The test set comprises IMO-AnswerBench and IMO-ProofBench
(
Luong et al., 2025
)
, and the December 2025 and January 2026 releases of ArXivMath
(
Dekoninck et al., 2026
)
. Text classification covers USPTO-50k (USPTO)
(
Schneider et al., 2016
)
, Symptom2Disease (S2D)
(
Gretel AI, 2023
)
, and LawBench (Law)
(
Fei et al., 2024
)
, using 130 training, 92 development, and 320 test tasks in total and a budget of 10,000 training and development actor calls. The labeled examples used to construct classification memories are separate from these optimization tasks; memory construction is excluded from the budget. Both methods share the same splits and initial harnesses. We use gpt-oss-20B as the Math-RAG solver and judge, gpt-oss-120B as the classification actor, and Codex with GPT-6-Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026
)
for the optimizer and Curator. Actors and coding agents use medium reasoning effort, while the math judge uses high reasoning effort. We run one optimization experiment per method and setting, then evaluate each development-selected harness with three samples per test task.

5.4
Efficiency optimization and Cost Analysis
While GEPA-Curator is designed with active agent involvement to demonstrate the potential of agent-designed curriculum as a promising direction for self-improvement, we also develope a more efficient variant and conduct a cost analysis to evaluate its practicality for cost-efficient deployment.
Implementation.
We introduce three modifications to improve the cost efficiency of GEPA-Curator while preserving its effectiveness:
(1)
Skip interval decision.
Instead of making a skip decision at every epoch, the Curator specifies the number of epochs to skip, eliminating repeated Curator calls during the skip interval.
(2)
Compact task history.
Each Curator call receives full trajectories from a configurable number of recent executions, while older executions are represented by compact summaries containing their epoch numbers, outcomes, and previous Curator assessments. This reduces the growth of the Curator’s input context as optimization progresses.
(3)
Successful trajectory retention.
Since complete task history is no longer available, we retain an optional full successful trajectory, which is always provided to the Reflector upon each failure when available. During task curation, the Curator can replace this reference with a better successful trajectory from recent executions.
Experimental setup.
We evaluate Efficient GEPA-Curator on the four Webarena websites, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and
τ
\tau
-bench.
The Efficient Curator retains full histories for the latest four execution units per task on WebArena and the latest one on the non-WebArena benchmarks. We use a shorter history for non-WebArena benchmarks to reduce curation costs, as their cleaner task environments require less complex considerations during curation. All other setups are the same as Section

6
Conclusion
In conclusion, we introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework which augments prompt optimization to select which agentic tasks should shape prompt optimization.
A Curator is used to agentically select and filter out tasks based on whether they can provide noisy or reliable training signals.
Furthermore, the Curator can retrieve and provide prior successful trajectories for failed tasks and gives them to the prompt optimizer to act as an anchoring context for reflections.
We show that this technique achieves consistent performance improvements over GEPA and ACE by up to 21.2% on Webarena, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and
τ
\tau
-bench.
We further extend our method to Meta-Harness and show that this agentic curation idea can even improve harness code as well.
AI use statement
LLMs are a core component of our paper.
Our method uses LLMs to curate data, retrieve robust successful trajectories, and propose improvements to prompts used by an LLM agent.
These LLM-generated artifacts are part of the system being studied and developed in the paper.
Furthermore, standard LLM tools were used for simple writing assistance such as grammar and formatting.
Ethics statement
This work presents a generic method for improving prompts for LLM agents, rather than a system designed for a specific domain.
Potential positive impacts include making agentic systems more reliable, adaptable, and accessible to researchers and practitioners.
Potential negative impacts are indirect: stronger LLM agents could be misused in harmful ways, or could cause harm if deployed in high-risk environments without proper human supervision.
We emphasize that optimized agents should be evaluated in the intended environment and used with appropriate human oversight, monitoring, and controls.
Reproducibility statement
The models, datasets, hyperparameters, and prompts that are used in the paper have been detailed and documented in Appendix
B
and Section
4.1

Appendix A
Details about Motivating Experiments
A.1
Selection of Dataset Composition
Before constructing the experimental datasets for the motivating examples, we use logs from several preliminary GitLab experiments to identify tasks corresponding to different labels. For
Easy
tasks, we select tasks that already achieve consistently high success rates with the seed prompt. For
Optimizable
tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve consistent success with the optimized prompt from at least one preliminary GEPA run, and then select, from this subset, those with the lowest success rates under the seed prompt. For
Impossible
tasks, we select tasks with the lowest success rates across all rollouts. For
Flaky
tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve roughly 50% success with both the seed prompt and the optimized prompts returned by the preliminary GEPA runs. We then manually inspect these tasks and prioritize cases where the LLM-as-a-judge produces inconsistent success and failure judgments despite similar or identical end states, particularly when even the best attainable end state does not yield consistently successful judgments.
A.2
A Concrete Example of Negative Transfer
We trace an accepted prompt mutation from iteration 7 of the
Optimizable
+
Impossible
condition. Two tasks from the
Impossible
partition had failed under the parent prompt. For “View the
split_silence.py
example for audio processing,” global search returned no useful result, and the evaluator suggested manually browsing projects and groups. For “Expand a subgroup in the hierarchy list to view nested subgroups,” the actor searched public groups containing no expandable subgroup, and the evaluator suggested checking the actor’s own groups instead. Both tasks are considered
Impossible
because their underspecified intents identify neither a target repository nor a group, leaving the actor to explore without direction, frequently exhausting its step budget before succeeding and making the tasks difficult to optimize through prompting. Reflection converted this feedback into a stronger exhaustive-search instruction:
Exhaustive Exploration:
Global code search is often limited or disabled. If a search yields no results, manually navigate through groups, projects, and repository file trees. Always check “Your groups”, “Your projects”, and your personal dashboard before defaulting to public “Explore” tabs, as task resources are usually associated with your account.
Its exhaustive-search instruction caused a regression on the
Optimizable
task “Check the guide to WCAG documents and standards.” Immediately before the mutation, the actor recognized The A11Y Project on its starting page, opened the repository, used
Find file
to search for
WCAG
, and reached
src/posts/wcag2-documents.md
in five actions. With the mutated prompt, instead of opening the visible A11Y Project directly, the actor first filtered its personal projects, then traversed Explore, Topics, Help, global search, and group pages. After eventually returning to the A11Y Project, it inspected the README and Wiki and manually traversed the repository tree. It exhausted all 30 actions in the
src
directory without reaching the guide.
The exhaustive-search instruction caused the regression by replacing the short repository-level search path with broad exploration across site sections and the repository tree. Nevertheless, the aggregate minibatch score increased from 8 to 9, so the mutation was accepted as candidate 5. This example provides a concrete mechanism for the trend in Figure
2
: feedback from difficult tasks can elicit an overgeneralized search strategy whose aggregate gain masks a regression on a solvable task.

Curator Prompts
The Curator agent in the full method makes task-selection and success-selection decisions jointly in one LLM call. For readability, we separate the shared task-selection prefix from the success-selection instructions appended when success evidence is enabled.
Task-Selection Instructions
You are a task curator allocating evaluation budget during text optimization. Judge this task independently: no other task is visible. Decide whether another rollout is currently useful for learning a better prompt or obtaining information about the task.
Use these definitions:
Mastered:
Multiple stable, clean successes across separate rollouts. The agent must complete the task correctly, not merely benefit from evaluator luck, leaked state, or an accidentally correct final page. There must be no recent regression. One success is not sufficient evidence of mastery.
Prompt-sensitive:
Before/after evaluation pairs show that prompt changes can improve the behavior, including partial behavioral correction even when the binary score does not change. Run these tasks.
Operationally impossible:
The available tools or UI genuinely lack the required capability, supported by the action schema, trajectory-derived diagnostics, reference evaluation, or evaluator evidence. A single unsupported actor claim is insufficient; repeated independent attempts consistently identifying the same missing essential capability are meaningful evidence.
No current optimization signal:
The same failure mode persists across multiple materially relevant prompt mutations, with no behavioral progress or new diagnostic information. Do not infer this merely because several mutations failed when they did not address the observed failure.
Flaky or uninformative:
Materially similar behavior and ending states repeatedly receive inconsistent outcomes without a credible relationship to prompt changes. Do not infer flakiness from one disagreement.
Evaluator-broken:
There is explicit evidence of an incorrect label, stale or contradictory target, or an evaluator expectation inconsistent with the user request. A brittle, unusually strict, or difficult evaluator is not necessarily broken.
Infrastructure failure:
Timeout, reset, network errors, or local-state/file collisions caused by missing resets provide no evidence about prompt quality. Do not interpret them as agent failures.
Uncertain:
Run rather than skip. A rollout has information value: use it to test uncertain mastery, suspected flakiness, possible regressions, or ambiguous failure mechanisms.
Run unseen or underexplored tasks and tasks with credible prompt-sensitive failures. Skip only when the history provides strong evidence that another rollout currently has little optimization or diagnostic value. A
mutation_comparison
records paired before/after evaluations even when the proposed mutation was rejected. Use an improved after result as evidence that the task may be prompt-sensitive, but when
mutation_accepted
is false, do not assume that behavior belongs to the current prompt or that the task is now mastered. A skip is revisited in a later epoch; it is not a permanent retirement. In the reason, cite the specific historical evidence supporting the decision.

Taken together, these analyses suggest that GEPA-Curator can identify tasks whose outcomes are unlikely to provide reliable optimization signals. Many of the tasks diagnosed as impossible or flaky are affected by inherent limitations of the execution harness or environment, or by faulty or underspecified task descriptions. By withholding these tasks from the corresponding training batches, GEPA-Curator prevents their potentially misleading outcomes from influencing those optimization steps.
Importantly, an impossible or flaky diagnosis does not permanently retire a task. The diagnosis may be uncertain, and subsequent prompt updates or further actor exploration may reveal that a task previously considered impossible is solvable. The Curator therefore reconsiders skipped tasks in subsequent epochs.
To analyze this behavior, we divide the complete training epochs into three phases and measure the consecutive skipped epochs preceding each rerun. As shown in Table
12
, impossible tasks are deferred the longest, with their mean skip streak increasing from 5.50 to 8.75 epochs.
Mastered tasks are also deferred longer over time because repeated stable successes reduce the expected value of additional rollouts, although they are periodically revisited to detect regressions.
Flaky tasks are revisited more frequently to resolve uncertainty.
Thus, curation adjusts task frequency rather than permanently excluding tasks.
Furthermore, skip streaks generally increase as task histories accumulate, making the Curator more confident that rerunning a task at the current stage is unlikely to provide new information for prompt optimization.
While the Curator diagnosed 75 of the 1,581 training tasks (4.7%) as impossible or flaky at least once during optimization,
its effect on optimization is non-trivial.

article.headline: GEPA-Curator：用任务策展改进提示优化
article.lede: GEPA-Curator 在优化前筛选任务并检索历史成功轨迹，多个智能体基准上最高较 GEPA/ACE 提升 20.7%
article.problem: 现有反思式提示优化器假设失败轨迹含有可泛化信号，但智能体失败也可能源于工具缺失、执行框架限制、随机性或评审噪声，未必该归因于提示。仅靠验证集门控在变异后筛选，无法阻止噪声进入反思。因此需要先策展任务与上下文。
article.method: GEPA-Curator 作为外循环 harness 维护每任务历史，包含任务策展与先验成功检索两个组件。任务策展优先探索不足任务，并临时跳过稳定成功、外部原因失败或评估不一致的任务，跳过任务会在后续 epoch 重访。先验成功检索为失败任务选择性提供过去可信成功轨迹，作为反思时的对照上下文；两者只作为额外元数据输入现有优化器，不改变优化器本身。
article.results: WebArena 上，以 Gemini 3.1 Pro 为优化器时 GEPA-Curator 总体成功率 82.1%，高于 GEPA 的 78.7%（seed 72.4），聚合提升 3.4%，单站最高提升 7.4%；以 Claude Opus 5 为优化器时总体 84.5%，高于 GEPA 的 79.5%（seed 73.1），聚合提升 5.0%。附加基准上，Gemini 优化器下平均较 GEPA 提升 14.3%、较 ACE 提升 5.0%；Claude 优化器下平均较 GEPA 提升 8.1%、较 ACE 提升 12.6%，其中 ALFWorld 98.4%、AppWorld Test-N 68.8%、Test-C 46.4%、τ-bench 82.9%（与 GEPA 持平）。GitLab 消融中完整方法 88.6%，仅任务策展 84.2%，仅成功检索 84.7%，GEPA 82.8%。效率版非 WebArena 总成本 173.98 美元，低于 ACE 的 768.69 美元，平均准确率高 9.2%，总优化成本约为 GEPA 的 1.31 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把“从哪些经验学习”提升为自改进智能体的核心问题，提示优化器可通过外挂策展减少噪声失败导致的错误更新。对构建更可靠的多轮智能体有实用意义。
article.limitations: 方法建立在简化的贪心 GEPA 上并去掉了 Pareto 候选选择，Curator 本身依赖 LLM 判断，可能误判或过度弃权。QA 类基准收益有限，HotpotQA 上还比 GEPA 低 1.3%，实验也限于有限基准和两种优化器模型。
article.figure_caption_zh: 系统示意图：Curator 作为外循环读取任务历史，筛选小批量任务并检索历史成功轨迹，再交给提示优化器执行和反思。

figure.caption: system diagram. The prompt optimizer takes in a minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories. The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer. The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal ( {sec:task_curation}). The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as a trusted reference example ( {sec:success_retrieval}). Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds.

page_papers.title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation

Abstract
Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity.
Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory.
To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval.
In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget.
To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
Figure 1:
15-second multi-shot videos autoregressively generated by
CineMem
. By combining clustered memory with fine-grained query-adaptive retrieval, CineMem maintains coherent semantic flow across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios. Project page:
https://uknowsth.github.io/CineMem/
†
†
footnotetext:
*
Work done during an internship at Shanghai AI Laboratory.
†
Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Building on bidirectional architectures and extensive pre-training, recent diffusion models
(
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Ho et al., 2020
;
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Song et al., 2020
)
deliver impressive visual quality, but at substantial computational cost for long-duration generation.
Autoregressive generation offers a natural alternative for streaming video synthesis, typically combining a sliding-window mechanism with memory routing to maintain long-range consistency and stable generation
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2025
)
. This capability is particularly important for multi-shot video generation
(
Guo et al., 2025b
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which aims to synthesize coherent, film-like narratives through frequent shot transitions accompanied by substantial viewpoint changes. Maintaining a continuous and coherent narrative flow across discrete shot boundaries naturally calls for a well-designed memory retrieval strategy, especially
when previously observed subjects, scenes, or viewpoints reappear after intervening shots.
Existing memory mechanisms for causal video generation remain generally coarse-grained. Basic sliding-window strategies are widely adopted in single-shot causal models
(
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2025
)
, inevitably discarding distant information as autoregressive rollout proceeds. In multi-shot scenarios, some methods preserve temporally predefined anchors as persistent memory
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
, such as the first frames of individual shots.
These designs follow fixed routing patterns determined by temporal structures rather than the model’s intrinsic memory-access patterns, limiting their ability to fully exploit historical information.
More recent studies introduce retrieval-based memory strategies
(
Meng et al., 2026a
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
, which typically augment fixed sinks and adjacent context with frame-level routing.
The resulting routing decision is shared across all query tokens.
Although such designs allow content-aware access to historical cues, they still rely on coarse temporal grouping and overlook heterogeneous memory requirements across queries.
Consequently, long-horizon autoregressive generation remains constrained by frame-level historical conditioning, leaving much of the available memory underutilized.
In this work, we explore how an autoregressive multi-shot video model can retrieve long-term historical information under a constrained memory budget by leveraging its intrinsic memory-access patterns.
Rather than merely preserving adjacent-frame information for pixel-level continuity, memory in multi-shot scenarios should support the recovery of previously observed visual content after multiple shot transitions, a setting we refer to as revisitation.
To this end, we propose CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
By adapting memory organization and retrieval granularity to attention-based selection patterns, CineMem enables more effective access to long-term history and improves long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, as illustrated in Figure
1
.
To investigate the intrinsic memory-access patterns of autoregressive diffusion models,
we first develop a training framework that converts a bidirectional video model into a long-duration autoregressive multi-shot generator operating in a chunk-by-chunk manner, while allowing each current chunk to attend to the full generation history.
To stabilize long-horizon rollout, we further incorporate an error accumulation mitigation strategy during adaptation.
We then analyze the attention distributions between query tokens in the current chunk and all historical memory tokens. We observe a clear clustering structure among historical memory tokens and substantial variation in retrieval preferences across query tokens and attention heads.
These observations motivate our designs for online memory organization and query-adaptive retrieval.
Specifically, our framework comprises two complementary designs, as illustrated in Figure
2
. First, we apply online clustering to the KV cache to organize historical memory throughout autoregressive rollout. As generation proceeds, historical tokens are grouped according to their semantic similarity, with each cluster serving as a retrieval unit.
In contrast to conventional frame-level schemes that partition tokens by fixed frame membership regardless of content, our design forms content-aware groups, which alleviates the redundancy introduced by retrieving entire frames, while avoiding the high computational cost of treating every historical token as an individual memory unit.
Second, we introduce query-adaptive memory access in a query-wise and head-wise manner. Given their heterogeneous retrieval preferences, each query-head pair selects its most relevant clusters from memory.
Under a fixed per-query memory budget, this individualized retrieval provides broader access to the generation history, yielding a larger effective attention receptive field without increasing the retrieval cost.
Together, these designs better match intrinsic memory-access patterns while balancing
retrieval granularity, historical coverage, and computational efficiency, enabling CineMem to maintain long-range consistency across frequent shot transitions.
For evaluation, we adopt a comprehensive protocol covering video-level quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. Since conventional similarity-based metrics can assign deceptively high inter-shot consistency scores to videos that fail to perform the intended shot transition, we further introduce a VLM-assisted evaluation protocol that jointly considers transition execution and semantic preservation. This provides a more faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency in multi-shot generation. Experimental results show that CineMem achieves superior consistency compared with existing autoregressive baselines while remaining competitive with large-scale bidirectional models.
Moreover, our attention-aligned retrieval designs are effective in a plug-in setting without additional fine-tuning, demonstrating their ability to better exploit historical information during autoregressive rollout.
Overall, our work highlights the importance of fine-grained memory organization and retrieval for coherent long-horizon autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Figure 2:
Overview of CineMem.
Existing autoregressive video generation methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level, which may result in redundant retrieval, inefficient memory utilization, and overlooked heterogeneous information needs across query tokens. CineMem combines an online-clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval to enable a finer-grained memory retrieval strategy. As illustrated by the attention receptive fields, CineMem provides broader (2/3 vs. 12/12) access to historical information under the same retrieval budget.
2
Related Work
Autoregressive Video Generation and Memory.
Diffusion-based autoregressive video generation enables streaming synthesis by progressively generating frames or chunks through autoregressive rollout
(
Gao et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2026b
;
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Guo et al., 2025a
)
.
Recent methods adapt pretrained bidirectional video models through post-training or distillation
(
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2026
)
, relying on fixed anchors, sliding windows, or coarse-grained memory retrieval to maintain long-range consistency
(
Ji et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
. OminiMem
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
further introduces a fine-grained head-adaptive retrieval framework, but primarily focuses on single-shot video generation.
Meanwhile, fine-grained KV-cache organization has been explored in LLMs
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026c
;
Zhu et al., 2025
)
mainly for inference acceleration in the text domain.
In contrast, our work investigates fine-grained retrieval over visual memory with the primary goal of preserving long-range consistency, which we study in the more demanding setting of autoregressive multi-shot video generation.
Multi-Shot Video Generation.
Multi-shot video generation aims to synthesize sequences with discrete shot transitions while preserving narrative, subject, and scene consistency. Most existing approaches are built upon bidirectional video models and can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: generating individual shots separately and subsequently composing them
(
He et al., 2023
;
Xie et al., 2024
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Long et al., 2024
)
, or directly modeling multi-shot sequences in an end-to-end manner
(
Guo et al., 2025b
;
Qi et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2026b
;
Wu et al., 2026a
;
Meng et al., 2026b
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Jia et al., 2026
)
. In autoregressive video generation, several methods enable dynamic content control by updating prompts during streaming synthesis, but primarily focus on single-shot generation
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Ji et al., 2025
)
. More recently, autoregressive approaches have begun to explore multi-shot generation. ShotStream
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
reformulates the problem as next-shot generation, while CausalCine introduces content-aware memory routing for accessing historical information
(
Meng et al., 2026a
)
. Nevertheless, their memory retrieval remains relatively coarse-grained, limiting the effective use of long-term historical information.
3
Method
In this section, we present the methodology and insights of CineMem. After introducing the preliminaries in Section

3.3
. Guided by these insights, Sections
3.4
and
3.5
present our online-clustered KV cache and query-adaptive memory retrieval mechanism. Figure

Long-Horizon Autoregressive Adaptation

Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. 3.3
Memory Selection in Attention Module
Based on the full-memory model, we analyze memory-access patterns during autoregressive rollout to guide the design of a fine-grained retrieval mechanism that best matches the model’s intrinsic selection behavior under full-memory attention. While conventional retrieval schemes typically define the retrieval unit at the chunk-to-frame level, we revisit the fundamental token-to-token memory selection process inherent in attention, which motivates our fine-grained retrieval design. For each generated chunk, memory selection is essentially the process by which current tokens, serving as queries, select relevant historical memory tokens through their keys and values.
For a query, highly attended keys receive higher attention probabilities, which mathematically correspond to larger normalized dot-product similarities. We therefore use this signal to study token-wise selection relationships and reveal the underlying memory-selection patterns.
Memory structure.
Efficient retrieval requires grouping, since treating each token as a separate group reduces retrieval to full-memory attention. Frame-level retrieval instead treats each frame as a group, implicitly assuming stronger correlations among tokens within the same frame. However, this assumption may not always hold, especially when a frame contains diverse content. To investigate this, we cluster the full-memory tokens and visualize the results in Figure
4(a)
. Clear clustering patterns emerge: highly similar tokens tend to form cross-frame clusters, while tokens within each cluster exhibit semantic consistency to some extent. We also observe stronger correlations among tokens from the first frame than among those from other frames, consistent with prior findings on the importance of the first latent sink
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
. These observations motivate grouping memory by token similarity rather than frame membership.
This is because frame-based grouping may introduce redundant information, as retrieving a group due to a few highly relevant tokens also includes many weakly related ones. Moreover, using a single centroid to represent semantically diverse tokens from the same frames can weaken their semantics and reduce retrieval precision.
Heterogeneous memory selection.
Turning to the query side, each query in attention independently computes its similarity to all keys, naturally motivating query-level retrieval.
In practice, different queries and attention heads attend to distinct memory tokens.
We visualize these selection patterns in Figure
4(b)
and observe clear heterogeneity across queries and heads. Even when each query-head pair selects only the top 30% most relevant memory tokens, their overall memory receptive field covers nearly the full memory, which indicates the necessity of query-wise and head-wise retrieval.
(a)
Clustering of full-memory tokens and representative patterns of selected clusters.
(b)
Heatmap of query-head memory preferences and memory coverage.
Figure 4:
Intrinsic memory-selection patterns under the full-memory setting.
Memory tokens exhibit semantically meaningful clustering structures, while different query-head pairs show distinct preferences over memory tokens. Although each query-head pair selects a subset of the most relevant tokens, their union covers nearly the entire memory. See Appendix
A
for more details.
3.4
Online Clustered KV Cache
To enable fine-grained memory grouping, we introduce an online cluster KV cache. During autoregressive rollout, memory tokens are dynamically grouped according to their cosine similarity, such that semantically related tokens are assigned to the same cluster.
This design leverages the semantic coherence within each cluster: tokens relevant to the same query are likely to share similar semantic information, reducing redundant retrieval while improving retrieval effectiveness.
To support fine-grained query-level retrieval, clustering is performed independently for each attention head.
We retain the first and latest chunks as memory anchors.

Query-level Retrieval
Considering the heterogeneous memory selection patterns discussed in Section
3.3
, we design a query-level retrieval mechanism, specifically query-wise and head-wise retrieval, for fine-grained memory access.
Conventional retrieval shares a single historical memory subset across all queries, which cannot capture diverse query and head preferences, causing redundant retrieval of irrelevant tokens and missing relevant historical information.
This motivates a more fine-grained retrieval unit. Instead of sharing, we allow each query-head pair to independently select relevant memory from the full history. Combined with the clustered KV cache in Section
3.4
, this design enables query-specific access to relevant memory clusters while maintaining the same retrieval budget, substantially expanding effective memory access and approximating full-memory attention under a constrained memory budget.

4.2
Evaluation and Results

Metrics.
To comprehensively evaluate streaming multi-shot video generation, we construct an evaluation set of 100 prompts and establish an evaluation protocol covering video-level, intra-shot-level, and inter-shot-level metrics. Video-level metrics assess fundamental properties of generated videos, including visual aesthetics
(
LAION-AI, 2022
)
, transition control
(
Soucek and Lokoc, 2024
)
, and text alignment
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, while intra-shot metrics
(
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Fu et al., 2023
)
evaluate consistency within individual shots. More importantly, inter-shot evaluation measures semantic consistency across shot transitions.
However, existing similarity-based inter-shot metrics suffer from an inherent ambiguity: a high similarity score may indicate either strong transition consistency or simply the absence of a meaningful transition. Consequently, models with weak transition control may receive deceptively high consistency scores.
To address this issue, we introduce a VLM-based metric
(
Achiam et al., 2023
)
, the Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score (PTCS), as illustrated in Figure
6
. PTCS rewards transitions only when they are successfully executed while preserving the required semantic consistency.
PTCS consists of two complementary components: Prompt-conditioned Continuity Preservation (PCP) and Prompt-conditioned Transition Alignment (PTA). Given a hierarchical prompt, we first construct a semantic state graph to identify the semantic elements that should remain unchanged and those expected to change across the transition. PCP measures whether the required elements are consistently preserved before and after the transition, whereas PTA evaluates whether the intended changes, such as modifications in focal subjects or camera configurations, are correctly realized. For each transition, PTCS is computed as the geometric mean of PCP and PTA and then averaged over the evaluation set. By jointly evaluating unchanged elements and intended changes, PTCS provides a more direct and faithful assessment of inter-shot consistency.

Figure
5

(
Yesiltepe et al., 2026
;
Ji et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026

(

(

Notably, we do not include CausalCine
(

Strong bidirectional baselines
(

Meng et al., 2026b

In contrast, CineMem generates stable multi-shot videos in an autoregressive setting while faithfully following the prescribed transitions and maintaining cross-shot consistency, including challenging revisitation scenarios.
Quantitative Results.
Table
2
reports the quantitative comparison on our evaluation set. CineMem achieves strong performance across video-level quality and intra-shot consistency metrics, demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality videos while maintaining stable shot-level content. For inter-shot evaluation, CineMem achieves the best performance on PTCS, which jointly considers unchanged elements and intended changes during shot transitions. Notably, models with high similarity-based inter-shot scores or PCP values often exhibit limited transition control, while models specifically designed for multi-shot generation may still receive relatively low scores on these metrics. This indicates that similarity-based or preservation-only metrics can overestimate inter-shot consistency when the intended transition is not properly realized. By explicitly considering both preserved and changing elements specified in the prompt, PTCS provides a more faithful evaluation of transition quality. Finally, CineMem achieves superior PTCS performance and even surpasses larger bidirectional models with substantially more parameters.
4.3
Ablation Study
To validate the effectiveness of different design choices in CineMem, we conduct ablation studies from three perspectives, with results summarized in Table
3
.
Training Strategy.
In Section
3.2
, we introduce resampled history context to simulate autoregressive error accumulation during training. Compared with the standard teacher-forcing strategy, resampling context training provides more consistent training conditions with autoregressive inference and achieves superior performance across different metrics, especially in long-horizon consistency.
Retrieval Strategy.
We analyze different retrieval strategies introduced in Sections
3.4
and
3.5
under a plug-in setting. Specifically, we compare our clustered KV cache and query-wise retrieval with frame-level grouping and shared retrieval. To isolate the effect of retrieval design, we directly apply different strategies to the adapted base model without additional training. As shown, query-wise retrieval consistently improves performance under both frame-level and clustered memory organization, demonstrating the importance of fine-grained memory access. Moreover, clustered KV cache further improves transition quality and inter-shot consistency over frame-level grouping, validating the effectiveness of semantic-based memory organization. Notably, without additional training, our retrieval strategy achieves comparable performance to full-memory attention while obtaining higher inter-shot consistency, demonstrating its effectiveness under a constrained memory budget.
Query-level Retrieval Variant.
We investigate a query grouping variant of our retrieval mechanism. Instead of performing independent retrieval for each query, this variant recursively partitions queries into groups according to their spatial and semantic similarity using an adaptive tree structure and shares retrieved memory within each group.
Although query grouping provides an effective approximation by exploiting query similarity, it remains slightly inferior to fully query-wise retrieval, further validating the importance of fine-grained query retrieval.
5
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduce CineMem, a fine-grained memory retrieval framework for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Combining an online clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval, CineMem enables broader historical access and improves long-range consistency in revisitation scenarios. We develop an autoregressive adaptation framework with resampled context to analyze intrinsic memory-access patterns, revealing semantic clustering among memory tokens and heterogeneous query-head preferences that motivate our design. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
Our results highlight the importance of fine-grained memory modeling for autoregressive video generation. Rather than relying only on recent frames, autoregressive models should exploit information throughout history. Advances in memory organization and retrieval will enable scalable long-horizon video generation.

A.2
Pre-RoPE Clustering vs. Post-RoPE Clustering
Figure 10:
Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE.
Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.
In Section
3.4
, we introduce an online clustering mechanism to organize memory tokens into semantic groups rather than predefined frame-based partitions. In practice, before entering each transformer block, token representations are augmented with positional encoding. Our clustering and retrieval operations are therefore performed before RoPE (Pre-RoPE). This design choice is motivated by the observation that positional encoding introduces strong absolute position information into token representations, which can obscure semantic similarity and weaken semantic clustering structures.
In fact, the visualization in Figure
4(a)
is obtained using token representations before positional encoding. To further investigate this effect, Figure
10
presents representative clustering results before and after applying RoPE. We observe that RoPE-transformed tokens exhibit stronger position-dependent similarity patterns, while the semantic grouping structure becomes less apparent. Therefore, performing clustering and retrieval after positional encoding may bias memory organization toward positional grouping and degrade into a behavior similar to frame-level partitioning, limiting the benefits of semantic-aware memory organization. These observations support our choice of conducting clustering and retrieval in the Pre-RoPE space.

Appendix C
Analysis of Efficiency
In this section, we analyze the efficiency of CineMem and compare it
with two representative memory access strategies. Full-history attention is
considered as an upper bound in terms of memory availability, as it provides
access to the complete historical context without retrieval constraints.
Meanwhile, frame-group retrieval serves as an efficient coarse-grained
baseline by selecting a fixed number of historical frames with shared routing.
In contrast, CineMem performs fine-grained query-head-wise retrieval over
online-clustered memory, aiming to achieve a better balance between retrieval
granularity and computational cost.
We evaluate these strategies from both theoretical and practical perspectives.

overhead, while the practical evaluation measures actual inference efficiency.

D.2
The effectiveness of Prompt-conditioned Transition-Consistency Score
As discussed in Section
4.2
, conventional similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics evaluate transitions by measuring feature similarity between frames from different shots. However, such metrics inherently favor cases where adjacent shots exhibit limited visual changes, assigning high consistency scores even when the intended transition is not successfully realized. This limitation explains why some methods can achieve high inter-shot consistency scores while exhibiting poor transition control. These observations motivate our design of PTCS, which explicitly considers both semantic preservation and prompt-specified transition changes. Given that PTCS serves as a key metric for evaluating the effectiveness of CineMem, we further analyze its validity in this section.
We visualize several multi-shot examples with PTCS evaluations in Figure
13
. Qualitatively, PCP successfully reflects transitions where semantic consistency is violated, while PTA captures both missing transitions, where the intended shot change is not realized, and unexpected changes introduced during transitions, including inconsistencies in style, character identity, spatial relationships, or even subtle local details. By jointly considering these two complementary aspects, PTCS provides scores that better align with the desired properties of shot transitions. In contrast, similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics may produce misleading evaluations: when the visual composition remains similar, they can assign high scores despite missing or incorrect transitions, while failing to distinguish valid and invalid transitions under substantial compositional changes.
Figure 13:
Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics.
The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.
To complement the quantitative evaluation, we conduct a user study to investigate whether PTCS aligns with human perception of inter-shot consistency. Specifically, we select 30 prompts for evaluation, and participants rate each generated video on a scale from 1 to 5 from three perspectives: overall video quality, intra-shot consistency, and inter-shot consistency. The mean opinion scores (MOS) are summarized in Table
4
.
As shown, the human evaluation results are consistent with the trends observed in PTCS. Methods with higher PTCS scores generally receive higher inter-shot consistency ratings from human participants, while models that achieve high similarity-based consistency scores but fail to perform the intended transitions receive substantially lower human scores. This agreement indicates that PTCS better captures human-perceived transition consistency by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes. Furthermore, CineMem achieves the highest MOS in inter-shot consistency and competitive overall video quality, demonstrating its ability to generate coherent multi-shot videos with controllable transitions.

. CineMem achieves the highest PTCS across all shot-count groups, while also consistently obtaining the strongest transition control and intra-shot consistency. Notably, its advantage is preserved for prompts containing six to seven shots, where autoregressive error accumulation and long-range dependency modeling become more challenging. This result indicates that our memory retrieval mechanism remains effective as the generation horizon increases.
Revisit distance.
Finally, Table
7
analyzes performance with respect to revisit distance, which directly reflects the temporal range over which previously generated content needs to be recalled.
CineMem maintains strong performance across all distance ranges and achieves the highest PTCS for the longest revisit range of 13-18 chunks.
It also consistently achieves the best transition control and intra-shot consistency across different revisit distances. These results further support the effectiveness of our fine-grained memory retrieval in preserving long-range historical information and maintaining consistency when previously observed content reappears after a long temporal interval.

Figure 17:
Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.
To further investigate the long-horizon generation capability of CineMem, we provide additional qualitative results on 30-second videos. As shown in Figure
17
, CineMem can continuously extend autoregressive generation while maintaining coherent visual content and long-range consistency across multiple shot transitions. These results highlight the potential of fine-grained memory retrieval for enabling more scalable autoregressive video generation over extended durations.
Appendix F
Limitation and Failure Case
Limitations.
Due to limited computational resources, our experiments are conducted on a relatively small-scale autoregressive backbone with a limited amount of training data for adapting a bidirectional model into a long-horizon autoregressive generator. Consequently, the visual quality of generated videos may lag behind that of large-scale state-of-the-art diffusion models with substantially larger model capacity and training data. Nevertheless, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed memory retrieval framework and reveal meaningful insights into memory utilization in autoregressive diffusion models. We expect that the proposed approach can further benefit from larger-scale models and datasets.
Figure 18:
A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios.
Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.
Failure Cases.
Our memory retrieval mechanism aims to approximate the intrinsic full-memory access pattern under a constrained memory budget by enabling more effective historical information retrieval. However, it still struggles in scenarios requiring complex multi-entity reasoning, as illustrated in Figure
18
. In the presented example, the generated video exhibits issues such as missing characters and inconsistent details across shot transitions.
Such failures are particularly challenging for autoregressive generation. In this case, an early chunk introduces four characters through its prompt, while a later chunk requires only three characters. The model must therefore generate a valid transition by adjusting the camera viewpoint while preserving the spatial relationships and identities established in previous shots. However, the earlier chunks are generated without knowledge of future shot requirements, making such coordinated transitions inherently difficult, especially when the initial composition does not provide sufficient flexibility.
Therefore, multi-entity scenarios with complex shot transitions remain challenging even for full-memory autoregressive generation or bidirectional models, as they require reasoning beyond historical information retrieval. While our proposed memory mechanism improves access to relevant historical content and achieves promising results on certain multi-entity scenarios (see supplementary project page), handling complex entity interactions remains an important direction for future work.
Appendix G
Future Work
Beyond the proposed online clustered KV cache and query-adaptive retrieval framework, several directions remain open for future exploration. For memory organization, more effective clustering strategies could further improve retrieval quality. Meanwhile, exploiting the shared retrieval patterns among queries may provide more efficient alternatives to fully query-wise and head-wise retrieval, as explored by the query-group variant in Section
4.3
. These directions may enable more scalable and efficient memory mechanisms for autoregressive video generation.
From the perspective of autoregressive video generation, integrating entity-aware or structure-aware memory retrieval could help address challenging multi-entity scenarios discussed in Section
F
. Furthermore, extending autoregressive generation to substantially longer horizons remains a promising direction toward more scalable long-form video synthesis.

article.headline: 细粒度记忆检索让自回归多镜头视频更连贯
article.lede: CineMem 把 KV cache 在线聚类，让每个 query-head 独立检索历史记忆，15 秒多镜头视频的 P
article.problem: 自回归视频生成靠记忆检索维持长程依赖，多镜头场景尤其需要在镜头切换带来的大幅视觉变化下保持语义连续。已有方法多在帧级别检索，且所有 query token 共享同一份历史上下文，忽略了不同 query 与注意力头对历史信息需求的异质性，造成检索冗余和历史记忆利用率低。
article.method: 作者先把双向视频模型经多阶段适配转为逐 chunk 的自回归多镜头生成器，并用重采样上下文训练缓解长程 rollout 的误差累积；在此基础上分析全记忆注意力下的 token 级记忆选择模式，发现历史 token 呈现跨帧的语义聚类结构，且各 query-head 的偏好差异明显。据此提出在线聚类 KV cache（按余弦相似度分组，用分裂/合并与负载惩罚保持簇均衡）和 query 级检索，每个 query-head 对独立选取最相关的簇。
article.results: 模型基于 Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B、用 16 张 NVIDIA H200 训练，在 15 秒多镜头视频上 PTCS 为 0.8242，高于 MultiShotMaster 的 0.7984 和 HoloCine 的 0.7385；过渡控制 0.9960、镜头内一致性 0.9716。理论效率上，聚类检索（K=28、S=1024）总 FLOPs 为 638.82 T，略低于帧级检索（K=20）的 650.02 T，明显低于全历史的 932.56 T。30 人评分实验（原文为 30 条 prompt 的用户研究）中，镜头间一致性均分 4.37±0.31（5 分制）。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明记忆检索的粒度应当对齐注意力本身的选择行为，而非沿用固定的帧级分组，这为在固定记忆预算下扩展自回归长视频生成提供了可复用的设计思路。
article.limitations: 实验基于 1.3B 的小规模骨干和有限训练数据，作者承认生成画质可能落后于大规模扩散模型；复杂多实体镜头切换仍会失败，例如角色消失和细节不一致，且 CausalCine 权重未公开，未能直接对比。
article.figure_caption_zh: CineMem 框架总览：多阶段适配把双向模型转为带记忆检索的自回归多镜头生成器，推理时每个 query-head 从首 chunk、相邻 chunk 和在线聚类检索出的候选簇中取记忆，训练时用重采样真值帧构造记忆输入以缓解误差累积。

figure.caption: {Our memory retrieval framework.} Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

page_papers.title: Q-Learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
page_papers.abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector--Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector--Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic's value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM's gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.

Introduction
Flow policies represent rich and multimodal action distributions, and they have become a common

(

;

)
.

against a learned action-value function
(

;

)
.
However, fine-tuning a flow policy to maximize a learned value function is not a trivial problem because of its multiple sampling procedure
(
Park et al., 2025b
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. Most methods therefore freeze the policy and work outside it, adding a separately learned residual to the actions it produces
(
Dong et al., 2026b
;
Xiao et al., 2026
)
or learning with RL which input noise to feed the frozen policy
(
Wagenmaker et al., 2025
)
, which leaves the pretrained policy intact during training. The improvement then rests on a separately learned component rather than on the generative model itself, so it is either bounded by what the frozen policy can express or forfeits the expressiveness of the flow policy. On the other hand, adjoint matching
(
Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025
;
Li and Levine, 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026c
)
provides a theoretically grounded alternative for directly updating the flow model with value functions. It propagates value information from the final action back to each flow step to guide the model’s updates. However, this requires a vector–Jacobian product through the policy at every step, so the computational cost grows with the number of flow steps and policy size.
In this work, we observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of a pretrained flow policy concentrates on its diagonal (
Figure
2
). This suggests that the vector–Jacobian product adjoint matching
pays for at every flow step may not be necessary. Inspired by this finding, we approximate the
Jacobian by a scalar multiple of the identity, under which the propagation admits a closed form that
scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time (
Proposition
1
). We call this
the scalar adjoint. It needs a single critic gradient at the sampled action and no vector–Jacobian
product through the policy, and
Section
4.2
shows that it preserves the qualitative trends
of the exact propagation.
We further find that the effectiveness of the scalar adjoint depends on the value-learning scheme. We investigate this dependence and identify the critic’s value at policy-generated actions as particularly important. Our regularization ablations isolate this dependency. Methods that regulate the
critic at these actions improve performance, while methods that act only on dataset
(
Kostrikov et al., 2022
)
or action distance
(
Tarasov et al., 2023
)
provide little improvement
(
Section
4.3
). Based on these findings, we propose
Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching
(SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at policy-generated actions.

(

)

Contributions.
We highlight the key contributions of our paper below:
•
We introduce SQAM, an off-policy fine-tuning algorithm for flow policies that reduces the
compute cost of adjoint matching by replacing its per-step vector–Jacobian products with the
closed-form scalar adjoint.
•
We show that the scalar adjoint makes performance depend on the value learning scheme, and we
find that what matters is controlling the critic’s value at the actions the current policy generates.
•
SQAM’s gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where it exceeds the
strongest baseline by
18
18
to
35
35
percentage points in success rate, and it extends to fine-tuning a
pretrained vision-language-action policy on a real robot.
