Comparison between Adjoints
Figure
4
explains why the scalar adjoint works even though it approximates the exact
adjoint. The approximation preserves the two properties the update relies on. In magnitude, both
adjoints contract in the same way as the flow time approaches zero, so the regression target in
Equation
2
has a similar magnitude at each flow step under either adjoint. In direction, the scalar
adjoint stays positively aligned with the exact adjoint at every flow time. These two properties allow
the scalar adjoint to stand in for the exact adjoint, but they do not make the two identical. The angle
between them is larger on the two manipulation domains than on the two locomotion domains, and these
are exactly the domains where the scalar adjoint alone underperforms (
Section
3.2
). Since
the scalar adjoint relies directly on the critic’s gradient, this correspondence led us to examine the
role of the value learning scheme in this framework, which
Section
4.3
presents.

Related work
Propagating value to intermediate flow steps.
A flow policy generates its action over many flow
steps, while the critic evaluates only the final action. Using the critic to steer the flow therefore requires propagating its value to each intermediate step, and existing methods differ mainly in how they do
so
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
. The most common approach evaluates the critic at a
Tweedie posterior estimate of the final action, and it is used for guidance at test
time
(
Chung et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2025
;
Zhou et al., 2026
)
.
Another line avoids the approximation and feeds the intermediate action to the critic directly, either
by matching the policy’s score to the critic’s action gradient at the intermediate
action
(
Psenka et al., 2024
)
or by learning a separate value at each noise
level
(
Oberai et al., 2026
;
Doo et al., 2026
)
. Adjoint
matching
(
Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025
;
Li and Levine, 2026
;
Dong et al., 2026c
;
Bergmeister et al., 2026
)
gives a theoretically
grounded answer, propagating the value gradient back to each flow step through the lean adjoint ODE.
For test-time guidance rather than fine-tuning, dropping the Jacobian has also been found to outperform
backpropagating through the exact Jacobian
(
Zhou et al., 2026
)
.
Critic regularization.
Many value learning schemes regularize the critic, and they differ
in where the regularization acts. CQL penalizes the critic’s value at the actions the policy prefers relative to the data
(
Kumar et al., 2020
)
, IQL fits a state value by expectile regression and trains the critic by TD regression toward it, using only dataset actions
(
Kostrikov et al., 2022
)
, and ReBRAC subtracts an action-distance penalty from the bootstrap target
(
Tarasov et al., 2023
)
. Fisher-BRC penalizes the action
gradient of the critic’s offset from a behavior model
(
Kostrikov et al., 2021
)
, which is close to the gradient-norm penalty we compare in
Section
4.3
, and Cal-QL calibrates the critic against a reference policy for offline-to-online fine-tuning
(
Nakamoto et al., 2023
)
.
Offline-to-online RL.
Pretraining a policy and a critic on offline data and then fine-tuning
them online is a standard recipe for sample-efficient
RL
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Hester et al., 2018
;
Hu et al., 2024
;
Kostrikov et al., 2022
;
Kumar et al., 2020
;
Lei et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2024
;
Nair et al., 2021
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Rajeswaran et al., 2018
;
Vecerik et al., 2018
)
.
A central challenge is the distribution shift at the transition, which destabilizes the value
function and can make the policy forget what it learned
offline
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Wołczyk et al., 2024
)
.
6
Conclusion
We introduced SQAM, which fine-tunes flow policies with off-policy RL without a vector–Jacobian
product through the policy. Motivated by the diagonal structure of the batch-averaged velocity
Jacobian, it replaces the exact adjoint with a closed-form scalar adjoint and pairs it with a value
penalty at the policy-generated actions. SQAM improves most on the four hardest OGBench domains
and extends to a vision-language-action policy on a real robot.
Our results also suggest a broader point. A rough approximation of the adjoint suffices, while the
value learning scheme largely determines how well it performs. The bottleneck of
off-policy RL with flow policies may therefore lie less in the policy update than in the critic. We
hope this encourages further work on value learning for flow policies.

Ethics statement
This work fine-tunes robot policies with reinforcement learning in simulation and on a robot in a
controlled laboratory setting. The real-robot experiments involve no human subjects and no personal
data, and an operator supervised the robot throughout. As with any method that improves a policy
against a learned value function, deployment beyond a supervised setting calls for the usual
safeguards.
AI use statement
We used generative AI tools to assist with writing, editing, and routine coding and plotting. We did
not use them to generate research ideas, experimental results, or claims. The authors reviewed all

Appendix E
Real-robot experiments: RB-Y1 with Wuji Hand 2
This appendix documents the real-robot experiments on a dual-arm RB-Y1
humanoid
(
Rainbow Robotics, 2024
)
equipped with two Wuji Hand 2 dexterous hands
(
Wuji Technology, 2025
)
. For
each of three manipulation tasks we follow the same pipeline: (i) behavior cloning (BC) of a
vision-language-action base policy on teleoperated demonstrations, (ii) collection of 30 rollout
episodes of the BC policy on the robot, (iii) offline RL for 15K steps on the demonstrations plus these
30 BC rollout episodes, (iv) online RL for a further 10K steps that continues from the offline
checkpoint while the robot collects new episodes, and (v) a 30-episode evaluation of every checkpoint.
The same protocol is run for our method (SQAM) and for the EXPO-FT
baseline
(
Dong et al., 2026a
)
.
E.1
Platform, observations and actions
Figure 9
:
Hardware setup: RB-Y1 humanoid with a Wuji Hand 2 on each wrist
and a head-mounted ZED Mini stereo camera.
Hardware.
We use a Rainbow Robotics RB-Y1
(
Rainbow Robotics, 2024
)
dual-arm humanoid with a 20-DoF Wuji
Hand 2
(
Wuji Technology, 2025
)
mounted on each wrist. The experiments use 54 of its degrees of freedom, the two 7-DoF arms and the
two 20-DoF hands, for bimanual tabletop manipulation. The torso and neck stay at fixed joint positions, and
the mobile base is not used. A single Stereolabs ZED Mini stereo camera
(
Stereolabs, 2018
)
mounted on the
head provides the visual input (
Figure
9
).
Observation space.
At every policy query the observation has three parts. The first is two ego-centric RGB images, the
left and right views of the ZED Mini stereo pair, captured at 30 Hz and resized to
192
×
320
192\times 320
. The
second is a 62-dimensional proprioceptive vector of measured joint positions. The third is the task instruction
(
Table
6
).
Action space.
Actions are absolute joint-position targets. The base policy predicts an action chunk of 24 steps, and
its first 16 steps are executed. RL acts only on these
16
16
executed steps and on the 54 arm and
hand joints. SQAM optimizes this sub-chunk by
updating the action head of the base policy, whereas EXPO-FT keeps the base policy frozen and adds a
residual to it through its edit policy.
Control loop.
The robot runs at a nominal control rate of 30 Hz and executes the policy synchronously. At each
policy query the current observation is sent to the actor and the returned 16 step chunk of
joint-position targets is executed step by step. A new observation is taken and the next chunk is
requested only after the chunk has been completed.

Appendix H
Limitations and future work
We see three directions that this work leaves open.
Value learning for flow policies.
Our results suggest that the value learning scheme largely
determines how well the scalar adjoint performs, and SQAM addresses this with a value penalty added
to a standard critic. A value learning method designed for flow policies from the ground up may make
this dependence more reliable than a penalty on top of an existing critic.
Multi-task fine-tuning.
Updating the generative policy itself, rather than a separately
learned component, should matter most when a single policy serves many tasks. Our real-robot experiments
fine-tune the policy on each task separately. Fine-tuning a single policy across many tasks, as in
Wang et al. (2026)
, would test this benefit more directly.
Why the Jacobian concentrates on its diagonal.
We observe that the batch-averaged velocity
Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal on every domain we measured, but we
do not explain why. A theoretical analysis of when this structure arises would clarify the conditions
under which the scalar adjoint applies.

article.headline: 用标量伴随替代雅可比积，加速流策略Q学习
article.lede: 预训练流策略的批平均速度雅可比近似对角占优，作者据此给出闭式标量伴随，省去逐步向量–雅可比积，并在OGBench与真机上
article.problem: 用离策略RL微调流策略时，评价函数只告诉最终动作好不好，需要把这一价值信息回传到每个流步。伴随匹配通过积分伴随ODE做到这一点，但每个流步都要对策略做一次向量–雅可比积，开销随流步数和策略规模增长，难以扩展到大型预训练策略。
article.method: 作者观察到预训练流策略的批平均速度雅可比集中在对角线上，于是把雅可比近似为标量的单位阵倍数，得到闭式解：每个流步的伴随只是最终动作处评价函数梯度乘以流时间τ，无需任何向量–雅可比积，称为标量伴随。由于该更新直接依赖策略自己生成的动作处的评价梯度，他们再加一项只在该动作上生效的价值惩罚（相对数据集动作的价值之差），构成SQAM。
article.results: 在OGBench 50个任务、8个种子的离线1M步评测中，SQAM总体成功率75%，最强基线TRQAM为68%；增益集中在四个最难的域，分别比各域最强基线高21、18、22、35个百分点，其中cube-quadruple上最强基线为19%、SQAM为54%。真实双臂机器人三个任务各30次留出评估：监督微调为15/30、7/30、4/30，SQAM离线转在线后为25/30、15/30、13/30。更新开销方面，论文报告精确伴随在每种策略宽度下都约慢一半，且差距随流步数增加而扩大（正文未给出具体秒数）。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明流策略的伴随不必逐步反传雅可比，一个粗糙的标量近似就够用；作者的结论是瓶颈更多在评价函数的学习方式，而不在策略更新本身，这为流策略的离策略RL指出了一个更廉价的改进方向。
article.limitations: 标量伴随建立在“批平均速度雅可比对角占优”这一经验观察上，作者明确表示并未解释该结构为何出现；在两个操作域上标量伴随与精确伴随的夹角更大，单独使用会掉点，必须靠价值惩罚补救，而cube-double上该惩罚反而降低离线成功率因此被关闭。真实机器人实验每任务仅30次评估且各任务单独微调，无法说明多任务共享一个策略时的收益；另外EXPO-FT基线在作者修改过的协议下运行，对比并非原样复现。

page_papers.title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
page_papers.abstract: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase

Abstract
Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input.
Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject’s unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a
fully automated
data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct
Showcase-4K
, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across
88
88
trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and
ShowcaseBench
, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video.
Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page:
justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase

1
Introduction
Subject-to-video (S2V) generation aims to create videos of a specified subject from reference images while preserving its appearance across time and viewpoints.
Recent video diffusion models generate photorealistic videos from text or a single image
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Kong et al., 2024
;
Wan Team, 2025
;
Brooks et al., 2024
)
, and S2V methods use reference images to preserve subject identity in generated videos
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Jiang et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2025
)
.
However, most S2V methods condition on a single reference image, which provides appearance information only for the visible surfaces and leaves other regions unconstrained.
As the camera reveals previously unseen sides, generated videos may exhibit inconsistent geometry and appearance, which can lead to changes in silhouette, structure, and surface details.
These ambiguities motivate the use of multiple reference views and explicit geometric information. The main difficulty is geometric rather than purely photometric since the model must infer 3D structure that is absent from the input.
Recent methods incorporate multiple reference views into S2V generation.
MV-S2V
(
Song et al., 2026
)
trains a feed-forward model using generated multi-view videos, whereas 3DreamBooth
(
Ko et al., 2026
)
performs per-subject optimization using static multi-view images.
These efforts motivate two complementary directions: training on geometrically consistent viewpoint changes and providing explicit 3D geometry during generation. For the latter, recent feed-forward reconstruction methods can recover 3D geometry from a few uncalibrated images
(
Wang et al., 2024a
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2026
)
, making explicit geometry available from the same sparse references used at inference.
We present
OmniShowcase
(Figure
), a framework that combines an automated data synthesis pipeline with geometry-aware conditioning.
The pipeline renders multi-view videos from 3D assets and composites them into realistic scenes.
For conditioning, we reconstruct geometry from the reference views and render a surface-normal sequence using the same procedure during training and inference.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce an automated data synthesis pipeline that renders subject views from 3D assets and composites them into realistic scenes to construct training videos.
•
We present
Showcase-4K
, a dataset of 4,000 videos paired with diverse source meshes, camera trajectories, reference images, and surface-normal sequences, along with
ShowcaseBench
, a held-out benchmark with ground-truth geometry and camera parameters for evaluating subject consistency across viewpoints. We will publicly release
Showcase-4K
,
ShowcaseBench
, and the associated data-synthesis code.
•
We propose a geometry-aware in-context conditioning mechanism that uses reference images and a reconstructed surface-normal sequence to guide video generation without requiring frame-wise alignment between the normal and target sequences.
•
We evaluate our method against single- and multi-view S2V baselines on synthetic and real-world subjects, achieving state-of-the-art performance in subject identity preservation and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality.
2
Related Work
2.1
Video Generation Diffusion Models
Diffusion models
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Rombach et al., 2022
)
are the dominant approach to visual content synthesis, and the shift from convolutional U-Nets to transformer denoisers
(
Peebles and Xie, 2023
)
with rectified-flow training
(
Esser et al., 2024
)
improved their scalability and sample quality. These advances carried over to video. Early video models extended pretrained image backbones with temporal layers
(
Singer et al., 2023
;
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Guo et al., 2024
)
; more recent systems use large diffusion transformers trained on web-scale corpora and generate high-resolution clips of steadily increasing length
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Kong et al., 2024
;
Wan Team, 2025
;
Brooks et al., 2024
)
. Image-to-video (I2V) variants add a starting frame as a condition, giving coarse control over appearance. Our framework builds on a pretrained I2V diffusion transformer and adapts it through low-rank tuning
(
Hu et al., 2022
)
.
2.2
3D Generation and Novel View Synthesis
Representing and rendering 3D content from images has been studied through neural fields
(
Mildenhall et al., 2020
)
and point-based splatting
(
Kerbl et al., 2023
)
. To synthesize unseen viewpoints without per-scene reconstruction, one line of work distills 2D diffusion priors into multi-view-consistent generators: image-conditioned models such as
Liu et al. (2023)
hallucinate novel views of an object, and multi-view diffusion models
(
Shi et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2024b
;
Voleti et al., 2024
)
jointly denoise several views to enforce cross-view coherence. These methods are mostly confined to isolated objects against clean backgrounds and do not model scene-level dynamics. In parallel, feed-forward geometry estimators build on monocular depth foundation models
(
Yang et al., 2024
)
and recover dense 3D structure from sparse, uncalibrated images in a single pass
(
Wang et al., 2024a
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2026
)
. This makes it practical to derive explicit geometry from multi-view reference images. We use this capability to supplement coarse 3D information of unseen views as a geometry cue.

2.3
Subject-Driven Video Generation
Personalizing generative models to a user-specified subject originates in the image domain, through identifier-based personalization
(
Ruiz et al., 2023
;
Gal et al., 2023
;
Kumari et al., 2023
)
and later encoder- or adapter-based conditioning that injects reference features without test-time optimization
(
Ye et al., 2023
;
Tan et al., 2025
)
. These ideas carried over to video, where subject-to-video (S2V) methods keep a reference identity stable throughout a generated clip. Optimization- and adapter-based approaches
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Wei et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2024
;
Yuan et al., 2025
)
preserve identity over time, and reference-conditioned frameworks
(
Liu et al., 2025
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Jiang et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
extend this to multiple subjects and flexible prompts. These methods primarily encode the subject through 2D appearance features, leaving viewpoints not covered by the reference unconstrained.
Closest to our setting are recent attempts to move beyond single-view conditioning. MV-S2V
(
Song et al., 2026
)
feeds multiple reference views into a video diffusion transformer and uses a shifted positional-encoding scheme to distinguish different views of the same subject. The references provide appearance information from several viewpoints, but do not explicitly encode the 3D surface structure underlying those views. Its training videos for object-centric generation are produced by a camera-controllable video generator, so viewpoint variation is not explicitly tied to a shared 3D asset. 3DreamBooth
(
Ko et al., 2026
)
uses static multi-view images for subject-specific adaptation, preserving the pretrained model’s temporal behavior but requiring optimization for each new subject. In contrast, OmniShowcase reconstructs geometry from the input views at inference and uses it directly as a conditioning signal, without subject-specific optimization. Our training data are designed to satisfy three requirements: subject identity preservation, geometrically consistent viewpoint changes, and explicit geometry for conditioning. A camera-controllable video generator does not guarantee these properties, because unseen surfaces are still synthesized by the generative prior. Real multi-view capture satisfies the first two but
leaves the third to an estimator. Rendering from a 3D asset satisfies all three
at once, because one mesh under known cameras produces every frame. However, direct rendering produces clean-background videos. We therefore add a separate scene-compositing stage to introduce realistic backgrounds corresponding to the camera motion.

5
Conclusion
We present OmniShowcase, which pairs an automated pipeline that renders omnidirectional
videos from 3D assets with surface-normal turntable conditioning reconstructed from
the reference views, requiring no temporal alignment with generated frames. OmniShowcase leads single- and multi-view baselines on subject identity and cross-view 3D
consistency on both
ShowcaseBench
and NAVI. Two limitations remain: the
background sometimes looks synthetic, and subjects that are not rigid across the four
references are not handled (Figure
, Appendix
).
We leave both to future work. We will release the data, benchmark, and code.
AI use statement
In the preparation of this work, we used LLMs to polish the text, including
grammar checking and phrase refinement, and to polish figure illustrations.
Generative models are also components of the data pipeline itself, where a
vision-language model gates asset and clip curation, a large language model
writes the scene vocabulary, and a video-language model captions each clip.
Appendices
and
state where each one is used
and give every prompt and rubric verbatim. No LLM contributed to the research
ideas, the method design or the analysis.
We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of
generative AI.
Ethics statement
This work includes a human preference study with
44
44
participants, as described
in Appendix
. Every 3D asset comes
from Objaverse, the Digital Twin Catalog or Google Scanned Objects under a
Creative Commons license, and none carries a NoDerivatives term, so the renders
may be released. A small fraction is NonCommercial, which the research-only
release respects. We ship the license and the original author of every asset
with the renders, and ShareAlike terms carry over to the renders that inherit
them. An asset whose terms the release cannot meet is replaced by a pointer to
the original and the code that reproduces our renders from it.
Reproducibility statement
We release the sources of the data generation, the exact modules composing the
pipeline, the method architecture, the VLM and LLM rubrics used for curation,
and the prompts that generate the captions, all in
Appendices
and
. The evaluation protocol is
fixed as described in Section
, and where a method requires a
deviation we state it, such as extending Phantom and MAGREF from single-view to
multi-view input and appending the camera-trajectory sentence that our model
consumes. The data-generation code and the dataset will be released publicly.

Appendix H
Failure Analysis
Figure 13:
Failure cases.
Left two.
Prompt adherence and the
commanded rotation both hold, but the surroundings render with flat shading
and little material detail, so the clip reads as slightly synthetic.
Right two.
Both receive four reference views of a subject caught in
four different poses. The upper one is prompted in the usual static style
and settles into an averaged pose that matches none of the references, while
the lower one is asked to follow the motion in step with the orbit and
tangles in 3D at the transitions between poses.
Analysis.
The two columns of Figure
fail for unrelated reasons. The
synthetic look of the background follows from how the training targets are
built. Only the subject is physically rendered, and the scene around it is
painted in afterwards by a video inpainting model conditioned on the prompt. The corpus
therefore pairs a physically shaded subject with a generated background, and the
light transport between the two was never consistent to begin with. The model
reproduces that statistic, so the subject holds while the surroundings inherit
the flat shading and thin material detail of their source.
The dynamic case is a property of the conditioning signal itself. The
surface-normal turntable is obtained by lifting the reference views into a
single static reconstruction and rendering that one shape from every
viewpoint. When the four views catch the subject in four different poses, the
reconstruction fuses them into one rigid body that corresponds to no pose the
subject ever held, and the condition handed to the generator is a static
representation of a subject that is not static. Under a static prompt the model
follows that condition faithfully, which is exactly why the output settles into
an averaged pose. Asking for motion in the prompt does not repair it. The text
now requests a pose change that the geometry condition does not encode, so the
two disagree, and the model has to interpolate between reference poses in image
space with no 3D correspondence to guide it. The tangles appear at those
interpolated transitions. Handling non-rigid subjects would require a
conditioning representation that varies over the generated sequence, which we
leave to future work.

G1: Asset Quality
Prompt
You are an asset QC reviewer for a 3D object dataset. I show reference render views (view0-3) of ONE 3D asset plus its category label. The bar is "good enough to show in a paper/demo" - NOT perfection. Score 6 criteria 0/1.
Criteria
(score each 0/1 with a short justification)
(1)
realism
(read this as ASSET CRAFTSMANSHIP, not "is the subject a real thing"): judge how WELL-MADE the 3D asset is.
- Being a figurine, plush toy, statue, or a stylized animal model is NOT a defect - many categories are inherently toy-like, and a well-crafted figurine is a good asset.
- The decisive test is MATERIAL AND DETAIL: a good asset has believable surface material (fabric weave, fur, metal, glaze, wood grain, paint with wear) and real modelled detail.
- Score 0 (reject) when the asset is low-effort or cartoon-flat: emoji-like or clip-art forms with flat uniform fills, crude blocky/faceted shapes, plastic-smooth surfaces with no material character, sloppy or melted geometry, or a shape so distorted you cannot tell what it is.
- Score 1 (keep) when the craftsmanship is solid - including figurines, sculpted animals, plush toys and other inherently toy-like SUBJECTS - as long as the asset itself shows real material and detail.
- So: a finely sculpted animal figurine = 1; a flat cartoon hamburger or a toy-car with uniform purple plastic = 0.
(2)
geometry
proper, complete geometry - NO low-poly/blocky faceting, holes, broken or degenerate mesh.
(3)
no_base_plate
LOOK AT WHAT THE OBJECT RESTS ON.
- Score 0 if the asset includes any surface/terrain the object merely sits on and that would not be carried with it: a scanned ground or dirt patch, sand/water/grass terrain, baked-in cast-shadow geometry, a cake board, a serving plate, a square showroom slab, or a fragment of surrounding wall or floor.
- A base that is an INTEGRAL part of the real object - a trophy’s plinth, a flower pot, a lamp base, a statue’s pedestal, a vase foot - is NOT a violation (score 1).
(4)
texture
has a proper material/color appearance - NOT a blank untextured grey/white placeholder mesh or an unfinished flat single-color surface.
- Smooth surfaces are FINE (car paint, metal kettle, glass) - score 0 only when it looks like an untextured/unfinished mesh.
(5)
category_match
score 0 if (a) the object is plainly a DIFFERENT KIND of thing than the label, or (b) the asset is not ONE instance of it - multiple copies bundled together (three bats), or the object plus surrounding structure / a mini-scene (a phone booth attached to a wall slab).
- Judge kind at the COARSE level: close relatives, subspecies, breeds, and stylized variants COUNT AS A MATCH (a wolf-like dog for ’wolf’, any motorcycle for ’dirt_bike’, any van for ’minivan’).
- Do not fail on fine-grained species/model distinctions.
(6)
standing_thin
score 0 ONLY in the specific failure case where the object is a THIN, PLATE-LIKE OR LOOP-LIKE form standing ON ITS EDGE, so that rotating 90 degrees makes its silhouette collapse to a narrow sliver - a ring or coin balanced on edge, an upright bat or pole, a hanging necklace/chain.
- Compare the 4 views: if one view is a full shape and the neighbouring view is a thin line, score 0.
- If the object has real volume from every angle (an animal, a vehicle, a cup, a shoe, a fish lying horizontally), score 1 even if it is somewhat slender.
- When unsure, score 1.
Rule
qualified only if ALL 6 = 1.

Prompt
You are a QC reviewer for an object-centric TURNTABLE video dataset. The camera ORBITS a central object in a fixed scene.
I will give you, IN ORDER: (1) the REAL ORIGINAL object as reference photos (view0-3) - ground truth; (2) the GENERATED video frames to CHECK.
The CAMERA orbits while the object stays FIXED in the scene, so seeing different ANGLES of the SAME place is EXPECTED - do NOT penalize that. But if the background is nearly STATIC while the object SPINS in place, that is a turntable spin, not a camera orbit - fail physical_plausibility.
Criteria
(score each 0/1 with a short justification)
(1)
authenticity
object grounded, NOT floating.
(2)
background_sharpness
the whole scene stays in focus.
- Score 0 if the background is blurred or bokeh’d into mush while only the object is sharp.
(3)
scene_consistency
the background must behave like ONE RIGID 3D place.
- Score 0 if structures appear/vanish between frames, the layout rearranges, floor/tile grids warp, or it becomes a DIFFERENT place.
- Seeing NEW parts of the same room as the camera moves is fine.
(4)
physical_plausibility
no non-physical deformation/flicker/fusion of the central object, and the object must be physically SUPPORTED by what it rests on - not floating, not in an impossible pose, not on a surface that could not hold it.
(5)
subject_shape
object is not paper/card/cloth/2D-planar.
(6)
object_integrity
FIRST, from the REFERENCE photos, note the original object’s parts (strap? pole/stand? flag? handle?).
- THEN check the GENERATED frames.
- Score 0 ONLY for a CLEAR STRUCTURAL change: a substantial new part attached to the object (a pedestal or stand under it, a frame around it), the object FUSED INTO a background structure (a bird becoming a fountain pillar), or its overall shape MORPHED into a different form.
- Do NOT fail on: parts that merely become visible from a new camera angle, small texture noise or thin stray artifacts, lighting and shadow differences, or nearby scene props that sit SEPARATELY next to the object without touching it.
- When the object still reads as the same item with the same silhouette, score 1.
Rule
qualified only if ALL 6 = 1.
Final user instruction
Now evaluate. Any part in GENERATED but absent in REFERENCE = object_integrity 0.
G3 is used only for training-data curation and is not applied during evaluation or inference.
G3: Reconstruction Quality
Prompt
You are a QC reviewer for 3D RECONSTRUCTION quality. A reconstruction of an object is rendered as a turntable video (camera orbits; the object should appear to spin in place). I will give you, IN ORDER: (1) the REAL ORIGINAL object as reference photos (view0-3) - ground truth; (2) the RECONSTRUCTION frames to CHECK.
Judge ONLY the reconstructed object’s GEOMETRY vs the reference. Object SIZE and POSITION in the frame are handled elsewhere - do NOT penalize framing/crop/margins.
Criteria
(score each 0/1 with a short justification)
(1)
identity_match
compare the object’s OVERALL PROPORTIONS / aspect ratio AND distinctive 3D FORM to the reference.
- 0 if proportions are distorted (e.g. a wide rectangular object reconstructed as a square/cube), if melted/morphed, or if reduced to a generic blob that lost the reference’s distinctive form.
- IGNORE surface text/printed labels/logos - MV-SAM3D cannot reconstruct fine print, so blurred/changed/flickering text is NOT a defect; judge by 3D shape and proportion only.
(2)
completeness
object is whole - no holes, no missing or collapsed STRUCTURAL parts.
- A flickering/blurred printed LABEL or surface text is NOT a completeness defect (surface print is expected to degrade); only missing 3D parts count.
(3)
no_floater
no floating fragments, stray blobs, or disconnected debris around the object.
(4)
rotation_integrity
object spins IN PLACE about its own axis.
- 0 if it SWINGS/ORBITS around an off-center point (revolves).
Rule
qualified only if ALL 4 = 1.
I.2
Category descriptions and scene vocabulary
Category descriptions and scene vocabulary are generated automatically
with Claude Opus 5 under the rules below. Each category has an appearance
sentence and a coarse type; the type selects compatible scene locations.
The scene bank contains
2,000
2{,}000
locations with surfaces, props, depth cues
and lighting used to assemble the compositing prompts
(Section
).
Category Descriptions and Scene Vocabulary
Category description
one sentence per category, written from the category name (not from a particular asset):
"A [adjective] [material] <category> with [distinguishing trait]"
- plus exactly one coarse type from {accessory, apparel, appliance, bag, beauty, decor, drink, electronics, food, furniture, sports, tools}
Scene vocabulary
one entry per location: a compatible set of surfaces, props, depth cues and lighting, with a tone label (cool, warm, neutral, green).
- no words implying defocus or bokeh
- no people or actions
- no description of the subject itself
I.3
Captioning
Tarsier2-7B captions the RGB reconstruction turntable and the composited
target with greedy decoding and a category hint. Before insertion into
[CONDITION]
, the reconstruction caption is stripped of turntable
narration and references to reconstruction and the white background.
The condition box below shows the resulting format; the target box gives
the captioning prompt.
Condition Caption Format
Stripping rule
Retain the object’s visible appearance and distinctive parts. Remove turntable-rotation narration, white-background phrases and reconstruction-specific narration.
Template
"The video starts with [object: shape, color, material, distinctive visible features]. [Optional additional appearance details.]"
Example
"The video starts with a black gargoyle statue with bat-like wings and a menacing expression, positioned on a stone base."
Output
The stripped object description is used after [CONDITION].
Target Caption Prompt
Prompt
In this video, a 3D object is placed in a real-world scene. Focus your description on the object, where it is placed, the surrounding scene, and any visible action or scene change.
Describe the video in 2 to 3 sentences. The first sentence MUST start with "The video starts with" and contain the object, its placement, and the scene. Follow this structure precisely:
Template
"The video starts with [object: shape, color, material, distinctive features] [placement phrase: e.g., placed on a wooden table / standing on a stone pedestal / resting on a tiled floor] in [scene location with lighting style]. [Optional second/third sentence: brief description of camera motion, scene change, or other notable action visible in the video]."
Example
"The video starts with a digital watch with a metal bracelet placed on a rusty riveted metal table in a brick-walled loft with warm natural light from arched windows. The camera gradually moves closer to the watch, revealing the textured brick walls and wooden floor in more detail."
Output
Respond ONLY with the description.
I.4
Inference prompts
The captioner does not reliably state how far the camera turns, so a fixed
sentence derived from the camera mode is appended to every target caption. At
inference our model receives an introductory sentence, the stripped condition caption
after
[CONDITION]
, and the target caption after
[VIDEO]
,
ending with the trajectory sentence; baselines receive only the text after
[VIDEO]
.
Inference Prompt
Trajectory sentence
Chosen from the motion and suffix vocabulary in Tables
--
and appended to the target caption.
Structure
intro sentence
+ [CONDITION] stripped condition caption
+ [VIDEO] target caption
+ trajectory sentence
Example
This video demonstrates a multi-view capture of a gargoyle, showcasing the object as it rotates and moves across different viewpoints.
[CONDITION] The video starts with a black gargoyle statue with bat-like wings and a menacing expression, positioned on a stone base.
[VIDEO] The video begins with a detailed view of a gargoyle statue situated on a stone base, surrounded by scattered autumn leaves on a cracked stone pavement, with a gothic architectural background featuring tall spires and intricate stonework. The camera rotates around the gargoyle, capturing different angles and perspectives [...] The camera circles all the way around the object while rising.
Baselines
the text after [VIDEO] only; for 3DreamBooth it is rewritten into its identifier format: "A video of a [rhs <noun>] ..."

article.headline: 用表面法线转台做主体一致的全向视频生成
article.lede: OmniShowcase 从 4 张参考视图重建 3D 几何、渲染表面法线转台作为条件，无需逐主体优化即可生成环绕主体的
article.problem: 主体到视频（S2V）生成多以单张参考图为条件，相机转到输入中不可见的表面时，模型只能靠生成先验推测几何与外观，轮廓和结构随之漂移。近期方法虽引入多张参考视图，却没有显式给出连接这些视图的 3D 结构，训练数据本身也不保证视角变化对应同一 3D 主体。
article.method: 作者用 3D 资产在 Blender 中渲染目标轨迹与 4 张参考视图，再用视频 inpainting 把主体合成进提示词驱动的背景，构建 Showcase-4K。条件端从参考视图前馈重建几何（点图加 3D 高斯），沿 15° 仰角渲染 25 帧表面法线转台，与参考图一起作为 in-context 序列送入 LoRA 微调的 Wan2.1 I2V 扩散 Transformer。法线与目标视频分别编码后沿时间轴拼接，因此不要求两者逐帧对齐。
article.results: 在 50 个主体的 ShowcaseBench 上，DINO 主体一致性为 0.799（最好的基线 3DreamBooth 为 0.707），CLIP 为 0.925 对 0.907，MEt3R 为 0.190 对 0.325，GT-CD 为 0.0824 对 0.1717；在 NAVI（35 个主体）上 DINO 为 0.828、GT-CD 为 0.0975。消融显示，去掉几何条件后 GT-CD 从 0.0824 升至 0.2092，把法线换成纹理渲染或把转台从 25 帧减到 9 帧也均变差。44 人用户研究中，该方法在四项标准上获 70.9%–79.4% 偏好，没有基线超过 12.7%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把显式 3D 几何作为与外观解耦的条件通道引入 S2V，并用渲染数据保证视角变化真的对应同一形状，为可控运镜的主体视频提供了可复现的数据与评测管线。
article.limitations: 作者自述两点局限：合成背景有时显得平板、缺少材质细节；法线转台来自把四张视图融合成单一静态重建，因此当四个参考拍摄到不同姿态的非刚性主体时，模型会收敛到一个没人摆出过的平均姿态。训练语料仅 4,000 段、2,593 个资产，远小于 Phantom 等的百万级真实视频。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从 4 张参考视图重建 3D 并渲染表面法线转台，与参考图一同注入 LoRA 微调的图生视频扩散 Transformer 参考通路，无需逐主体优化即可生成目标视频。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} From $N{=}4$ reference views, we reconstruct 3D geometry and render a surface-normal turntable. The reference images and normal condition are injected into the reference pathway of a LoRA-tuned image-to-video diffusion transformer. The model uses appearance information from the reference views and 3D structure from the normal condition to generate the target video without per-subject optimization.

page_papers.title: Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes
page_papers.abstract: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) is essential for latency-sensitive applications. However, current causal systems face two coupled gaps. First, standard benchmarks fix the number of speakers at two and ignore the near-/far-field interference, reverberation, and sudden noise of real scenes. Second, high-performance causal architectures are too heavy for edge deployment. Lightweight alternatives try to reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, which offsets the savings. To address the first gap, we release RealSSA, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1--5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10--15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. To address the second gap, we propose Falcon, a causal AVTSE method. Its Separator performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder--decoder pass. We train Falcon with an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. This loss suppresses near-field leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across backbones. Falcon achieves state-of-the-art extraction quality on RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix. Compared with the causal AV-TFGridNet baseline, it cuts parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2 times, and GPU inference latency by 11.1 times. Code and demo are available at https://cslikai.cn/Falcon/.

Second, high-performance causal architectures are too heavy for edge deployment. Lightweight alternatives try to reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, which offsets the savings. To address the first gap, we release RealSSA, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1–5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10–15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. To address the second gap, we propose Falcon, a causal AVTSE method. Its Separator performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder–decoder pass. We train Falcon with an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. This loss suppresses near-field leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across backbones. Falcon achieves state-of-the-art extraction quality on RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix. Compared with the causal AV-TFGridNet baseline, it cuts parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2

1
Introduction
Audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) leverages a speaker’s visual stream, typically lip movements, as enrollment cues to separate the target speaker’s voice from a multi-speaker mixture
[
1
,
2
]
. Although this setting has often been described in prior work as audio-visual speech separation
[
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
]
, these methods all condition on the visual stream of a single target speaker, which by definition is target speaker extraction; therefore, we use the term AVTSE throughout this paper.
Many latency-sensitive applications now demand
causal
AVTSE, such as video conferencing
[
7
]
and hearing-assistive devices
[
8
]
. However, the current causal AVTSE methods fall short along two axes: the data used to train and evaluate causal models, and the architecture of the causal model itself.
(a)
Small Rooms
(b)
Coffee Shops
(c)

(d)
Outdoor Streets
Figure 1
:
Real-world AVTSE scenarios motivating RealSSA. The four scene types, ranging from small rooms to outdoor streets, cover varying number of speakers, near-/far-field interference, reverberation, and sudden environmental noise beyond standard fixed-speaker benchmarks.
Existing AVTSE benchmarks do not reflect the acoustic conditions of deployment. Some benchmarks built on LRS2
[
9
]
, LRS3
[
10
]
, and VoxCeleb2
[
11
]
fix the number of speakers at two, draw mixtures at controlled SNRs, and hold room acoustics and background noise constant, leaving out the near-/far-field geometry, reverberation, and sudden noise events that characterize everyday recordings (Figure
1
)
[
12
,
13
]
. None of them are paired with a real-recorded evaluation set, and reported gains offer little evidence that a causal model will hold up once deployed. Therefore, the AVTSE task requires a benchmark that can simulate simultaneous changes in the number of speakers, spatial geometry, and noise, while also providing real recordings to evaluate real-world deployment performance.
On the model side, current causal AVTSE faces an efficiency gap. Causal variants of strong non-causal architectures preserve the extraction quality. Some methods include AV-TFGridNet
[
14
]
, AV-Mossformer2
[
15
]
, and RTFSNet
[
16
]
, obtained under the protocol of SwiftNet
[
17
]
. However, their parameter counts and per-frame FLOPs push inference latency beyond real-time budgets on edge hardware. Lightweight alternatives such as SwiftNet
[
17
]
recover capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator after audio-visual fusion. Yet each additional cycle multiplies per-frame computation and erodes the latency savings of the smaller module. On the training side, SI-SNR penalizes deviation from the clean target
[
18
]
, but does not explicitly push the estimate away from near-field speakers. This leaves residual leakage from spatially close talkers, and the leakage grows with the number of simultaneously active near-field speakers in realistic scenes
[
1
,
19
]
.
To close this data gap, we release
RealSSA
, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1–5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers across four scene types; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10–15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. We jointly sample room reverberation, ambient noise, and sudden noise events, so that the number of interfering speakers, spatial geometry, and environmental acoustics vary together rather than one axis at a time. RealSSA-Real further allows causal models trained on simulation to be evaluated on deployment-side distributions without adaptation.
To close the model-side gap, we propose
Falcon
, a single-pass causal AVTSE method. At its core, the
Separator
applies an encoder–decoder trunk to the audio-visual fused feature. In a single decoder traversal, it performs frequency-axis, time-axis, and joint time-frequency modeling, assigned to different decoder levels from coarse to fine scales. We further introduce an
encoder-space speaker contrastive loss
, computed in the separator’s STFT encoder space against the clean target and each near-field interferer. This loss suppresses residual leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across AVTSE backbones. On RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix
[
9
]
, LRS3-2Mix
[
10
]
, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix
[
11
]
, Falcon matched or exceeded the strongest causal baselines
[
14
,
15
,
17
,
20
]
in separation quality (Table
3
). On RealSSA-Real, it achieved competitive perceptual quality, WER, and target-speaker similarity. Meanwhile, it reduced parameters, computational cost, and GPU inference latency by 91.9%, 20.2
×
\times
, and 11.1
×

relative to the causal AV-TFGridNet

14

Related Works
2.1
AVTSE Benchmarks
AVTSE benchmarks can be organized along three axes: speaker configuration, acoustic conditions, and evaluation realism (Table
1
). Along the first axis, LRS2-2Mix
[
9
]
, LRS3-2Mix
[
10
]
, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix
[
11
]
fix two near-field speakers per mixture, and therefore do not expose models to varying counts of near- and far-field interferers. These three corpora are used by most AVTSE models
[
4
,
6
,
5
,
16
,
20
]
and their causal variants
[
17

. Along the second axis, these corpora inherit acoustic conditions from the source videos, and offer no controlled reverberation or sudden noise events. The LRS3+WHAM! noisy protocol, reused by
[
21

[

[

2.2
Causal Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction
Causal AVTSE methods mainly differ in two aspects: separator architecture and training objective. On the architecture side, causal evaluation largely follows the protocol of SwiftNet
[
17
]
, which provides a recipe for converting non-causal AVTSE backbones into their causal counterparts by restricting temporal operations to past and current frames; earlier time-domain separators
[
25
,
26
,
27
,
6
]
and recent time-frequency separators are causalized under this protocol. Among the time-frequency family, AV-TFGridNet
[
14
]
and AV-Mossformer2
[
15
]
retain strong extraction quality at the cost of large parameter counts and heavy per-frame computation, while SwiftNet and the causalized RTFSNet
[
16
]
and AVLiT
[
21
]
variants reuse a single compact block across multiple iterative cycles, trading parameters for per-frame FLOPs. Falcon instead employs level-specific time-frequency blocks within a single encoder–decoder forward pass.
On the training side, AVTSE systems were typically optimized with waveform reconstruction losses such as SI-SNR
[
18
]
, and prior attempts to suppress residual interferers either adjust the training mixture distribution or add routing-level gates over the separator output
[
19
,
14
]
rather than explicitly separating the estimate from each interfering speaker. Falcon instead adds an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss, discarded at inference time.
3
The RealSSA Dataset
RealSSA consists of two parts: RealSSA-Sim, a controllable simulated-scene suite used for training, validation, and testing, and RealSSA-Real, a held-out real-recorded evaluation set used to assess generalization under non-simulated acoustic conditions. RealSSA-Sim provides systematic control over speaker configuration, source distance, reverberation, environmental noise, and sudden noise events, while RealSSA-Real reflects raw on-device recordings in everyday acoustic environments.
RealSSA-Sim: Simulated Scene Suite.
RealSSA-Sim defines four acoustic scene types that span a wide range of room sizes, reverberation levels, and noise conditions (Table
2
). Small meeting rooms have short RT60 and only near-field interferers, representing close-range conversations. Medium indoor spaces introduce far-field speakers and moderate reverberation. Large public spaces further increase RT60 and the number of interferers, reflecting scenarios such as lecture halls. Outdoor environments have minimal reverberation but high ambient noise levels. Across the four scenes, the number of near-field interfering speakers varies from 1 to 5; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10–15 far-field interfering speakers. Each scene independently samples RT60, near-/far-field geometry, environmental noise, and sudden noise events. We classify an interferer as
near-field
when it lies within
3

far-field
otherwise; this threshold approximates the critical distance in typical indoor rooms, beyond which reverberant energy dominates the direct path

28

RealSSA-Real: Real-World Evaluation Set.
In addition to the simulated suite, we collect a real-recorded evaluation set, denoted as RealSSA-Real, to assess generalization under non-simulated acoustic conditions. RealSSA-Real covers everyday indoor, public, and outdoor environments with natural background noise, room reverberation, and uncontrolled interfering speech. It is recorded with a single mobile device and preserves the raw acoustic conditions of real on-device capture. The recordings are post-processed only to match the input format used by the AVTSE pipeline, including audio resampling to 16 kHz, video conversion to 25 fps, and extraction of 96
×
\times
96 grayscale mouth regions.
RealSSA-Real is used exclusively for evaluation and is never used for training or validation. We assess perceptual quality with DNSMOS and NISQA, speech recognizability with WER, and target-speaker consistency with speaker similarity. Detailed recording protocol, environment composition, and privacy processing are provided in Appendix
A.4
.

7
Conclusions
RealSSA combines RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real to benchmark AVTSE under variable speaker counts, near-/far-field geometry, reverberation, and sudden noise, with held-out real recordings for evaluating generalization. Falcon performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder–decoder pass and uses an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss that suppresses near-field leakage, transfers across backbones, and adds no inference cost. Across RealSSA-Sim, RealSSA-Real, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix, Falcon matches or surpasses strong causal baselines. Relative to causal AV-TFGridNet, it reduces parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2
×
\times
, and GPU inference latency by 11.1
×
\times
, supporting progress toward low-latency on-device AVTSE.
Limitations.
Both the separator and the encoder-space speaker contrastive loss in Falcon operate on a single channel, and we leave the four-element array simulated in Appendix
A.2
to future multi-channel extensions. RealSSA-Real covers approximately
84
84
minutes over
10
10
participants and eight environments, which is sufficient to reveal cross-architecture trends and can be scaled up in follow-up releases. The contrastive loss currently relies on clean per-source waveforms of near-field interferers available in simulation, and adapting it to unlabeled real recordings is a natural direction for future work.

Scene design rationale.
The four scene types in Table
2
are not arbitrary. They are chosen to cover an acoustic gradient that separators must traverse in deployment, with three controlled axes: room volume, reverberation time, and the presence of far-field interferers. Small meeting rooms have the shortest RT60 (0.3–0.6 s), match the scale of two-person to small-group offices, and contain only near-field interferers because no point in the room is beyond the 3 m near-/far-field threshold; this makes them the “clean” end of the gradient. Medium indoor spaces (e.g., kitchens, living rooms) introduce moderate reverberation (0.5–0.9 s) together with the first far-field talkers, since the room becomes large enough for some speakers to fall outside the critical-distance neighborhood of the microphone
[
28
]
. Large public spaces such as cafeterias and lecture halls extend RT60 to 1.0–2.0 s, which is the regime in which reverberant energy dominates the direct path and in which far-field speech becomes the harder interferer to suppress. Outdoor environments invert the indoor pattern: very low RT60 (0.05–0.1 s) but high environmental SIR difficulty, so that the stress test moves from reverberation to wide-band ambient noise. Together the four scenes span the regime in which residential and on-the-go AVTSE systems are deployed, and the RT60 ranges fall within the values reported for occupied rooms of comparable size in standard architectural-acoustics references
[
28
]
.

Semantic noise selection from Hive.
Hive provides a label hierarchy over sound events; we use it to ensure that the noise pool of each scene is semantically consistent with the scene type rather than uniformly drawn. Table
12
lists the environmental and sudden-noise labels assigned to each scene. The mapping follows three rules: continuous mechanical noise (air conditioning, refrigerator, microwave) is restricted to indoor scenes whose physical setting plausibly contains such sources; pedestrian and traffic events (footsteps, sirens, vehicle pass-bys) are restricted to large-public and outdoor scenes; and a small pool of generic transient events (key jangling, coin dropping, slam, bang) is shared across all scenes since they occur ubiquitously regardless of room type. The label-to-scene assignment is fixed in the released metadata and is the only step in the pipeline that draws on human knowledge of the sound-event taxonomy.

Ethics statement.
All recordings were collected under written informed consent. Participants were informed of the academic purpose of the data, were free to withdraw their contribution at any time, and were offered the option to redact specific segments before release. Appendix F
Causalization of Dolphin and AV-Mossformer2 Baselines
Dolphin
[
20
]
and AV-Mossformer2
[
15
]
were originally released as non-causal AVTSE models. To compare them against Falcon under a common causal protocol, we re-implemented both baselines with the minimal modifications required to remove future-context access at every layer, while preserving their parameter counts, block topologies, and training objectives. Both baselines used the common optimizer and learning-rate schedule described in Section
5.2
. This appendix lists, for each model, the operations that needed rewriting; every module not listed is already causal in the released code and was kept unchanged.
Across both models we used four rewriting primitives
[
17
]
.
Causal self-attention
adds a lower-triangular mask before the softmax.
Causal convolution
replaces symmetric padding by left padding only, with the same kernel size and dilation.
Causal pooling and interpolation
replaces full-axis adaptive average pooling and nearest-neighbor interpolation along time by their one-sided (past-only) variants.
Streaming-causal layer normalization
replaces full-axis LayerNorm or GroupNorm along time by the frame-local
LN
c
\operatorname{LN}_{\text{c}}
of Section
4.2
. Frame-wise operators, including pointwise convolutions, element-wise gates, and LayerNorm on the feature axis, were kept as released.
F.1
Dolphin Causalization
Visual encoder and refinement.
The DP-LipCoder visual encoder
[
20
]
was frozen during AVTSE training, as in the original paper. Inside it we added causal masks to the temporal axis of every dual-path attention block, while the spatial axes remain bidirectional, and we rewrote every temporal downsample and upsample as a causal convolution. The post-encoder visual refinement block uses dilated depthwise convolutions with symmetric padding, which we rewrote as causal convolutions.
Audio-Visual Fusion.
The fusion module has three paths: a resize path that upsamples the visual feature to the audio frame rate by nearest-neighbor interpolation, a key-value path that multiplies a pointwise-projected audio feature by the upsampled visual feature, and an attention path that softmaxes a projected visual feature over its time axis and upsamples the result to the audio time axis. The two non-causal operations are the nearest-neighbor upsamplings, which we rewrote as one-sided, and the softmax over the visual time axis, which we rewrote as a causal softmax that masks visual frames later than the current audio frame. The element-wise sum of the three paths is unchanged.
U-shape Separator.
The Separator alternates Global Attention and Local Attention blocks across encoder and decoder stages, joined by injection-based skip fusion and a global Bottleneck. Global Attention compresses the input by adaptive average pooling along time, applies relative-position multi-head self-attention, and restores the resolution by nearest-neighbor upsampling; we rewrote the pooling and the upsampling as one-sided, added a causal mask to the inner attention, and tightened the relative-position clip to non-positive offsets. Local Attention contains Heat Diffusion Attention, which as released applies a discrete cosine transform (DCT) along the full time axis, a per-frequency exponential decay, and an inverse DCT. We replaced the full-sequence DCT pair with a causal windowed DCT on a past-only window of length
W
W
, so that the heat-diffusion interpretation is restricted to a finite past and the transform pair becomes a causal convolution of effective kernel
W
W
. The surrounding depthwise convolutions and GroupNorm layers in this block were rewritten as causal convolutions and as
LN
c
\operatorname{LN}_{\text{c}}
, respectively. The Bottleneck aggregates encoder-stage outputs by adaptive average pooling along time before applying multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward network; we rewrote the aggregation pool as one-sided, added a causal mask to the attention, and rewrote the feed-forward depthwise convolution as causal. The injection-based skip fusion modules align the global feature to each skip’s resolution by nearest-neighbor interpolation along time, which we rewrote as one-sided; the projection sub-modules inside the injection module reuse Heat Diffusion Attention and inherit its causal windowed DCT rewrite.
Audio encoder and decoder.
The strided 1D audio encoder and its transposed-convolution decoder were rewritten as causal convolutions along the time axis.
F.2
AV-Mossformer2 Causalization
Pre-separator audio-visual fusion.
The visual encoder was frozen as in the original paper
[
15
]
. The pre-separator fusion layer upsamples the visual feature to the audio frame rate by nearest-neighbor interpolation, which we rewrote as one-sided; the pointwise projection and the element-wise gated sum that follow are unchanged.
MossFormer block.
Each MossFormer block runs a quadratic intra-group attention with squared-ReLU scores in parallel with a linearized cross-group attention. The released code already exposes a causal switch: when enabled, it adds a strictly upper-triangular mask to the squared-ReLU score tensor inside each group, and replaces the bidirectional cross-group statistics by one-sided cumulative sums followed by a one-step shift that excludes the current group from its own summary. We enabled this switch on every MossFormer block, and no further modification was required to the joint attention path.
Gated FSMN.
The Gated FSMN module is already causal in the release: its memory taps span only past frames, the surrounding pointwise convolutions have time receptive field
1
1
, and the cumulative LayerNorm computes statistics only over past frames. The block was therefore kept unchanged.

Three patterns emerge from the grid. The scene axis did not follow a simple monotone difficulty ordering with respect to reverberation time. Outdoor cells consistently yielded the highest SI-SNRi for every architecture because the near-anechoic propagation of Table

leaves the target direct path largely intact, so that the separator only needs to suppress wide-band ambient noise and a small number of geometrically well separated interferers. Large public cells were the next easiest on average, since the dominant interference is reverberant rather than spatially co-located with the target and the visual enrollment cue is sufficient to disambiguate far-field talkers. Medium indoor cells lay in the middle and combine moderate reverberation with the first far-field interferers. Appendix J
Visualization of Encoder-Space Speaker Embeddings
To further analyze the effect of the proposed encoder-space speaker contrastive loss, we visualized speaker embeddings extracted from models trained with and without this loss. We selected the top-15 target speakers with the most utterances from the RealSSA-Sim training set, resulting in 5–8 utterances per speaker. For each utterance, we extracted an encoder-space speaker embedding using the speaker pooling head and projected all embeddings into two dimensions using principal component analysis (PCA).
As shown in Figure
9

In contrast, with the proposed contrastive loss, same-speaker embeddings became more compact and different speakers were more clearly separated. This visualization supports that the proposed loss introduces a speaker-discriminative structure in the encoder space, which helps the separator distinguish the target speaker from near-field interferers.

article.headline: Falcon：单次前向的因果视听目标说话人提取
article.lede: 团队发布 RealSSA 真实场景基准与 Falcon 因果提取模型，参数 0.5M，GPU 延迟 51.3 ms。
article.problem: 现有因果视听目标说话人提取基准几乎都把说话人数固定为两人，声学条件恒定，缺少近场与远场干扰、混响和突发噪声，也没有真实录音评测集。模型侧则相反：高性能因果架构参数与每帧计算量过大，难以部署到边缘设备，而轻量方案靠反复调用小分离器换容量，反过来抵消了延迟收益。此外，SI-SNR 只拉近目标、不显式推开近场干扰，说话人越近泄漏越严重。
article.method: 作者发布 RealSSA 基准，其中 RealSSA-Sim 覆盖小型会议室、中型室内、大型公共空间与户外四类场景，近场干扰说话人 1 到 5 个，有远场干扰的场景再加入 10 到 15 个远场说话人，并联合采样混响、环境噪声与突发噪声；RealSSA-Real 是单台手机录制的留出评测集。模型 Falcon 采用非对称 U-Net 分离器，在单次编码器–解码器前向中完成频率轴、时间轴与联合时频的多尺度建模，取代 SwiftNet 式的多次迭代。训练时额外加入编码器空间说话人对比损失，以干净目标和各近场干扰的编码特征作为正负参考，推理阶段完全移除，因此不增加推理开销，并可迁移到其他骨干。
article.results: 在 RealSSA-Sim 上 Falcon 取得 7.7 dB SI-SNRi（AV-TF-GridNet 为 7.6 dB），在 LRS2-2Mix、LRS3-2Mix、VoxCeleb2-2Mix 上分别为 16.4、10.5 dB 等最佳值，其中 VoxCeleb2-2Mix 相对 Swift-Net-12 提升 1.1 dB；RealSSA-Sim 上 WER 为 25.47%，比 AV-TF-GridNet 低 1.84 个百分点。在 RealSSA-Real 上 DNSMOS 为 3.276，WER 为 32.74%（在提取系统中排第二，落后 AV-Mossformer2 0.74 个百分点），目标说话人相似度 42.23 为最高。效率方面参数 0.5M、10.6 G MACs、GPU 延迟 51.3 ms，相对 AV-TF-GridNet 参数减少 91.9%、MACs 减少 95.0%、GPU 延迟减少 91.0%；对比损失在 Falcon、SwiftNet-12、Dolphin 上分别带来 0.4、0.2、0.3 dB 的 SI-SNRi 增益。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「更真实的评测条件」和「能上边缘设备的因果模型」放在同一项工作里，说明轻量单次前向架构在拥挤近场场景下可以追平甚至超过重量级因果基线。对视频会议、助听设备这类低延迟应用，这类基准与效率数据比单一仿真集上的分数更有参考价值。
article.limitations: 分离器与对比损失都只处理单通道，作者把四元麦克风阵列留作后续工作；RealSSA-Real 仅约 84 分钟、10 名参与者、8 个环境，规模有限，且对比损失依赖仿真中才有的干净近场干扰源波形。此外模型高度依赖视觉输入：在 500 个样本上完全去掉视觉帧后 SI-SNRi 跌至 −9.91 dB，连续遮挡比随机丢帧损伤更大。

page_papers.title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
page_papers.abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.

1
Introduction
Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) enables generalist robot policies to learn from physical interaction and improve on deployment tasks
(
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
.
Initialized from offline expert demonstrations, a policy aims to maximize cumulative task rewards
(
Luo et al., 2024
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
and optionally learns from human-intervention data during deployment
(
Luo et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
However, current real-world RL methods face limitations in data reuse and policy-update frequency.
On-policy updates primarily use fresh rollouts, limiting the reuse of historical experience
(
Chen et al., 2025a
)
.
Iterated offline RL separates data collection from optimization, delaying feedback from newly encountered states
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
.
Besides, partial observability poses another challenge.
With limited observation histories, visually similar states may require different actions.
Meanwhile, value functions provide compact task-progress estimates, but typically serve as filtering scores or optimization weights
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
.
We therefore ask whether value estimates on observation histories can augment policy inputs to mitigate partial observability, and how an online RL system can exploit a learned value function to incorporate offline demonstrations, off-policy data, and on-policy rollouts for joint adaptation of the policy and value functions with high sample efficiency and rapid closed-loop feedback.
To this end, we introduce
Value as Memory (VaM)
, an offline-to-online RL system with two key features.
First
, we propose value caching, which extends value predictions beyond training supervision by supplying their recent history as an additional policy input.
Alongside visual and proprioceptive histories, this cache indicates whether estimated progress improves, stalls, or declines, helping distinguish states requiring different actions.
Second
, VaM uses a hybrid training data scheme that combines offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient joint adaptation of policy and value models.
Our training regime progresses from offline RL warmup through human-assisted collection to autonomous learning with sparse rewards.
Across real-world tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulations, VaM improves mean absolute success rate by
29.4
%
29.4\%
over its variant without value caching.
It gains
32.8
%
32.8\%
in mean absolute success rate over its offline RL counterpart under matched training budgets.
The evaluated online schedule performs
8
×
8\times
as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than
2
×
2\times
lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
These results support value caching for mitigating partial observability and our online RL system with a hybrid training data scheme for improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.
Our contributions are twofold:
1.
We propose value caching to condition policies on recent task-progress estimates, with theoretical analysis and real-world ablations supporting its role in mitigating action ambiguity under partial observability.
2.
We develop an online RL framework that reuses offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for joint policy and value adaptation, improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.

3.1
Method Overview
VaM uses a distributional value expert to supply recent progress predictions to the action expert through a value cache and advantage labels for policy post-training.
Training proceeds through four stages: offline demonstration initialization, offline RL warmup, Online DAgger, and Learn from Experience (LfE).
The value and action experts are updated in parallel during online RL.

;
Chen et al., 2025a
)
.
Likelihood-based, hierarchical, and latent-space formulations support optimization of generative policies
(
Ren et al., 2025
;
Lei et al., 2026
;
Wagenmaker et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025a
)
, while world models reduce physical interaction by providing imagined or synthetic experience
(
Yang et al., 2026
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
GigaBrain Team et al., 2026
)
.
To learn from a robot’s own experience, some prior methods learn an additional value function to filter out suboptimal segments.
General-purpose reward and critic models learn transferable evaluations from robot trajectories or vision-language supervision
(
Liang et al., 2026
;
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhai et al., 2026
)
, while advantage-oriented methods derive relative progress from temporal relations in demonstrations and trajectories
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Yu et al., 2026a
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
RECAP combines demonstrations, policy rollouts, and human interventions to estimate value and annotate data for advantage-conditioned policy extraction through CFGRL
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
.
However, learning value estimates from fixed or periodically refreshed datasets can leave the critic stale as the deployment distribution changes between updates.
In addition, when value predictions serve only as rewards, filtering scores, annotations, or optimization weights, the deployed policy does not receive them as inputs.
Without this explicit task-progress information, visually similar observations can obscure different stages of execution, leaving the policy with partial observability of task progress.
VaM instead continually updates value from online rollouts and human interventions and uses its predictions both as policy-learning supervision and an explicit policy input.
5.2
Human-in-the-loop Online Adaptation
Human operators intervene during deployment to correct uncertain or failing policy behavior
(
Luo et al., 2025b
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
.
Methods such as HG-DAgger and Sirius use interventions as corrective demonstrations for policy improvement
(
Kelly et al., 2019
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
Fleet-DAgger, SiriusFleet, and ARMADA scale intervention collection by allocating operators or requesting assistance only when necessary
(
Hoque et al., 2023
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Yu et al., 2026b
)
, while recent fleet-scale systems combine online robot rollouts with human corrections across multiple robots and tasks
(
Pan et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
VaM further uses intervention trajectories to update a value model that guides policy learning and conditions the policy input.
5.3
Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Offline-to-online RL stabilizes policy improvement by retaining or replaying offline data during online training
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Peng et al., 2019
;
Nair et al., 2020
;
Li et al., 2025
)
.
RLPD mixes offline and online samples, Cal-QL calibrates an offline value function for online fine-tuning, and Warm-Start RL initializes online learning with replay data that preserves pretrained behavior
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
.
In real-world robotics, SERL and HIL-SERL combine behavior-cloning initialization with off-policy learning for physical manipulation
(
Luo et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2025a
)
.
VaM combines offline demonstrations, historical off-policy intervention data, and current on-policy experience for sample-efficient online adaptation.
6
Discussions and Conclusions
Though VaM demonstrates improvement over prior methods in sample efficiency and mitigates partial observability in generalist robot policies, it has several limitations that suggest directions for future work.
First, value caching depends on a value function that closely tracks actual task progress, making offline RL warmup necessary for stable online training.
The cached history consists of the value expert’s own predictions, so its usefulness as task-progress memory depends on the quality of those predictions.
Second, our real-world RL framework is currently limited to a single robot.
Our experiments do not establish how the framework scales when multiple robots contribute data.
Scaling VaM to robot fleets with shared experience is a promising direction for further improving sample efficiency.
In conclusion, we presented VaM, a framework that uses recent value predictions as task-progress memory and combines offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and on-policy rollouts for online policy and value adaptation.
Value caching addresses action ambiguity under partial observability, while the offline-to-online RL pipeline supports continued learning from deployment experience.
Together, these components offer a practical approach to post-training generalist robot policies.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
Figure
8
summarizes the real-robot platforms and task workspaces, while Table
3
reports the episode counts used for offline demonstrations, offline RL warmup, and each Online RL collection round.
A.1
Task Procedures
Box Assembly
.
A cardboard box is placed in a random pose on the table.
The robot grasps one of its front flaps to bring the box upright.
The other arm then slowly folds a side flap inward and clamps it in place.
Finally, the robot lays the box flat and repeats the inward fold-and-clamp operation on the opposite side.
We evaluate the task on four tablecloths that differ in both texture and appearance.
The task is successful if, within the 120 s time limit, both side flaps are fully locked in place and the box lies horizontally on the table.
Laundry Folding
.
A crumpled garment is randomly arranged at a corner of the table.
The robot first moves it into its workspace.
It repeatedly locates the garment seams and progressively spreads the garment flat.
If necessary, the robot rotates the garment to a horizontal orientation.
It folds both sleeves inward, rotates the garment back to a vertical orientation, and folds it in half.
It then pushes the folded garment to the table corner.
The task is successful if the robot completes the procedure within 240 s and pushes the garment to the table corner while keeping it folded.
Magnetic Bus Assembly
.
The robot starts with six magnetic blocks scattered across the workspace and first identifies the three base blocks of the bus.
It sequentially aligns and magnetically joins their narrow side edges to form a horizontal base.
The robot then identifies the three body blocks labeled “V”, “A”, and “M” and attaches them magnetically to the base in that order, placing each block flush against its neighboring body block.
The task is successful if, within 300 s, all six blocks form the bus, with a connected horizontal base and tightly adjoining body blocks spelling “VAM”.

article.headline: VaM：用价值缓存做机器人在线强化学习
article.lede: 上海交大等提出 VaM，把近期价值预测作为策略输入，并用真实世界在线强化学习后训练通用机器人策略。
article.problem: 通用机器人策略在真实世界后训练时，部分可观测性让视觉相似状态可能需要不同动作，动作选择存在歧义；离线后训练又把部署反馈与策略更新隔开，数据复用和策略迭代频率受限。现有方法常把价值函数用作过滤分数或优化权重，而不是策略的显式输入。
article.method: VaM 用分布式价值专家预测任务进度，并把最近若干步的价值预测组成缓存，与视觉、本体感受历史一起输入动作专家；同时用离线示范、离策略干预和在线 rollout 联合更新价值与策略。训练分四阶段：示范初始化、离线 RL 预热、Online DAgger 和从经验学习（LfE）。
article.results: 在三个真实长时程任务上，价值缓存使最后三个在线检查点的平均绝对成功率提升 29.4%；按任务看，Box Assembly 为 96.7% 对 81.7%，Laundry Folding 为 88.9% 对 48.9%，Magnetic Bus Assembly 为 76.7% 对 43.3%。相比匹配训练预算的离线 RL，在线自主学习平均提升 32.8%；所有 LfE 检查点平均的缓存增益为 31.3%。在线调度在相同梯度步预算下完成 8× 的策略迭代，单梯度步记录时间平均降低 57.8%。
article.why_it_matters: 如果价值缓存能缓解部分可观测性，通用机器人策略就有望在部署中持续从稀疏结果奖励中改进，而不必反复离线重训。论文给出的在线与离线时间对比也说明，异步并行的数据采集与训练可能让真实机器人 RL 更实用。
article.limitations: 价值缓存依赖价值函数紧密跟踪真实任务进度，因此离线 RL 预热对稳定在线训练是必要的；缓存的是价值专家自身预测，预测质量差时会误导策略。实验仅限单台机器人、三个任务，尚未验证多机器人共享经验时的扩展性。
article.figure_caption_zh: VaM 的四阶段离线到在线训练流程，以及价值专家如何把历史价值预测写入缓存并条件化动作专家。
