The bottom panel shows how the distributional value expert turns previously computed value predictions into the value cache that conditions the action expert.

page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.
page_papers.content:
Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
Haipeng Liu
Yang Wang
†
†
thanks:
Yang Wang is the corresponding author
Meng Wang
Affiliation:
School of Computer Science and Information Engineering
Affiliation:
Hefei University of Technology, China
Email:
hpliu_hfut@hotmail.com
yangwang@hfut.edu.cn
eric.mengwang@gmail.com
Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from
https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM
.

Introduction
Figure 2
:
(a) Comparison of the generated results, as well as the attention score map of text prompts and image references, between IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
and MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
for image customization. (b) Comparison of the generated results between InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
and StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
for style transfer. (c) Comparison of generated results guided by different frequency band of the image reference.
Personalized image generation focuses on synthesizing text-driven images conditioned on reference images, which enjoys remarkable progress, benefiting from the powerful denosing capabilities of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)
Ho et al. (2020)
;
Liu et al. (2024)
;
Liu et al. (2025a)
,
e.g.
, Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
;
Esser et al. (2024)
;
Podell et al. (2023)
;
Qian et al. (2022)
;
Qian et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024c)
. Typically, the personalized image generation involves two key subtasks,
i.e.
,
image customization
and
style transfer
. Given text prompts, image customization
Xiao et al. (2025)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Pang et al. (2024)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Kumari et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2025b)
;
Ma et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2022)
;
Cao et al. (2026)
;
Jiang et al. (2026)
aims to generate images by substituting the foreground semantics in the text prompts with the foreground extracted from the reference images, while preserving the background of the text prompts. In contrast, style transfer
Qin et al. (2025)
;
Rout et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2023)
;
Sohn et al. (2023)
;
Zhu et al. (2025)
;
Qi et al. (2024)
;
Hertz et al. (2024)
;
Lei et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Xing et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Wang et al. (2024a)
;
Jeong et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2022)
focuses on disentangling style (
background
) from reference images and aligning the foreground with the text prompt. However, prior arts have struggled to align the generated image with the text prompts within each individual subtask.
Figure 3
:
Illustration of our proposed
Dual-FDM
pipeline (a); For customization style transfer (b), we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Sec.
2.3
). For the color style transfer (c), we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Sec.
2.4
). Each of the two personalized image generation tasks are conducted in the early and late stage of the whole denoising process guided by text prompts as illustrated in Eq. (
1
).
For image customization, substantial efforts
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
aim to
emphasize dense image references of the foreground while overwhelming sparse text prompts of the background, especially for complex ones
,
e.g.
, a degraded “
flower wreath
” and the missing “
coffee
” in the IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
of Fig.
2
(a). Building on this, layout-based methods
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
exploit spatial layouts to explicitly constrain reference concepts to the foreground, while assigning background regions to text prompts.
This preserves the foreground identity, but the explicit separation of foreground and background in the layout disrupts overall consistency, leading to the misalignment with (complex / long) text prompts.
As illustrated in the MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(a), the generated spatial arrangement of “
flower wreath
” and “
coffee
” diverges from the prompt and instead resembles
“A flower wreath around a dog near a coffee”
.
When coming to style transfer, during the early stage of the denoising process with high-level noise, the foreground is reconstructed from sparse text prompts,
the dense style information intended for the background often leaks into the foreground, resulting in misalignment with the text prompts
,
e.g.
, the incorrect number of “
woman
" in the InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
of Fig.
2
(b). To resolve such issue, StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
applies style via instance normalization
Huang and Belongie (2017)
in the cross-attention layers and leverages layout to preserve foreground in the self-attention layers. Nevertheless, self-attention score maps highlight only the most salient regions, implying that the extracted layout can align only with simple text prompts (
i.e.
, “
a dog
") rather than the multi-objects (“
two pillows and one lemon
" in the StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(b)) text prompts, thereby
preventing it from handling the complex text prompts
.
So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.
2
Methodology
Central to our proposed Dual-FDM cover the following aspects: 1) how to pop up the background of the image references (Sec.
2.2

2.3

2.4

2.5

Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

Appendix A
Frequency Variation During the Denoising Process
As mentioned in Sec.
1
of the mainbody, We claim that
during the denoising process, images recover low-and-mid frequency bands first, followed by high-frequency details
. To validate the claims via frequency analysis, we experimentally measure the changes in both low- and high-frequency bands at different timesteps during the denoising process. The results are reported in Tab.
5
:
•
Low-frequency information.
We adopt
Mean Gray
,
Mean HSV-V
, and
Mean Luma
, which primarily capture global brightness and luminance structure. These metrics quantify the stability of the low-frequency bands throughout the denoising process.
•
High-frequency information.
We use
Average Gradient
,
Variance
, and
LBP Variance
, which are sensitive to edge sharpness, local contrast, and texture complexity. These metrics reflect the recovery of high-frequency details.
The low-frequency metrics remain nearly unchanged from the beginning (e.g.,
Mean Gray varies only slightly from 119.5 to 120.9
). In contrast, the high-frequency metrics increase steadily throughout the reverse process (e.g.,
Avg Gradient rises from 59.01 to 233.88
), confirming that high-frequency details are refined gradually during denoising. This is consistent with
Sec.
1
of the mainbody
.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

1.
Claims

[No]
or

[Yes]

•
The answer
[N/A]

[No]
means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

•
The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
•
The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
•
The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
•
The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
•
If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.
•
While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. of the Appendix and carefully described the experimental metrics in the experimental chapter. The information we provide is sufficient and detailed for replication purposes.

article.headline: 解耦双参考图像：频域扩散模型新框架
article.lede: Dual-FDM 用 DCT 掩码分离低中高频，分别处理定制与颜色风格迁移。
article.problem: 个性化图像生成需要同时利用参考图与文本提示，但现有扩散模型在图像定制和风格迁移中常出现文本对齐失败。作者观察到，问题源于去噪过程中低、中、高频段相互纠缠：低中频在早期高噪声阶段占主导，并压制文本提示的引导。
article.method: Dual-FDM 将参考图映射到 DCT 频域，用掩码分离低、中、高频段。定制风格迁移把定制参考前景的中频段替换到风格参考背景中；颜色风格迁移则把颜色参考前景与背景的低频段替换到风格参考背景中。方法还用 SVD 反转奇异值构造背景矩阵，并以替换频段的信息熵比值自适应划分去噪早期与晚期。
article.results: 在定制风格迁移中，Dual-FDM_cust 的 CLIP-T 为 0.3194、CLIP-TC 为 0.5031、HPS 为 2.6007，高于 MS-Diffusion 的 0.3123、0.4680 与 2.5436；颜色风格迁移的颜色类 CLIP-TS 达 0.5015、CLIP-S 达 0.7178、DINO-S 达 0.4970，优于 StyleAligned 的 0.4832、0.6904 与 0.4437。效率方面，Dual-FDM_cust 推理时间为 10.26 秒，显存占用 12.48 GB。
article.why_it_matters: 它把双参考解耦放到频域，为同时控制文本对齐、定制身份与风格相似度提供了可复用思路，并覆盖定制风格迁移和颜色风格迁移两类任务。
article.limitations: 论文自述的失败案例是：当风格参考包含极稀疏的线条结构时，替换中频的定制线索会削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整。此外，作者未报告误差棒或统计显著性检验，结论的稳健性仍需更多验证。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
Chunyu Luo
Hongyu Zhao
Guangyi Ni
Yue Song
Lingkai Kong
The University of Hong Kong  Beihang University
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen  Independent Researcher  Tsinghua University
Correspondence to:
lingkaikong@hku.hk
.
Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).
2
Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.

article.headline: 一步生成策略DriftSpread提升在线RL效率
article.lede: 论文提出DriftSpread，把MaxEnt策略改进拆成critic引导的Drift和熵驱动的Spread，用同一个a
article.problem: 扩散和流策略能表达复杂动作分布，但通常需要迭代采样，训练与推理成本高。在线最大熵RL要从critic定义的Boltzmann目标学习，而隐式策略没有可处理密度，熵项难以直接计算。
article.method: DriftSpread从负MaxEnt目标导出两个更新：Drift沿critic梯度移动动作，并用动作回归让actor拟合；Spread用适当尺度的独立噪声近似熵诱导扩散，再以MMD和特征函数做分布匹配。两个更新顺序作用于同一个actor，无需从Boltzmann目标采样，也无需策略密度或score估计。
article.results: 在五个MuJoCo-v3任务、每任务100万次环境交互和5个随机种子下，DriftSpread在13个基线中取得最高聚合归一化回报；平均推理时间为0.15 ms/action，低于DIME的1.24 ms和两步MeanFlow策略MFPO的0.36 ms，训练成本也低于扩散、流和MeanFlow基线。
article.why_it_matters: 它给在线RL提供了一步生成策略，在保留生成式策略表达能力的同时显著压低采样开销，让这类策略更接近实际训练和部署需求。
article.limitations: 理论收敛依赖固定critic、精确拟合以及小步长和长时间极限，实际训练不保证满足；实验仅限MuJoCo仿真，扩散噪声分布和尺度训练中固定，且聚合回报以DriftSpread自身均值为归一化参考，跨方法比较需谨慎。

page_papers.title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
page_papers.abstract: Robot foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, motivating low-cost offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To test this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to robotics and make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

Introduction
Robot foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models
[
4
,
3
]
, video models
[
50
]
, and world action models
[
15
,
28
,
5
]
. Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation
[
30
,
33
]
or the real world
[
1
,
9
]
, where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for policy capability.
A natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs
[
31
,
57
]
or pixel-level video quality for world models
[
18
,
52
,
23
]
. However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether a representation is organized for action
[
59
,
24
,
47
,
35
]
. Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, a model must produce different motions across tasks even in similar scenes. This requires aligning the sensory representation with the motor representation.
This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
21
]
, which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to a shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces.
For example, images and text are two projections of the same underlying world.
As vision and language models scale,
they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points.
We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical robot motion be viewed as another projection of that same world, such that more capable embodied models better align their vision and language representations with the structure of motion trajectories?
We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space.
We formalize this as
Sensorimotor Alignment
(
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free metric, illustrated in
Figure
1
. For each episode in a robot dataset, a model’s image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episode’s nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment.
In
Section
3
, we show that
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the task success of the resulting VLAs, more strongly than their visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs),
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
likewise correlates more strongly with task success than video-quality metrics such as FID
[
18
]
, SSIM
[
52
]
, and PSNR
[
19
]

S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
computed offline correlates with physical-robot task success on a shared set of tasks. Across these settings, sensorimotor alignment correlates with task success more closely than VQA or video-quality metrics.
Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closed-loop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
to supply that explanation, as shown in
Section
4

S

of their vision features, not their text features.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose a new view of embodiment: more capable embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with the structure of motion trajectories. To test this, we introduce
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
, a training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations.
•
Across model families, in simulation and on real robots,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with task success, making it a low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation.
•
Furthermore, we use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
to explain, at the representation level, several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs that were previously observed only through closed-loop results, making it a diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models.
We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

5
Related Work
Representation learning in robotics.
Many robotics studies pretrain visual representations to improve task performance
[
34
,
40
,
32
]
. However, there remains limited understanding of which representational properties lead to downstream task success. A few studies ask what makes a pretrained vision encoder useful for robot learning.
Hu et al. [20]
evaluate 14 frozen vision encoders and find that the correlation between an encoder’s offline score and downstream task success rate is not stable across policy-learning methods.
Burns et al. [8]
find that emergent segmentation predicts manipulation success under visual distribution shifts, but only for Vision Transformers. Theia
[
43
]
hypothesizes that higher feature-norm entropy improves robot learning, but reports the supporting correlations only within separate groups of encoders. These studies examine only vision encoders rather than a broader range of embodied models, and none of them accounts for the trajectories the robot executes when measuring the representation. By contrast,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
compares
k
k
-nearest-neighbor sets in sensory and motor spaces. The same
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
measure correlates with task success across VLAs, raw VLMs, WAMs, and the encoders that
Hu et al. [20]
evaluate.
Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Recent work has applied the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)
[
21
]
to several new domains. In image generation, REPA
[
54
]
aligns diffusion-transformer features with self-supervised vision encoders, improving training speed and quality. CREPA
[
22
]
extends this recipe to video diffusion. In multimodal understanding, VIRAL
[
53
]
re-aligns multimodal large language models (LLMs) with their vision encoders, recovering visual detail lost in multimodal training. For cross-modal alignment,
Schnaus et al. [42]
match independently trained vision and language encoders through their shared geometry, without paired data. PRH has not yet been brought into robotics; we extend it to robotics by treating robot trajectories as another projection of the world, and find that more capable embodied models align their sensory representations more closely with it.
6
Conclusion
We introduce Sensorimotor Alignment (
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
), a training-free offline metric of alignment between sensory representations and end-effector trajectories. Across VLAs, raw VLMs, and WAMs in simulation, and across real-robot policies,
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates positively with downstream task success, supporting a PRH-inspired view of embodiment.
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
correlates more strongly with task success than VQA scores and video-quality metrics, and explains, at the representation level, VLA and WAM phenomena previously observed only through closed-loop results: modality dominance, the performance drop from freezing the vision encoder, the small task-success cost of skipping iterative denoising, and the importance of mid-depth blocks for semantic reasoning. We use
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
only offline as a low-cost model-selection and diagnostic tool before closed-loop evaluation, but this correlation motivates optimizing embodied models directly for sensorimotor alignment.
Limitations.
Our study has three main limitations. (1) The positive relationship between
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
and task success is correlational across the tested models; we have not yet demonstrated that sensorimotor alignment can be used directly during training to improve task success rates. (2) Models with similar
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
values can still achieve different success rates, so
S
2
\mathrm{S}^{2}
is best used as a low-cost offline proxy for identifying promising models and VLM backbones before costly fine-tuning or closed-loop testing, which remains the final step of model selection. (3) Our evaluation covers limited model families, benchmarks, and training recipes, few models per comparison, and a single real-robot setting; broader generalization remains to be tested.

article.headline: S²：运动对齐关联机器人策略成功率
article.lede: 新论文提出免训练离线指标S²，衡量视觉-语言表征与末端轨迹几何的对齐，并在多类模型和真机上与任务成功率正相关。
article.problem: 机器人基础模型通常要靠昂贵的闭环仿真或真机 rollout 评估，速度慢、噪声大且依赖基准。现有离线代理多测VQA或视频质量，反映的是被动感知或生成质量，而非表征是否为动作组织。作者受Platonic Representation Hypothesis启发，追问运动轨迹能否作为另一种模态，使更强的具身模型其感官表征更贴近物理运动结构。
article.method: S²完全免训练：从DROID、BridgeDataV2或ALOHA采样片段，用模型视觉与文本编码器得到感官嵌入，用未来h步末端执行器位姿与夹爪状态构成运动表征。它分别按余弦距离和DTW找k近邻，再用共享近邻比例（centered normalized CKNNA，k=10）衡量两种邻域的重合度。
article.results: 在12个微调VLA上，S²与SimplerEnv成功率Pearson r=+0.717（模型bootstrap 95% CI +0.436至+0.912）；8个原始VLM的S²与微调后VLA成功率r=+0.681、p=0.031，而VQA分数为r=-0.154。6个WAM上r=+0.718、p=0.054；5个真实机器人策略上r=+0.831、p=0.041。负对照把参考数据从双机械臂ALOHA换成单臂DROID后，3个WAM的相关从r=+0.999降到+0.246；冻结视觉编码器使S²降41%、成功率降40%。
article.why_it_matters: 若能在闭环评测前用S²筛模型和VLM骨干，可降低评估成本，并提供成功率之外的表示层诊断。作者认为这也指向直接优化感官-运动对齐的训练方向。
article.limitations: 作者明确承认证据以相关性为主，尚未证明把S²当训练目标能提升成功率；模型家族、基准和训练配方覆盖有限，每类比较模型数少，真机仅一个设定。更需注意的是，真机r=+0.831来自探索性horizon h=110，预设的h=7只有r=+0.429、p=0.236，WAM的p=0.054也未达0.05。
article.figure_caption_zh: S²在微调VLA、原始VLM、WAM和真实机器人策略上均与下游任务成功率正相关，支持其作为离线代理指标。

Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution
in Autoregressive Video Generation
Ruopeng Gao
1,∗
, Yukun Huang
2,‡
, Jiarui Hu
3
, Shuai Wang
1
,
Wenbo Hu
2
, Ying Shan
2
, Limin Wang
1,†
1
Nanjing University
2
ARC Lab, Tencent IEG
3
Zhejiang University
Project page:
https://hellorpg.github.io/looking-ahead/
Code:
https://github.com/TencentARC/Looking-Ahead
Abstract
Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve.
Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution.
We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context.
Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged.
Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution.
Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
1
Introduction
Autoregressive video generation
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Yuan et al., 2026
)
has emerged as an important direction in video generation, offering a flexible paradigm in which visual sequences can be extended continuously.
It typically operates through chunk-wise temporal rollout, where each new chunk is generated conditioned on preceding visual context.
As an important pathway toward generative world modeling
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Valevski et al., 2025
)
, such a history-conditioned generator is expected not merely to produce plausible successive chunks, but also to model how visual scenes evolve over time.
However, the ability to extend a video does not by itself guarantee that the model has learned how the scene should evolve.
We argue that a key reason is standard teacher forcing, where the current chunk is denoised given ground-truth history.
Due to the strong temporal redundancy in videos, neighboring chunks often share highly similar appearance and motion patterns.
As a result, the model may rely heavily on local visual continuity to recover the current chunk, creating a shortcut that provides limited pressure to capture the underlying dynamics of scene evolution.
This motivates us to seek supervision that goes beyond what can be readily inferred from local visual continuity.
A natural place to look is farther into the future.
As the prediction target moves farther from the observed history, local appearance and motion continuity provide less direct support for recovering the target, thereby placing greater pressure on the model to capture temporal progression.
Importantly, this supervision comes directly from the training video itself, without requiring external pretrained representations or semantic alignment
(
Yu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
.
Motivated by this intuition, we introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), a simple auxiliary objective for autoregressive video diffusion training.
In addition to denoising the target chunk under standard teacher forcing, FCP uses the learned intermediate representation to predict a target beyond the current chunk, without exposing the model to the intervening ground-truth visual context.
This complementary objective places additional training pressure on the learned representations to capture information relevant to visual evolution, a capability fundamental to effective temporal rollout in autoregressive video generation.
Importantly, FCP is introduced only during training and leaves the original autoregressive inference process unchanged.
To assess whether this additional supervision improves the modeling of visual evolution, we focus on physical plausibility as a concrete and challenging evaluation dimension.
Our method demonstrates improved physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training under matched data exposure and training budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision.
These results highlight the potential of exploiting richer predictive supervision from existing video data, rather than relying solely on increased training resources.
Beyond the improvements in generation quality, we further examine how FCP affects the intermediate video representations.
Interestingly, the introduced supervision induces more pronounced spatiotemporal organization in the representation space, suggesting that FCP also meaningfully reshapes the representations learned during training.
This finding highlights the potential of future prediction for learning representations better suited to autoregressive video generation, which may further benefit generative world modeling.
2
Related Work
2.1
Autoregressive Video Diffusion
Conventional video diffusion models typically synthesize fixed-duration clips in a single denoising process
(
Ho et al., 2022
;
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Team, 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
Autoregressive video diffusion instead extends video chunk by chunk, conditioning on preceding visual context
(
Voleti et al., 2022
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Teng et al., 2025
)
.
This formulation supports streaming generation and provides a basis for interactive visual simulation and generative world modeling
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Valevski et al., 2025
)
.
Prior work addresses rollout quality by adapting bidirectional models into causal few-step generators through distribution matching or adversarial training
(
Yin et al., 2025
;
Lin et al., 2025
)
, exposing models to self-generated histories or extended student rollouts
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, and examining the causal compatibility of teacher supervision with student generation
(
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Zheng et al., 2026
)
.
Other approaches manage historical context through active windows, cached states, or global anchors
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, while selective retrieval and cache compression balance long-range consistency against computational and memory costs
(
Cai et al., 2025
;
Samuel et al., 2026
;
Ji et al., 2026
)
.
Our approach complements these directions by adding future-chunk supervision to teacher-forced training without prescribing rollout distillation or inference-time context management.
2.2
Representation Alignment for Generation
Aligning intermediate diffusion features with vision foundation models can accelerate training and improve generation quality
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
.
Video extensions use cross-frame and multi-feature alignment
(
Hwang et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2025
)
, or relational supervision targeting physical plausibility
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
.
These methods rely on targets from external pretrained encoders
(
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
, which may complicate scaling to large video corpora.
Our approach instead derives supervision from future chunks in the training videos, without an additional pretrained vision model, offering a data-native path toward scaling.
Our work was developed independently of and concurrently with Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, the closest related approach. We include relevant comparisons in our experiments and provide a more detailed discussion in the appendix.

4.1
Future Chunk Prediction
Building upon the teacher-forced formulation in Section
3.3
, each target chunk is denoised conditioned on its temporally contiguous ground-truth history.
As discussed in Section
1
, the strong temporal redundancy of video allows this immediately preceding correct context to provide substantial support for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to capture temporal progression and potentially hindering the learning of representations that capture visual evolution.
This observation suggests a simple design principle: we seek a learning signal that is less directly supported by such immediately preceding context, yet remains intrinsic to the training video itself, allowing the supervision to scale naturally with video data without relying on external pretrained representations.
To this end, we introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), which supplements next-chunk denoising with an auxiliary task of predicting temporally more distant chunks from the same video.
By excluding the intervening chunks from the visual context, this task discourages reliance on local temporal continuity and encourages stronger predictive representations of visual evolution.

For the autoregressive generator, we use a standard video diffusion model

Feature Conditioning.
To capture information at different semantic levels, we extract features from multiple generator layers, concatenate them along the channel dimension at corresponding token positions, and fuse them with an MLP.
Inspired by prior AdaLN-based conditioning designs
(
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Pan et al., 2026

Wang et al., 2026a
)
, we inject the fused features into every auxiliary DiT block through token-wise AdaLN modulation, preserving fine-grained conditioning across spatiotemporal positions.
Asymmetric Text Conditioning.
Unlike the text-conditioned main generator, the auxiliary predictors omit text cross-attention from every DiT block.
Consistent with equation
6
, this asymmetry blocks a direct pathway through which text prompts could leak cues about future events, encouraging the predictors to rely on the generator’s source representations instead.
This design also reduces the predictors’ parameter count and computational cost.

Inference.
At inference, we discard all FCP-specific modules, retaining the same autoregressive generator and rollout procedure as the teacher-forcing baseline without additional overhead.
Qualitative visualizations of the auxiliary predictors suggest that they capture plausible future evolution despite limited visual fidelity.
We leave their potential use for sampling acceleration through early-stage denoising or generation enhancement through prediction ensembling to future work.

5.1
Implementation Details
We initialize our autoregressive generators from official Wan checkpoints
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
For our implementation, we choose the image-to-video setting, treating the initial frame as fixed clean context and generating subsequent chunks of three latent frames.
Each auxiliary predictor contains three DiT blocks initialized from the corresponding generator; the generators and predictors are then jointly optimized.

5.6
Representation Space Analysis
Beyond physical-plausibility evaluation, we visualize the generator’s intermediate representations using query-to-token similarity maps.
As shown in Figure
5
, teacher forcing produces diffuse responses extending into unrelated regions, whereas FCP yields more selective responses aligned with the queried object and visually related instances.
Figure
6
further shows that high-similarity regions remain aligned with corresponding content as it moves across frames.
Together, these visualizations suggest that FCP-trained representations capture clearer spatial structure and meaningful temporal correspondence.
We believe that such semantically structured representations may provide a useful foundation for future world models.
6
Conclusion
We introduced Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective that predicts temporally separated chunks from the same training video in autoregressive video diffusion.
Optimized jointly with the standard teacher-forced denoising objective, FCP provides complementary supervision to the generator’s intermediate representations without requiring an additional pretrained encoder.
The auxiliary predictors are removed at inference, leaving the autoregressive generation process unchanged.
Controlled comparisons show improved physical plausibility across model scales and conditioning settings.
More surprisingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP also induces a more structured representation space, which we believe may be important for autoregressive world models.
Together, these findings support future prediction as a promising training principle for autoregressive video generation.

The 1.3B and 5B configurations may appear to follow different design principles.
These differences arise from choices made at different stages of development.
For source-layer selection, the 1.3B configuration evolved from an early single-layer variant using layer 15, subsequently expanded to include both shallower and deeper features.
For the 5B model, we select approximately evenly spaced layers backward from the final block to provide direct auxiliary supervision across the generator’s depth, while excluding the earliest blocks whose features may not yet be sufficiently semantically informative.
Computational constraints have prevented a systematic comparison of these source-layer selection strategies, which we may revisit in future scaling efforts.
For auxiliary initialization, the 1.3B configuration follows the early variant using source features from layer 15, with blocks 17–19 used to initialize the auxiliary predictor.
For the 5B model, we instead initialize from the final backbone blocks, decoupling this choice from the source-layer configuration and simplifying subsequent scale-up.
These blocks are also closer to the output and are chosen to better match the output head, which is likewise initialized from the original generator.
Preliminary experiments suggest that this initialization strategy may offer a modest improvement in early-stage convergence.

Appendix C
Limitations and Discussions
C.1
Comparison with Next Forcing
As discussed in Section
2.2
, Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
explores a closely related future-prediction idea.
Importantly, our work was developed independently of and concurrently with Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
. The initial FCP prototype design was completed before the Next Forcing paper became publicly available. While both works explore future prediction for autoregressive video generation, we target different tasks and adopt distinct methodological and experimental designs. First, Next Forcing is primarily framed around world-action modeling and robotic action learning, whereas we focus on autoregressive video generation as a pathway toward generative world modeling.
Conditioning Context and Efficiency.
Second, Next Forcing conditions its auxiliary predictors on the full visible history
𝐡
≤
k
\mathbf{h}_{\leq k}
, whereas ours use only
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
. As discussed in Section
4.1
, this choice encourages the source-chunk representation itself to compactly encode information predictive of future evolution. Beyond this design rationale, we test the context choice with a full-context FCP variant shown in Figure
4
. At matched training steps, the two FCP variants achieve comparable IQ scores, but ours requires roughly 40–50% less training compute to attain the same performance. Our source-chunk-only design thus offers a more efficient and scalable form of future-prediction supervision, an important consideration when training larger video generators.
Parallel versus Chained Prediction.
Third, Next Forcing adopts a chained prediction architecture inspired by language-model MTP
(
DeepSeek-AI, 2024
)
, whereas our offset-specific predictors operate in parallel from
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
. Unlike discrete-token prediction, diffusion-based video prediction gives each auxiliary predictor a partially noised future latent. Chaining may therefore pass information from an intermediate future chunk to later predictors along the red path in Figure
2(a)
, weakening the intended predictive supervision on
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
.
Consistent with this concern, the chained variant retains a gain at 1.3B with three offsets, but offers only a marginal I2V gain and no V2V gain at 5B models. This decline suggests that information leakage in chained prediction may become more consequential at larger model scales, as higher-capacity models can more readily exploit intermediate future information and thereby weaken the intended supervision.
Parallel prediction, by contrast, remains effective in both settings (Tables
4
and
2
), supporting its use for visual future prediction.
Other Differences.
Our different task emphasis also shapes several design and evaluation choices.
We supervise both clean-context and noisy-target representations, and use token-wise AdaLN to inject source features into the auxiliary predictors, drawing on prior experience in visual generation
(
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Pan et al., 2026
)
.
Our evaluation focuses on the physical plausibility of generated videos, reflecting our interest in visual evolution rather than action-planning performance.
C.2
Potential Inference-Time Applications
Figure
11
suggests that the auxiliary predictors can anticipate future dynamics, although their outputs do not yet reach the visual fidelity expected of final video generation.
Replacing the main generator with these branches throughout denoising may therefore compromise output quality.
One possibility is to use them during early, high-noise denoising before handing the sample to the main generator for refinement, potentially reducing sampling cost.
Alternatively, combining their predictions with those of the main generator may improve the reliability of the resulting future evolution.
These inference-time applications remain untested and are left for future work.
C.3
From-Scratch Pretraining and Further Scaling
Due to computational constraints, our experiments do not cover larger model scales or training on substantially longer videos.
We therefore leave broader scaling and evaluation across longer temporal horizons to future work.
All current models are initialized from pretrained bidirectional video diffusion checkpoints rather than pretrained from scratch.
In our experiments, adapting these checkpoints for autoregressive training led to early-stage performance degradation.
We suspect that bidirectional and autoregressive models may organize their representations differently, so this initialization could limit the extent to which FCP’s benefits emerge.
We aim to investigate large-scale from-scratch pretraining with FCP as a native objective for autoregressive world models, together with more diverse, higher-quality data tailored to this setting.

article.headline: 让自回归视频模型预测更远的未来块
article.lede: 南京大学与腾讯ARC等提出FCP：训练时让模型跳过中间片段预测更远的未来块，推理零额外开销，物理合理性提升。
article.problem: 自回归视频扩散模型按块滚动生成，但标准教师强制训练下，视频强烈的时间冗余使模型可以靠相邻块的局部外观与运动连续性「抄近路」完成当前块的去噪，缺少建模场景如何演化的压力。能续写视频，并不等于学到了世界该如何变化。
article.method: 作者提出未来块预测（FCP）作为辅助目标：在标准教师强制去噪之外，用生成器对应块 k 的中间隐状态 h_k 去预测时间上相隔 Δ 个块的未来块，且不给模型看中间那些块，从而削弱对局部连续性的依赖。实现上采用独立参数的轻量 DiT 分支，多个偏移量并行预测，互相不传递信息，也不接文本交叉注意力，仅通过 token 级 AdaLN 注入主干多层特征；辅助损失回传到主干隐状态。推理时全部 FCP 模块被丢弃，生成流程与基线完全一致。
article.results: 在 Physics-IQ Verified 上，1.3B 模型的 IQ 从 27.6 提升到 30.9；5B 模型的 I2V 从 30.4 升到 33.8、V2V 从 40.6 升到 44.4。消融显示，只正则化干净上下文或噪声目标分别带来 1.2 和 2.3 的 IQ 增益，两者合用增益 3.3；并行预测比链式预测高 0.8（30.1→30.9），加入文本条件反而使 IQ 下降 1.1。训练效率上，要达到相同 IQ 29 和 30，本文设计估计比使用全历史表示 h_≤k 的变体少 42.6% 和 50.7% 的训练算力。其他基准上，WorldModelBench 总分 7.22→7.64，PAI-Bench-G 领域分 81.13→82.38，PhyGround 提升较小（物理项 2.75→2.80）。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明提升自回归视频生成可以靠从现有视频中挖掘更强的预测监督信号，而不必只靠堆算力或引入外部预训练编码器，且推理零成本。可视化还显示 FCP 训练出的表示空间有更清晰的空间选择性与跨帧对应关系，这对构建自回归世界模型可能有用。
article.limitations: 所有模型都从预训练的双向视频扩散检查点（Wan）初始化，而非从头训练，作者自己怀疑双向与自回归表示组织方式不同，可能限制 FCP 效果的发挥；消融主要在 1.3B 上完成，链式变体在 5B 上几乎没有增益甚至不涨，说明规模变大后信息泄漏问题更严重。此外表示结构化只是定性可视化，与 Next Forcing 属同期独立工作，训练数据含不可公开的内部语料，跨模型对比也难以归因于方法本身。
article.figure_caption_zh: FCP 总览：自回归主干的多层中间表示经 MLP 融合后，通过 token 级 AdaLN 调制并行的辅助 Transformer 块，用于预测未来块。

Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Thanks:
§
Work done while interning at Amazon FAR
Thanks:
†
Amazon FAR team co-lead
Sihang Li
Xiaofeng Guo
Jinkun Cao
Charlie Cheng
Ruihan Yang
Chen Feng
Guanya Shi
Haozhi Qi
Affiliation:
Amazon FAR (Frontier AI & Robotics) New York University Carnegie Mellon University University of Chicago
Abstract
Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present
FLoRe
, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website:
https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/
.
I
Introduction
Humanoid robots offer a general-purpose embodiment for working in environments built for people. Many tasks in these environments, such as pushing a cart, moving a heavy box, and wiping a surface, require the robot to control contact force as well as motion. However, learned humanoid loco-manipulation is commonly formulated as generating and tracking motion references
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
. Tracking a demonstrated hand trajectory alone does not reproduce the demonstrated force, which also depends on contact geometry, stiffness, and object motion. Unlike a fixed-base arm, a humanoid must stay balanced under these contact loads, coordinating its hands, torso, and legs while regulating force.
Two difficulties stand in the way. The first is data: imitation learning requires scalable demonstrations that record contact force alongside motion. Existing robot-free interfaces for whole-body demonstration collection record motion but not force
[
4
,
5
]
.
The second is execution: the robot must accurately apply the desired force. Current learned humanoid whole-body controllers track motion alone, or treat force as a disturbance to reject or a stiffness to lower
[
6
,
7
]
. Tracking a commanded contact force has been shown only on quadrupedal manipulators, using estimated rather than measured force
[
8
,
9
]
, which is not accurate enough. A humanoid instead needs to track force at both hands together with whole-body motion while maintaining balance.
We present
FLoRe
, a framework for learning
force-reactive
humanoid loco-manipulation. Its robot-free force-annotated data collection system records contact force with each demonstration; the policy learns to predict this force, and the controller tracks it. The system pairs two UMI-style handheld grippers
[
10
]
with a chest tracker and two ankle trackers
[
4
,
11
]
. Each gripper carries a wrist camera, a pose tracker, and a six-axis F/T sensor
[
12
,
13
]
. The applied wrench is thus recorded alongside hand, torso, and foot motion. The robot uses the same gripper–sensor assembly.
For the high-level planner, we propose a force-reactive diffusion policy
[
14
]
. It observes wrist images, robot state, and the measured wrench at each hand, then predicts a chunk
[
15
]
of action, gripper widths, and per-hand desired force. Force enters as both an input and an output. The input lets the policy react to interactions that images do not reveal. The output is commanded to the controller
[
13
]
, rather than used only as an auxiliary target
[
16
]
. This connects the force measured during demonstration to the deployed force.
To track the commanded forces, we develop a whole-body controller with hybrid compliance. It outputs only joint positions, so each hand’s force command becomes a shift of its position target. In contact, an integral of the force error measured at the wrist adjusts this shift until the hand exerts the commanded force, whatever the contact stiffness. Along uncommanded axes, the same integral lets the hand yield to external pushes. Each hand thus tracks force along the commanded direction and complies along the others, without switching modes. We train the controller in simulation
[
17
]
and deploy it on the robot using wrist F/T measurements.
We deploy
FLoRe
on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three whole-body contact-rich tasks: pushing a gantry hanging another robot, bimanual box rotation, and board wiping. In simulation, the controller realises in-contact force error of about 1 N per hand while tracking whole-body motion. On the real robot,
FLoRe
succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller with force commands disabled. Withholding only the force command reduces success to 36.7%, while removing only the force observation reduces it to 66.7%. Both contribute to the final performance.
Our key contributions are:
•
A robot-free pipeline for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation from demonstrations that record both motion and contact wrench.
•
A learned whole-body controller that tracks per-hand force together with keypoint motion while remaining compliant to external forces and maintaining balance.
•
Evaluation in simulation and on three contact-rich tasks on a Unitree G1, where force commands and force observations both improve task success over position-only control.
II
Related Work
II-A
Force Sensing for Loco-Manipulation Data Collection and Policy Learning
Robot-free data collection builds on UMI
[
10
]
. Force-aware variants add wrist or fingertip sensing, but deploy on fixed-base arms with analytic impedance or admittance control
[
12
,
13
,
18
]
. Humanoid extensions instead collect whole-body motion and execute it with learned trackers, but do not record contact force
[
4
,
11
]
. WT-UMI is the closest interface for humanoids, although it measures only a scalar normal force at each palm and relies on paired teleoperation data
[
19
]
. Our interface records a six-axis wrench at each hand together with torso motion, and its demonstrations require no robot-side data.
Measured force has been used to condition visuomotor policies
[
20
,
21
]
. Other work predicts stiffness, admittance gains, or virtual position targets that are executed by an impedance controller
[
22
,
23
,
24
,
12
]
. More closely related methods predict a wrench trajectory together with pose, but execute it on fixed-base arms through analytic force controllers
[
13
,
25
,
26
]
. On humanoids, WT-UMI passes a scalar normal-force prediction to an admittance rule
[
19
]
. UniFP is the closest formulation. It predicts 3-D force commands, but deploys end-effector force control only on a quadrupedal manipulator. Its humanoid interface exposes force only at the base
[
9
]
. Our planner instead predicts per-hand pose, gripper, and wrench trajectories from handheld demonstrations, then sends the predicted force to a learned humanoid whole-body controller.
Fig. 1:
Overview of our
FLoRe
framework.
(B)
Two handheld UMI-style grippers with F/T sensors and three additional trackers record images, motion, and contact force without a robot.
(C)
A force-reactive diffusion policy takes images, state and measured force as input and outputs keypoint motion and desired force commands at 30 Hz.
(A)
The hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking converts the force command into a shift of the target along the force direction, so that one RL policy tracks motion and force simultaneously while remaining compliant along other directions.
II-B
Force for Low-Level Control
Learned legged and humanoid controllers usually either withstand external force or yield to it through commanded stiffness or damping
[
6
,
27
,
28
,
29
,
7
,

IV
Experiments
We evaluate whether a humanoid can learn force-reactive loco-manipulation from robot-free demonstrations. Experiments in simulation and on the robot test four capabilities:
•
Whole-body force tracking
: tracking per-hand force commands and whole-body motion with one learned controller.
•
Sustained contact
: making contact and holding an appropriate force while the hands move with or along the object.
•
Bimanual and whole-body coordination
: applying force with both hands while the torso and legs balance and walk.
•
Robustness to force variation
: completing tasks when resistance changes within or across episodes but is not visible in the images, e.g., a heavier load or box mass.

IV-C
Push Gantry
Task.
As shown in Fig.
b, the robot places both hands on a heavy wheeled gantry, from which a second humanoid hangs, and walks it forward to a target distance. The demonstrated hand motion does not specify how hard to push, yet the gantry does not move until the push overcomes its static friction. This is the only task recorded with ankle trackers, so the policy predicts all five keypoints. A rollout succeeds if the gantry reaches the target distance without a stop.
Capabilities.
Bimanual and whole-body coordination:
the legs and torso produce the push while the two hands balance their forces; otherwise the gantry drifts from its heading.
Sustained contact:
both hands must keep contact as the gantry accelerates and the robot steps.
Robustness to force variation:
the hanging humanoid swings as the gantry rolls, so the resistance changes over time.

F2: Force-reactive policies resolve failures that motion alone cannot distinguish.
With the same demonstrations and controller,
DP

FLoRe
in 80% (Table

V
Conclusion
We presented
FLoRe
, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation from robot-free demonstrations that record both motion and contact wrench. Our hybrid compliance whole-body controller tracks the learned force commands, allowing the humanoid to sustain contact, coordinate both hands, and apply force while walking and balancing. On three tasks, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy. By making force a shared interface between demonstrations, policies, and whole-body control,
FLoRe
extends robot-free imitation learning to contact-rich skills that motion alone cannot specify.

article.headline: FLoRe：无机器人演示学习力反应人形全身操作
article.lede: FLoRe 用带六轴力/力矩传感器的手持夹爪采集无机器人演示，让扩散策略预测每手力指令，并由全身控制器跟踪。
article.problem: 许多日常任务不仅要跟踪运动，还要控制接触力；人形机器人需双手与全身协调施力并保持平衡，单靠运动轨迹无法指定力。无机器人演示接口通常只记录运动不记录力，而现有人形全身控制器多只跟踪运动，或把力当作扰动/降低刚度，难以准确跟踪双手力指令。
article.method: FLoRe 用两个带六轴 F/T 传感器、腕相机和位姿跟踪器的手持 UMI 式夹爪，配合胸部与脚踝跟踪器采集无机器人演示。力反应扩散策略以腕图像、机器人状态和实测力为输入，预测关键点运动、夹爪宽度和每手力指令。混合柔顺全身控制器把力指令转成沿力方向的目标偏移，并用实测力误差积分跟踪力，在其他方向保持柔顺。
article.results: 在仿真中，控制器对 5–25 N 的每手力指令达到 1.03–1.06 的跟踪增益，接触力误差约 1 N，但无力指令时传感器仍有 1.25–1.50 N 底噪。真实 Unitree G1 上，FLoRe 在三个接触密集任务中成功率为 80%（24/30），位置-only 策略为 26.7%（8/30）；去掉力指令降至 36.7%（11/30），去掉力观测降至 66.7%（20/30）。真实力跟踪中，x 轴稳态力约达指令的 91%，平均稳态误差约 1.1 N，平均 1.8 s 进入 ±1 N 带，稳态波动约 ±0.3–0.5 N。
article.why_it_matters: 把力作为演示、策略和全身控制之间的共享接口，使无机器人模仿学习能覆盖仅靠运动无法指定的接触密集全身操作。对推车、搬箱和擦表面等需要持续接触的任务具有直接意义。
article.limitations: 局限包括：训练中的虚拟接触面无摩擦、力指令仅为法向，切向载荷未在训练中出现；真实部署需将低于 1.5 N 的指令置零并限幅 25 N，横向和向下力增益较低且会串扰到其他轴。此外每任务仅 10 次 rollout，去掉力观测的下降（66.7%）只是趋势，统计显著性主要见于去掉力指令。
article.figure_caption_zh: FLoRe 框架总览：两个带 F/T 传感器的手持 UMI 式夹爪和三个跟踪器无机器人记录图像、运动与接触力，力反应扩散策略以图像、状态和实测力为输入、以 30 Hz 输出关键点运动和每手力指令，混合柔顺全身控制器把力指令转成目标偏移以同时跟踪运动与力并保持其他方向柔顺。

figure.caption: {Overview of our framework.} {(B)}~Two handheld UMI-style grippers with F/T sensors and three additional trackers record images, motion, and contact force without a robot. {(C)}~A force-reactive diffusion policy takes images, state and measured force as input and outputs keypoint motion and desired force commands at 30\,Hz. {(A)}~The hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking converts the force command into a shift of the target along the force direction, so that one RL policy tracks motion and force simultaneously while remaining compliant along other directions.
