Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation
Yucheng Mao
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Chongjian Ge
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Zhuowen Tu
Affiliation:
University of California, San Diego
Hao Tan
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Hanwen Jiang
Affiliation:
Adobe Research
Abstract
Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained
pixel details. We propose a learning paradigm that assigns these roles to
autoregressive pretraining for knowledge acquisition and diffusion post-training
for high-fidelity rendering.
Within this framework, we study the objective, representation, and scaling of knowledge acquisition and rendering.
Controlled comparisons identify autoregression as the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, improving both learning efficiency and final generation
quality. We further find that AR-only generation quality does not necessarily correlate with final performance; semantic quality matters more. This motivates a
purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone, without an
image decoder or reconstruction loss. We establish compute-optimal scaling laws
for knowledge acquisition and rendering, and find that autoregressive pretraining
lowers the fitted asymptotic rendering loss compared with pixel diffusion models trained from scratch. Guided by the laws, we train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, achieving 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench and validating the proposed paradigm at scale.
Figure 1:
Strong visual generation with compute-efficient training.
Left
: DPG-Bench versus training compute; marker size denotes model
size. Our 3B model achieves competitive performance with only 6,600 H100
GPU-hours (
48
×
48\times
less
than Z-Image-Base).
Right
: Text-to-Image generated samples.
1
Introduction
Visual generation has advanced primarily through two modeling paradigms:
autoregressive models predict discrete visual tokens
(
Sun et al., 2024
;
Tian et al., 2024
;
Pang et al., 2024
)
, while latent diffusion
models (LDMs) and pixel diffusion models (PDMs) denoise continuous signals
(
Ho et al., 2020
;
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Peebles and Xie, 2023
)
. They are
typically compared as competing paradigms, asking which produces better images.
Yet this comparison asks each paradigm to solve two distinct learning problems:
acquiring high-level visual knowledge
and
rendering it into detailed images
.
We therefore argue that these problems need not favor the same objective, and look beyond
their competition to uncover the synergy between autoregression and diffusion.
We find that the two problems indeed favor different objectives:
autoregression for visual knowledge acquisition and diffusion for
rendering
. This specialization gives rise to a natural
pretraining–post-training paradigm
, where autoregressive pretraining
provides the foundation on which diffusion is post-trained for rendering. This
mirrors modern language models, where broad knowledge is first acquired and
subsequently adapted toward desired behaviors. At inference, the autoregressive
rollout provides a structured visual representation that conditions diffusion,
connecting the two learning processes. Across the evaluated protocols and
compute budgets, this specialization consistently yields stronger generators,
revealing the synergy between the two objectives.
Specializing autoregression for knowledge acquisition changes what it should
learn. In visual autoregressive models, the tokenizer defines the
prediction target and therefore shapes the information the model is
incentivized to capture. Conventional tokenizers preserve low-level appearance
for image reconstruction. Once rendering is delegated to diffusion, however,
the autoregressive representation no longer needs to support reconstruction or
standalone image generation. Across different tokenizers, we find a striking
dissociation: neither reconstruction quality nor AR-only generation quality
determines post-training generation performance; semantic quality does. This
motivates
Semantic-LM
, a semantic tokenizer trained through language
supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. Visual
tokenization thus shifts from preserving pixels for reconstruction to providing
semantic learning targets for autoregressive knowledge acquisition.
Separating knowledge acquisition from rendering introduces a new question for scaling visual generation: how should compute be allocated between the two stages? We establish scaling laws for autoregressive pretraining and diffusion post-training that characterize the effects of model size, data, and compute and guide compute-optimal allocation. These laws also reveal a broader benefit of autoregressive pretraining. At matched model and data scales, diffusion post-training achieves both lower loss and a lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss than PDM trained from scratch. This finding suggests that autoregressive pretraining improves the attainable performance of diffusion rendering beyond accelerating convergence speed.
Given an available training budget of approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, we
use our scaling laws to select a roughly 3B-parameter model and allocate compute
between pretraining and post-training. The resulting model achieves strong
text-to-image generation (Fig.
1
), reaching 0.86 on
GenEval
(
Ghosh et al., 2023
)
and 87.78 on
DPG-Bench
(
Hu et al., 2024
)
. This performance is achieved with approximately
1/48
of the estimated training compute of
Z-Image-Base
(
Z-Image Team et al., 2025
)
, while attaining comparable DPG-Bench
performance.
2
Method
As shown in Fig.
2
, our framework assigns visual
knowledge acquisition and rendering to distinct learning objectives. During
pretraining, a frozen visual tokenizer converts images into discrete tokens,
which a text-conditioned autoregressive (AR) model learns to predict. We then
freeze the AR backbone and add trainable pixel-diffusion modules that reuse its
attention projections and representations for rendering. During post-training,
the renderer conditions on tokens from ground-truth images; at inference, these
are replaced by tokens generated autoregressively from the text prompt.

Autoregressive pretraining acquires visual knowledge through discrete token prediction. The pretrained backbone is then frozen and augmented with diffusion modules that reuse its attention and representations to render high-fidelity images. This division of labor specializes autoregression for knowledge acquisition and diffusion for rendering.

Autoregressive image models predict learned visual tokens

Combining autoregression and diffusion.
Several works combine autoregressive and diffusion modeling within a single
generative framework. MAR
(

)
uses diffusion as the conditional

5
Conclusion
We propose a visual generation paradigm that separates knowledge acquisition from rendering: autoregressive pretraining learns visual knowledge, and diffusion renders it into pixels. Through controlled experiments and scaling analysis, we identify three advantages of this approach. First, semantic tokens provide effective pretraining targets without requiring image reconstruction or standalone AR generation. Second, stage-specific scaling laws guide compute allocation, while the lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss suggests benefits of the pretrained pipeline beyond faster convergence. Third, these findings translate into a compute-efficient text-to-image generator that achieves 0.86 on GenEval and 87.78 on DPG-Bench with approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours of training. Together, our results support a practical approach to visual generation that tailors the learning objective, representation, and compute budget to each stage.

Semantic-Recon.
An IBQ codebook quantizes the frozen post-merger visual features, and a transformer decoder reconstructs the input
image from the quantized representation. The decoder has 12 layers, hidden
width 768, and 12 attention heads. We train the codebook and decoder on
in-house training data for 80,000 updates. The objective combines image
reconstruction, VGG-based LPIPS perceptual supervision, and quantization
loss, with respective weights 1, 0.5, and 1, together with the entropy
regularizer specified above. The pretrained visual feature extractor remains
frozen. We maintain an exponential moving average of the trainable parameters
with decay 0.9999 and a 2,000-update warmup.
Semantic-LM.
We freeze Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, including its visual feature extractor and
language model, and train only the IBQ codebook. Quantized visual features
condition the frozen language model, and next-token cross-entropy on the
supervised text targets provides the codebook’s training signal. This
language-modeling objective is not restricted to image captions. We train
for 40,000 updates on the 200B version of
DataComp-VLM
(
Farina et al., 2026
)
, using the shared optimization and
resolution settings above. The objective combines language-modeling
cross-entropy with entropy regularization at weight 0.05. No image decoder
or image reconstruction loss is used.
A.2
Controlled Generation Comparisons
Model capacity.
For the direct-pixel and AR controls, we match the total parameter count
of the final generators at approximately
400M total parameters. The PDM has width 1408, 16 layers,

feed-forward dimension, but only eight layers. Diffusion post-training adds
randomly initialized rendering modules, including separate diffusion
feed-forward layers, while keeping the AR parameters frozen. The AR-pretraining
backbone has approximately 250M parameters, and the rendering modules add
approximately 150M, giving a final generator of approximately 400M that matches
the PDM. This matched size refers to the final
generator, not to the number of parameters used during pretraining. Total parameter counts include the
frozen AR backbone and trainable rendering modules, count shared weights
once, and exclude external frozen text encoders and tokenizers.

A.9
Final Model Recipe and Evaluation
Final-model training.
The large-scale AR backbone has width 2304 and 27 layers. It uses frozen
Qwen3-4B text features from layers 9, 18, and 27, concatenated to 7680 dimensions;
feature extraction stops at layer 27 and uses BF16. AR pretraining uses a
global batch size of 2048 and a caption mixture of 70% flattened long
captions and 30% canonical structured captions.
The 150k-update AR curriculum uses 50k updates at the 256-resolution tier,
ramps toward a 50/25/25 mixture of the 256/512/1024 tiers over the next 50k,
and holds that mixture for the last 50k. These proportions count examples
within the global batch. This final-model recipe is separate from the
controlled comparisons in Tab.
2
.
We then freeze the AR backbone and train the diffusion modules for 100,000
updates with global batch size 512. Diffusion uses four times as many
visual target tokens per image as AR pretraining, so we reduce its image
batch size by a factor of four. This balances visual-target throughput
per update at a matched resolution. Guided by the prescribed
3
:
2
3{:}2
stage allocation, we use a matching ratio of pretraining to post-training
updates.
Post-training follows the diffusion resolution curriculum, preserving its
resolution proportions while reducing each resolution-specific batch size
proportionally to give global batch size 512. We use AdamW with weight decay
0.01 and base learning rate
8
×
10
−
4
8\times 10^{-4}
, selected by the post-training
learning-rate search in Appendix
A.5
.
Training cost.
The total training budget is approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours. Following
the prescribed
3
:
2
3{:}2
allocation, the nominal stage budgets are approximately
3,960 GPU-hours for AR pretraining and 2,640 GPU-hours for diffusion
post-training. These are budget allocations rather than separate measurements
of stage runtime.
Evaluation sampling.
We use an exponential moving average (EMA) of the trainable diffusion
parameters, with decay 0.9999 starting at update 20,000; the frozen AR
parameters remain unchanged.
We set AR classifier-free guidance (CFG) to 3 and use a 50-step Euler
sampler for diffusion, with AR-conditioning CFG 3 and text-conditioning
CFG 4. GenEval uses 553 prompts with one image per prompt and seed 42;
DPG-Bench uses 1,065 prompts with four images per prompt and seeds
42–45.
We use LLM-assisted prompt rewriting and select prompt variants using evaluation scores under fixed seeds.
Qualitative examples.
Fig.
11
presents 32 generations result from
the final text-to-image model.
A.10
Discussion: Semantic inference and rendering in frontier models.
Our results suggest a broader interpretation of the separation between knowledge
acquisition and rendering. We suspect that frontier visual generators
(
OpenAI, 2026
;
Ideogram,
;
Reve, 2026
)
increasingly perform substantial
semantic inference before committing to pixel generation. An autoregressive
process can expand a user request into a richer specification through text or
visual tokens, structured representations, retrieved information, or agentic
interaction. Prompt rewriting and long textual rollouts are simple instances of
this principle
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
: additional context progressively
specifies the desired image and reduces the ambiguity left to the renderer.
Under this view, the role of autoregression is not necessarily to produce an
image that can already be decoded, but to resolve
what
should be
rendered; diffusion can then focus on realizing this specification in pixels.
Semantic-LM admits a similar interpretation.
Its discrete visual tokens are trained through language supervision and need not
reconstruct or directly generate an image. They can instead be viewed as a
compressed semantic state between inference and rendering. In this sense, a
semantic visual rollout and a long textual rollout may serve related purposes:
both enrich the renderer’s conditioning context, but visual tokens may encode
the relevant information more compactly and in a spatially grounded form. This
perspective also raises a question not resolved by our current experiments.
Semantic-Recon retains reconstruction-oriented visual information, whereas
Semantic-LM more directly aligns its representation with language semantics.
Without explicit textual rollouts, our results do not determine which interface
is preferable when a generator already has access to rich language or agentic
context. We suspect that Semantic-LM may be particularly compatible with such
inference, while Semantic-Recon may preserve complementary visual information.
Understanding how textual, visual, structured, and agentic representations
should interact—and how much uncertainty each should resolve before
rendering—is an important direction for future visual generation systems.

article.headline: 先学后画：AR预训练加扩散渲染
article.lede: AR预训练学语义，扩散后训练做渲染；3B模型用6600 H100小时，GenEval 0.86、DPG 87.78。
article.problem: 视觉生成既要高层语义知识，又要细粒度像素细节。现有工作常把自回归与扩散当作竞争范式，要求同一目标同时承担知识获取与渲染。论文追问：两阶段是否应采用不同学习目标，AR应预测什么，算力又该如何在两阶段间分配。
article.method: 先用随机顺序的自回归离散token预测做预训练，学习语义知识；随后冻结AR backbone，加入像素扩散模块，用flow matching做渲染后训练。Semantic-LM tokenizer仅用语言监督学习码本，不需要图像解码器或重建损失。作者分别拟合预训练与后训练缩放定律，并据此给出约3:2的预训练/后训练算力分配。
article.results: 在最终约400M参数的受控比较中，AR→PDM取得GenEval 65.51、DPG-Bench 71.11，高于PDM的61.16/62.56、LDM的57.34/64.33和LDM→PDM的56.61/60.01。Tokenizer对比显示，重建最好的Recon后训练仅54.67/62.98，Semantic-Recon为65.51/71.11，无解码器的Semantic-LM为64.84/67.72。缩放拟合覆盖18个AR模型（55.71M–2.43B）和14个后训练模型（25.1M–2.03B），后训练拟合渐近损失约0.0701，低于从零PDM的约0.0788；导出的后训练算力占比r≈0.40。最终约3B模型用约6,600 H100 GPU-hours，取得GenEval 0.86、DPG-Bench 87.78，约为Z-Image-Base估计训练算力的1/48。
article.why_it_matters: 把知识获取与渲染解耦，让两个阶段分别选择目标、tokenizer和算力预算，为视觉生成提供了类似语言模型预训练-后训练的缩放配方。结果也显示，语义预训练可能降低扩散渲染的可达损失下限，而不只是加速收敛。
article.limitations: 作者提醒，跨系统分数比较因文本编码器、训练数据和评估设置不同而只能近似，且未证明算力分配最优；渐近损失比较把预训练权重与目标图像条件token作为整体，未分离各自贡献。此外，Semantic-LM没有图像解码器，不能独立生成图像。

Abstract.
The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions.
To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK).
Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns.
We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions.
Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model’s general capabilities.
Warning: this paper contains examples of unsafe content.
1.
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed in multilingual applications across diverse domains, yet their safety capabilities remain uneven across languages
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Shen et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2025b
)
. The same harmful request may be safely refused in one language but elicit an actionable unsafe response when reformulated in another. This inconsistency suggests that safety alignment does not transfer reliably across linguistic contexts and makes cross-lingual reformulation a potential means of bypassing model safeguards
(
Qi et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. Understanding how safety behavior is internally implemented across languages is therefore important for improving the cross-lingual safety of LLMs.
Figure 1.
Motivation of the Safety Kernel.
(a) Existing approaches improve multilingual safety through external alignment signals, while the shared internal target remains unclear.
(b) We identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel.
Existing work
(
Deng et al., 2024
;
Zhao et al., 2025a
;
Bu et al., 2026
;
Liang et al., 2026
)
has sought to improve multilingual safety through multilingual safety data, preference optimization, cross-lingual consistency constraints, and safety capability transfer. As illustrated in Figure
1
, these approaches primarily improve model behavior through external alignment signals, without explicitly localizing a shared internal target that can support safety intervention across languages. Whether LLMs contain a compact set of safety-related neurons that is shared across languages and amenable to direct intervention, thereby providing a common locus for modulating safety behavior in different languages, remains insufficiently explored.
To address this question, we analyze the cross-lingual safety behavior of LLMs at the neuron level and identify a set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, which we term the safety kernel (SK). Rather than anchoring discovery to English, we identify safety-related neurons independently in each language and extract their shared intersection to obtain the SK. Two complementary activation interventions show that suppressing the SK weakens safe refusal behavior across multiple languages, whereas injecting an SK activation state estimated from safe refusal generation reduces unsafe responses in other languages. These results indicate that the SK is not merely a statistical overlap across language-wise safety-neuron sets, but a shared neuronal subset that is functionally associated with cross-lingual safety behavior and amenable to direct intervention.
Building on the unified neuron locations provided by the SK, we further propose SK-Masked LoRA, which restricts safety fine-tuning updates to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK. We evaluate our approach across multiple LLMs and multilingual safety benchmarks. Experimental results show that the SK accounts for only a small fraction of the analyzed neurons, yet suppressing it causes substantially greater safety degradation than suppressing an equal number of randomly selected neurons. Transferring the SK activation state across languages reduces unsafe responses, while SK-Masked LoRA lowers attack success rates across multiple languages and exhibits a degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our findings reveal a shared neuronal structure associated with multilingual safety behavior and demonstrate its utility for cross-lingual safety intervention and targeted fine-tuning.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We identify language-wise safety neurons from parallel safe and unsafe prompts, and define their intersection as the cross-lingually shared safety kernel.
•
We verify the functional role of the SK in cross-lingual safety via activation suppression and state transfer interventions across multiple languages.
•
We propose SK-Masked LoRA, restricting updates to SK-aligned FFN outputs, improving safety and reducing attack success rates, including unseen languages.
2.
Related Work
Multilingual Safety and Cross-Lingual Alignment.
Large language models exhibit persistent safety disparities across languages, producing unsafe responses more frequently to malicious prompts in lower-resource languages
(
Shen et al., 2024
)
. XSafety
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
, MultiJail
(
Deng et al., 2024
)
, and subsequent evaluations
(
Friedrich et al., 2025
;
Kumar et al., 2025
)
further show that safety alignment does not transfer uniformly across linguistic contexts.
Existing approaches improve multilingual safety through preference optimization, cross-lingual alignment, parameter modification, and inference-time defense. General objectives such as DPO
(
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
, KTO
(
Ethayarajh et al., 2024
)
, R-DPO
(
Park et al., 2024
)
, and SimPO
(
Meng et al., 2024
)
are widely used for safety adaptation. Multilingual Refusal Alignment
(
Krasnodębska et al., 2026
)
shows that multilingual supervision provides broader refusal transfer than English-only alignment, while MPO
(
Zhao et al., 2025a
)
and MLC
(
Bu et al., 2026
)
improve cross-lingual safety through reward-gap reduction and consistency constraints. Layer-wise Swapping
(
Shin and Hwang, 2026
)
, SmoothLLM
(
Robey et al., 2023
)
, LDFighter
(
Dong et al., 2024
)
, and Sparse Weight Editing
(
Liang et al., 2026
)
further enhance safety through module replacement, inference-time defense, or sparse parameter updates. However, these methods do not explicitly identify a shared neuron-level intervention target across languages.
Internal Mechanisms of Multilingual LLM Safety.
Mechanistic interpretability studies localize model behavior to internal modules, activation directions, and sparse features
(
Meng et al., 2022a
;
Meng et al., 2022b
;
Zou et al., 2023
;
Cunningham et al., 2023
)
. For safety, refusal-direction studies
(
Arditi et al., 2024
)
identify low-dimensional refusal representations, while Safety Neurons
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
and related work
(
Zhao et al., 2026
)
localize neurons associated with safe refusal and jailbreak vulnerability. However, these analyses remain largely monolingual or English-centric.
Multilingual studies further distinguish shared and language-specific neurons
(
Tang et al., 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
, reveal language-independent representations in factual processing
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, and show that refusal directions can transfer across aligned languages
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. SS-Neuron
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
adopts an English-centered formulation, treating neurons shared between English and each target language as bridges for safety transfer.

Overview of the proposed framework.

Activation suppression and activation-state transfer provide two complementary views of the SK’s functional role. The former examines whether removing the shared coordinates weakens model safety, whereas the latter tests whether a safety-related state estimated from safe refusals can reduce unsafe responses in target languages. As shown in Table
2
, suppressing the SK increases ASR across multilingual harmful requests. Figure
3
shows that transferring the source SK state reduces the average ASR of the target languages across all three backbones. The average ASR decreases from 20.21 to 11.96 for Qwen3-8B, from 35.98 to 30.69 for Llama-3.1-8B, and from 5.18 to 3.17 for Gemma-2-9B-it. The magnitude of the improvement varies across models, but the direction of the effect remains consistent across all models. This result is complementary to activation suppression: removing the SK state weakens multilingual safety, whereas adding a state estimated from safe-response generation shifts target-language behavior toward safer outputs. Together, the two interventions show that the SK is associated not only with the presence of safety-related coordinates, but also with the activation states expressed through those coordinates during generation.

Experiments And Analysis
4.1.
Experimental Setup
Datasets.
We use AdvBench-x
(
Yong et al., 2023

and MultiJail
(

)
to evaluate multilingual safety. Unless otherwise specified, the SK is discovered from six languages: English (EN), Chinese (ZH), Italian (IT), Korean (KO), Thai (TH), and Bengali (BN). (
Hendrycks et al., 2020
)
and MGSM
(
Shi et al., 2022

Evaluation Metrics.
We use attack success rate (ASR) as the primary safety metric, defined as the proportion of harmful prompts judged to elicit successful attacks among all harmful prompts. Lower ASR indicates better safety performance. GPT-4o
(
Hurst et al., 2024

(

4.2.
Compare With SOTA Methods
Quantitative Results.
To quantitatively evaluate multilingual safety, we compare SK-Masked LoRA with representative safety methods on AdvBench-x and MultiJail in Table
3
. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA achieves the best or second-best average ASR across all four model–benchmark settings. Specifically, it reduces the average ASR from 28.22 to 1.20 and from 29.44 to 4.35 on Llama-3.1-8B, and from 3.42 to 0.34 and from 10.16 to 1.35 on Gemma-2-9B-it, with clear reductions also observed in Korean and Bengali. These results support the effectiveness of restricting safety fine-tuning to the FFN output dimensions corresponding to the SK in cross-lingual settings.
Qualitative Results.
To qualitatively examine the resulting behavioral change, we compare responses from the default model and SK-Masked LoRA to the same harmful request in Figure
4
. The example shows that SK-Masked LoRA produces a safer response than the default model. Specifically, the default model generates an unsafe response, whereas SK-Masked LoRA generates a safe refusal. This comparison is conducted under the same input prompt to ensure a controlled evaluation setting. Overall, this example illustrates a response-level change consistent with the quantitative ASR reductions reported in Table
3
, providing an intuitive view of how SK-constrained adaptation affects model behavior across multiple languages.
Generalization beyond SK Discovery Languages.
To evaluate whether SK-Masked LoRA generalizes beyond the languages used for SK discovery, we test it on Vietnamese, Javanese, German, Japanese, and Russian, none of which is used for language-specific safety-neuron identification or SK construction, as reported in Table
4
. The results show that SK-Masked LoRA reduces ASR across all five evaluated languages. Specifically, the average ASR decreases from 14.41 to 8.95 on Qwen3-8B and from 18.67 to 4.76 on Llama-3.1-8B. These results indicate a certain and measurable degree of generalization to languages excluded from SK discovery, without implying that they contain identical language-specific safety-neuron sets.

5.
Conclusion
This work reveals a safety kernel in multilingual LLMs at the neuron level, showing that cross-lingual safety behavior is closely associated with a compact, shared, and intervenable set of neurons. Activation suppression and state-transfer experiments further establish the functional relevance of the SK to model safety behavior. Building on this finding, SK-Masked LoRA effectively reduces attack success rates across multiple models and multilingual safety benchmarks, while extending the resulting safety improvements to languages excluded from SK discovery. Overall, our study advances the understanding of the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual safety and provides a new direction for more targeted and interpretable cross-lingual safety alignment.

article.headline: 跨语言安全核：只占0.12%的FFN坐标
article.lede: 研究者定位跨语言共享“安全核”，它仅占FFN输出坐标0.12%–0.15%，抑制它可保留约九成语言级安全效果。
article.problem: 大模型的安全能力在不同语言间明显不均衡，同一有害请求在一种语言被拒绝，换一种语言却可能得到可执行的回答，跨语言改写因此成为绕过安全护栏的捷径。现有对齐方法多依赖多语言安全数据、偏好优化或一致性约束等外部信号，没有明确指出一个跨语言共享的内部干预靶点；已有的神经元级安全研究又大多以英语为中心或只做单语分析。
article.method: 作者用多语言平行的安全与不安全提示，对每个FFN输出坐标计算SCAR分数，把标准化后的安全/不安全均值差与合并标准差之比，以及标准化均值差相加，每种语言取top-k=5000作为候选安全神经元，再对六种发现语言取交集得到安全核（SK）。随后通过抑制SK坐标、跨语言注入由安全拒答估计的SK激活状态这两种干预，检验SK与安全行为的功能关联。最后提出SK-Masked LoRA：冻结基座模型，只训练低秩适配器，并用二值掩码把适配器引起的输出变化限制在SK对应的FFN输出维度上。
article.results: 在MultiJail上，逐语言抑制SCAR选出的top-5000神经元使ASR升至69.63–81.06（Qwen3-8B）和69.52–81.27（Llama-3.1-8B-it），而随机抑制等量神经元时ASR接近默认（16.40→16.88、26.51→25.40）。SK仅占所分析FFN输出坐标的0.12%和0.15%，抑制它使平均ASR分别上升52.65和45.13点，保留约90%的语言级抑制效果。SK-Masked LoRA把Llama-3.1-8B-it在AdvBench-x与MultiJail上的平均ASR从28.22和29.44降到1.20和4.35，把Gemma-2-9B-it从3.42和10.16降到0.34和1.35；在未参与SK发现的五种语言上，平均ASR从14.41降到8.95（Qwen3-8B）、从18.67降到4.76（Llama-3.1-8B-it）。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一个可复用的内部干预靶点，把跨语言安全对齐从“堆多语言数据”转向“改对神经元坐标”，并且掩码只改动极小比例的坐标，有望降低多语言安全微调对通用能力的附带损伤。
article.limitations: SK由top-k交集定义，对发现语言集合与k值敏感：排除任一发现语言后SK规模平均增加8.3%，单语言排除的增幅从+4.0%（意大利语）到+17.6%（孟加拉语）不等；实验也只在8B–9B级开源模型和GPT-4o自动裁判下完成。消融显示标准LoRA的ASR更低（Qwen3-8B为5.50、Llama-3.1-8B-it为4.71），但通用能力下降更大（Qwen3-8B的MGSM从0.560降到0.444），说明该方法是在安全与能力之间做取舍。
article.figure_caption_zh: 所提框架总览：(a) 由不安全与安全提示的激活差计算SCAR分数，逐语言识别安全神经元集合并取跨语言交集得到SK；(b) 通过神经元激活抑制与跨语言安全状态迁移检验SK的功能相关性；(c) SK-Masked LoRA把微调引起的输出变化限制在SK坐标上。

figure.caption: {Overview of the proposed framework.} (a) Language-wise safety-neuron sets are identified using SCAR scores computed from activation differences between unsafe and safe prompts, and their cross-lingual intersection forms the SK. (b) The functional relevance of the SK is examined through neuron activation suppression and cross-lingual safety-state transfer. (c) SK-Masked LoRA restricts fine-tuning-induced output changes to the SK coordinates for multilingual safety adaptation.

Abstract
Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the
real-world
contact dynamics essential for task success. We present
CARD
: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving
contact force targets
.
CARD
unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand–contact representation and generates explicit
contact force targets
in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay,
CARD
also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present
Vid-HACO
, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset,
CARD
maintains contact on
43
43
–
78
%
78\%
of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on
<
10
%
<10\%
and
22.5
%
22.5\%
of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12% to 32% on GRAB
[
70
]
. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via
CARD
is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
1
Introduction
Human demonstrations are the most scalable source of data for dexterous manipulation, yet nearly every way we collect them today, whether teleoperation
[
89
,
77
,
10
]
, wearable exoskeletons
[
11
,
87
,
79
]
, or kinesthetic teaching
[
63
,
8
]
, forces humans to act through a robot embodiment, limiting dexterity to what the interface allows. Retargeting natural human motion removes this bottleneck. However, existing methods
[
22
,
56
]
treat retargeting as a kinematic problem of mapping fingertip positions or joint angles. Further, retargeting often requires scene reconstruction followed by heavy optimization in simulation, and even recent contact-centric formulations
[
33
,
84
,
66
]
still presuppose an object model or a simulator. For manipulation with contact, reconstructing kinematics alone is not enough: millimeters of embodiment mismatch decide whether a replayed trajectory hovers, slips over, or crushes the object.
We present
CARD
, a retargeting framework that treats
contact force targets
as a first-class citizen. Instead of relying on object geometry,
CARD
uses per-link
contact force targets
extracted from a human demonstration, comprising a center of pressure, a push direction, and a force, to solve for robot configurations that place semantically matched robot links on every contact force target inside the demonstrated friction cone.
CARD
produces contact force targets alongside the joint trajectory without relying on object information, therefore it needs no simulator, object mesh, or object pose estimate. Consequently, rigid, articulated, and deformable objects need no special handling.
CARD
is agnostic to the demonstration source: any modality containing hand pose and contact can be used. To make heterogeneous sources interchangeable, we introduce a
unified hand–contact representation
that turns monocular video (through Vid-HACO, our video contact model), tactile gloves, and marker-based motion capture into a common interface: a MANO mesh sequence with one
contact force target
per hand region. Because every contact force target is bound to the human hand surface, retargeting to a new robot requires only a semantic map from hand regions to robot bodies.
On hardware,
CARD
pairs retargeting with a
tactile tracking controller
, an integral admittance loop over joint impedance that maintains the demonstrated contact forces during replay. Together they enable
open-loop replay
of dexterous human demonstrations on multiple robot embodiments mounted on a 7-DoF arm. Here
open-loop
means no object pose estimate and no learned policy. The only feedback is the fingertip force loop that maintains the demonstrated contact forces. We prioritize open-loop replay to demonstrate the retargeting quality of
CARD
over policy learning, since a closed-loop policy confounds retargeting fidelity with other issues such as learning error, partial observability and the like.
Concretely, our contributions are:
•
Contact-Anchored Retargeting:
A simulator and object-free formulation that optimizes contact reach, friction-cone alignment, force weighting, and contact stability per frame with a fast GPU sampling optimizer.
•
Unified Hand–Contact Representation:
A shared interface that maps video (through Vid-HACO, our video hand-contact model), tactile gloves, and motion capture into contact force targets with whole-clip force synthesis for sources that measure no force.
•
Tactile Tracking Controller:
A real-world force tracking controller with feedforward force that replays contact-rich tasks open-loop faithfully on physical hardware.
•
Cross-Embodiment Generalization:
Cross-embodiment retargeting through a semantic map, shown on four robot hands from a 22-DoF dexterous hand down to a parallel-jaw gripper.
Across video, glove, and motion-capture sources,
CARD
achieves state-of-the-art contact fidelity, matching demonstrated contact on 43–78% of contact frames where kinematic retargeting reaches under 10%, while retargeting methods needing object information
[
18
]
only reach 22.5%. Further, our trajectories transfer to the real world through open-loop replay, where the tactile tracker raises success from 4 to 25 of 30 trials over position-only replay.
2
Related Work
Kinematic retargeting.
DexPilot
[
22
]
established the
fingertip-vector cost
used by most dexterous teleoperation systems since, including AnyTeleop and
dex-retargeting
[
56
]
, learned pose imitators
[
67
,
86
]
, and VR and exoskeleton interfaces
[
10
,
15
,
83
,
87
]
. All these approaches retarget hand configuration to hand configuration. Two recent geometric retargeting methods, TopoRetarget
[
76
]
and Morphometric Imitation
[
62
]
, go beyond fingertip matching, although their optimization still relies on an object reference. Neither had released code at the time of submission, so we cannot compare against them.
CARD
keeps the optimization view but optimizes contact locations, push directions, and forces.
Contact-based retargeting.
Contact Transfer
[
32
]
and its sequel
[
33
]
transfer contact areas instead of joint angles. Concurrent work anchors retargeting on contact structure, under the same name
[
84
]
or in the object frame
[
66
]
, or on demonstrated forces
[
78
,
2
]
. Each needs an object model, a simulator, or a learned tracker.
CARD
needs none, and adds a push direction and a force to every contact.
Dynamic retargeting.
A complementary line transfers demonstrations through simulation with the object in the loop
[

,
39

[

[

CARD
needs neither, since its contact force targets are obtained directly in the real world.
Learning from human data.
Many pipelines recover hand and object pose from video or wearable capture devices and retarget kinematically for imitation or RL

Dexterous hand controllers.
Tactile and force feedback improve multifingered control, from contact-event grasp controllers
[
60

and tactile-driven policies

to tactile servoing and grasp-force regulation
[

CARD
outputs tactile targets from a demonstration, so a robot hand can replay it open-loop.
Contact and force from vision.
Dense hand contact has been predicted from hand–object geometry
[
20
]
and from images
[
30
]
, and concurrently from video together with pressure
[
29
,
47
]
or force
[
28
]
. Forces have also been fitted to the tracked object’s wrench
[
52
,
53
]
.
CARD
consumes any contact source and synthesizes forces from grasp balance without an object model.

3.2
Vid-HACO: Contact from Monocular Video
For monocular video, we introduce Vid-HACO, a video-based hand–object contact estimation model that predicts contact probabilities for all 778 MANO vertices, enabling video demonstrations to be converted into our unified hand–contact representation. Given an 8-frame clip ending at frame
t

[

[
48
]
and a DPT decoder
[
57

extract multi-scale features. Two prediction heads estimate vertex-level contact logits and a frame-level binary contact indicator, respectively. Temporal context helps distinguish contact transitions during approach, grasp, and release.
Following HACO
[
30
]
, we use a 10 mm distance threshold to label vertices as contacting the touched surface and set the probability threshold to 0.52 for contact prediction. We train on 1.55M frames from 12 datasets spanning egocentric, third-person, and web views, holding out 10% of each dataset for validation. We fine-tune the encoder end to end with HACO’s class-balanced vertex loss
[
13
]
and an additional binary cross-entropy loss on the frame head, retaining contact-free frames during training. Dataset and implementation details appear in
Appendix

Results.
Table
1
compares contact fidelity across both datasets. Kinematic baselines establish the demonstrated contact on only 3–10% of anchor-frames, with a median gap of 10–23 mm. In contrast,
CARD
establishes contact on 61% of anchor-frames on video, 78% on the glove and motion-capture clips, and 43% on GRAB, while reducing the gap to 1.4–3.6 mm. Importantly, nearly all established contacts occur on the correct finger, and over half of anchor-frames also satisfy the in-cone constraint. On GRAB, where ground-truth object meshes allow us to measure penetration,
CARD
reaches 43% contact against 22.5% for ReGrind, which takes the object mesh as input, and also produces the least object penetration (7.96 mm) (
Fig.
4
). We also find that contact fidelity correlates with contact signal quality:
CARD
can achieve 89% contact on the tactile glove clips, where contact is measured, 76% on motion capture, 61% on video, where it is inferred, and 43% on GRAB, where contact is calculated from geometric proximity (
Appendix
H
).
4.2
Open-loop replay on hardware
To directly evaluate the fidelity of
CARD
’s retargeted actions, we replay the trajectories open-loop on real hardware, eliminating confounding factors such as policy learning. Under this setting, task success depends directly on the faithful reproduction of task-critical contacts and forces.
Fig.
7
shows sequential snapshots of our hardware replays, including picking up a deformable card from a deck and rotating an articulated Rubik’s Cube with a single finger. All tasks use our tactile tracking controller to preserve contact forces. Full videos are available on our project website.
Tactile tracker ablation.
We replay identical
CARD
trajectories on the SHARPA Wave with and without the tactile tracker on three real-world tasks, 10 trials each (
Fig.
6
). Position-only replay succeeds on 1/10 hammer lifts, 3/10 cup lifts, and 0/10 mustard dispenses: the hammer and cup slip out during the lift while the bottle is lifted but not squeezed. With the tactile tracker the same trajectories succeed on 8/10, 10/10, and 7/10 respectively. Reproducing the joint motion alone does not reproduce the intended contact forces.

5
Conclusion
We presented CARD, a simulator- and object-free retargeting framework that preserves task-critical contacts and forces across diverse human demonstration sources and robot embodiments. Combined with a tactile tracking controller, CARD enables faithful open-loop hardware replay across rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Our results demonstrate substantial gains in contact fidelity and task success, establishing contact preservation as a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
Limitations and future work.
Retargeting quality is bounded by the input demonstration, and open-loop replay cannot recover from a large object displacement. We will use
CARD
-generated data to train closed-loop sensorimotor policies that close this gap, and to scale human demonstrations into contact-preserving robot data.

B.2
Evaluation Details and False Contacts
Benchmarks and metrics.
The validation split (172.9k frames) measures in-distribution accuracy. HRDexDB
[
37
]
, which no model saw in training, measures generalization: 434 egocentric videos of a hand grasping 94 objects (111.9k frames), with ground truth from the same 10 mm rule. All models see the same hand crops and are thresholded at 0.52. Vertex precision, recall, and F1 are pooled over all vertices of all frames, so contact predicted on a contact-free frame lowers precision. AP is threshold-free, and frame F1 scores whether a frame is in contact at all.
Fewer false contacts.
Both HACO models over-predict contact, trading 11 points of precision for 3 to 5 points of recall on HRDexDB. Their class-balanced sampling removes nearly every contact-free frame from training, so they flag contact on every frame and score exactly the trivial always-in-contact frame F1, where Vid-HACO reaches 98.3 and 95.3.
This matters downstream:
CARD
turns contacting vertices into
contact force target
, so contact hallucinated during a reach pulls fingers onto empty space.

A semantic map lists, for every human region of

Figure
10
shows the four maps we instantiate. SHARPA Wave and Wuji Hand 2 are five-fingered hands with three links per finger, so their maps are one-to-one: each of the 15 finger regions goes to the robot link of the same name (distal region to fingertip pad, middle to middle link, proximal to proximal link) and the palm to the palm body, and SHARPA additionally receives the pinky base on its metacarpal body. The Unitree Dex3-1 has three fingers, so its map is many-to-one: the human thumb maps to its thumb and the index to its index, while the middle, ring, and pinky regions all map to its third finger. Distal and middle regions land on the matching tip and middle pads, and when several of the grouped fingers touch at once their anchors are merged into one by a force-weighted centroid. The parallel-jaw gripper has two pads: the thumb maps to one jaw and the four fingers to the other, with the distal, middle, and proximal regions landing on the tip, middle, and base zones of the jaw, so the within-link location is still carried. Human regions without a counterpart, such as the palm on the Dex3-1 and on the gripper, carry no
contact force targets

article.headline: 接触锚定重定向: 无需物体模型的灵巧手迁移
article.lede: CMU与亚马逊FAR提出CARD, 把人手演示中的接触力目标直接重定向到机器人, 不需物体模型或仿真器, 接触保持率43
article.problem: 遥操作、动觉示教与外骨骼采集都要求人通过机器人本体动作, 人的灵巧性被接口限制。重定向可以绕开这一瓶颈, 但现有方法只映射指尖位置或关节角这类运动学量, 忽略真实世界的接触动力学; 毫米级的本体差异就决定回放轨迹是悬空、滑过还是压碎物体。
article.method: CARD把接触力目标当作一等公民: 每条语义手部区域带一个由压力中心、推压方向和力大小组成的目标, 用GPU上的采样优化(退火CEM, 每帧1024个候选、16次迭代)求解机器人构型, 同时惩罚接触距离、摩擦锥夹角和跨帧滑移, 全程不需要物体网格、位姿或仿真器。作者提出统一的手–接触表示, 把单目视频(经新模型Vid-HACO)、触觉手套和动捕都转成带接触力目标的MANO网格序列; 跨本体迁移只需一张从人手区域到机器人连杆的语义映射表。硬件回放时, 一个积分导纳环加前馈力的触觉跟踪控制器负责在开环轨迹上维持演示的接触力。
article.results: 在自采视频、手套加动捕数据和GRAB上, CARD在43%–78%的接触帧上保持接触: 视频61.4%、手套加动捕77.7%、GRAB 43.1%, 其中手套单独为89.1%; DexPilot与AnyTeleop两种运动学基线均低于10%(3.8%–9.7%), 需要物体网格的ReGrind在GRAB上为22.5%。接触目标到指腹的中位间隙降到1.4–3.6 mm, 运动学基线为10–23 mm。硬件开环回放三个任务各10次: 仅位置回放共成功4/30, 加触觉跟踪后为25/30(锤子8/10、杯子10/10、芥末瓶7/10)。把该表示接入基于物理的重定向后, GRAB上的严格任务成功率从12%升到32%, 动捕数据从40%升到52%。视频接触模型Vid-HACO在12数据集验证集上顶点F1为84.3, 在留出的HRDexDB上为67.2, 比原版HACO高3.9个点。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「保持接触」做成一个与本体和物体无关的接口, 意味着普通手机视频或触觉手套采集的人类演示, 可以较低成本地转成接触保真的机器人数据, 为后续训练闭环策略提供数据来源。
article.limitations: 重定向质量受输入演示本身限制, 开环回放无法从较大的物体位移中恢复; 在接触靠几何近邻推算的GRAB上接触率只有43.1%、摩擦锥内比例仅16.2%, 说明接触信号质量直接决定上限。此外Unitree Dex3-1与Wuji Hand 2没有触觉传感, 前者靠把抓取动作放大1.2倍、后者靠柔性内表面被动贴合, 触觉跟踪并未真正闭环; TopoRetarget与Morphometric Imitation因未开源而未做比较。

Abstract
Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. Together, these results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

. More ambitiously, recent work pursues the grand unification of multimodal modeling by representing images as discrete tokens analogous to text

Beyond serving as a common modeling interface, discrete visual representations can also function as visual chains of thought

Yang et al., 2026

Wang et al., 2026

, providing explicit guidance for image generation, spatial understanding, and depth estimation within unified multimodal models.
However, quantizing continuous visual features into a finite codebook inevitably incurs quantization error, which is widely assumed to entail semantic loss. Under this view, discrete representations cannot serve as a semantically faithful proxy for the original visual signal, making continuous visual representations a natural upper bound on downstream performance.

In this work, we challenge this common assumption. We use multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, since a representation that provides the information needed to answer any image-centric question can be regarded as semantically lossless with respect to the original visual signal
(
Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026
)
. Our experiments reveal that a discrete representation with an order-of-magnitude larger quantization error can nevertheless achieve substantially better understanding performance. This result demonstrates that quantization error is not a reliable measure of semantic fidelity, raising a fundamental question:
What determines the semantic fidelity of discrete visual representations?
Returning to first principles, raw visual signals, continuous features, and discrete representations are all finite-bit encodings in digital systems, whose nominal capacities can be characterized by their bit budgets, as illustrated in Fig.
2
(right). The semantic content of raw visual signals can in principle be represented with far fewer bits owing to their high redundancy, suggesting that discrete representations may approach semantic completeness with a sufficiently large bit budget. For discrete representations, the bit budget grows linearly with the number of codebooks
L
L
but only logarithmically with the size of each codebook
C
C
, making multi-codebook quantization a more efficient scaling strategy. To test this hypothesis, we systematically scale the bit budget and observe steady improvements in downstream multimodal understanding, as shown in Fig.
1
(a).
However, existing multi-codebook quantizers face a scaling bottleneck as additional codebooks become less semantically informative. Residual vector quantization (RVQ)
(
Lee et al., 2022
)
assigns later codebooks to progressively smaller residuals, whereas product quantization (PQ)
(
Jégou et al., 2011
;
Ma et al., 2026a
)
partitions the feature into increasingly narrow channel groups. Consequently, the effective semantic capacity fails to keep pace with the nominal bit budget, limiting further scaling.
The observed saturation motivates quantizer designs that continue to provide newly added codebooks with informative views as the bit budget grows. As one approach to alleviating this bottleneck, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), illustrated in Fig.
3
, which constructs complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the same visual feature and quantizes them with symmetric parallel codebooks. Fig.
1
(a) shows that FVQ continues to improve with larger bit budgets after RVQ and PQ saturate, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding.
Moving beyond small-scale feasibility studies, we train our model on industrial-scale multimodal data. The resulting model achieves competitive performance with flagship multimodal models across a broad suite of benchmarks, demonstrating the data scalability of discrete visual representations and supporting their potential to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows.
•
We show that quantization error does not determine semantic fidelity. Starting from the first-principles observation that digital RGB images are themselves discrete finite-bit signals, we further demonstrate that a sufficiently large effective bit budget enables discrete representations to match continuous ones in downstream understanding.
•
We introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), which provides one approach to alleviating the high-budget saturation observed in existing multi-codebook quantizers. FVQ quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the same visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks and sustains gains as the bit budget increases.
•
We demonstrate the data scalability of our model through industrial-scale multimodal training, achieving state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models with relative improvements of 22.8% over UniAR and 59.2% over Emu3-Chat on a nine-metric average. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first discrete-representation model to achieve competitive performance against flagship continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL. Beyond these empirical results, we distill the key principles and a practical recipe that make such competitiveness possible, further supporting the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

2.1
Rethinking Quantization Error and Semantic Fidelity
Finding 1: Quantization Error Does Not Determine Semantic Fidelity.
Representations with similar errors can exhibit substantially different understanding performance, whereas those with markedly different errors can retain comparable semantic information.
In this section, we challenge the common assumption that continuous visual representations form an intrinsic upper bound for their discrete counterparts. A prevailing view holds that mapping continuous visual features to a finite codebook inevitably introduces quantization error and that this distortion necessarily entails semantic loss. Under this view, discrete representations are inherently weaker than continuous ones.

The results reveal a counterintuitive pattern. Although the odd-group variant omits the coarse component captured by group 0 and incurs substantially greater reconstruction error, it markedly outperforms VQ and performs comparably to the even-group variant in understanding performance. Conversely, the even-group variant exhibits reconstruction error comparable to VQ but achieves much stronger understanding. Together, these contrasting cases show that reconstruction error does not determine semantic fidelity, raising a more fundamental question: what governs the semantic capacity of a discrete representation?

Bit-Budget Scaling in Discrete Visual Representations
Finding 2: Larger Bit Budgets Improve Semantic Capacity When Added Codes Remain Informative.
Increasing the discrete bit budget improves semantic fidelity and downstream multimodal understanding, ultimately enabling discrete representations to match the understanding performance of continuous visual representations.
Returning to first principles, raw visual signals, continuous features, and discrete representations are all finite-bit encodings in digital systems, and their nominal capacities can be characterized by their per-patch bit budgets
(
Yu et al., 2026a
)
, as summarized in Fig.
2

Despite this trend, both RVQ and PQ saturate at high bit budgets. Increasing the number of codebooks from 8 to 16 doubles the nominal bit budget but yields only marginal gains in understanding performance. We attribute this saturation to diminishing information per codebook, as later RVQ groups receive weaker residuals and PQ partitions features into increasingly narrow channel groups. The nominal capacity therefore grows without a corresponding increase in effective semantic capacity, showing that additional bits help only when the added codes remain semantically informative. This observation motivates quantizer designs that continue to provide informative representations to newly added codebooks as their number grows. In the next section, we introduce FVQ as one such approach.

From Bit-Budget Scaling to Quantizer Design
3.1
Overview
The preceding analysis shows that a larger nominal bit budget is insufficient when the information available to each codebook diminishes as their number grows. A scalable multi-codebook quantizer should therefore assign symmetric roles to its codebooks, provide each with a fixed-dimensional view derived from the full feature, and collectively preserve the original feature before quantization. Guided by these principles, we introduce
Factorized Vector Quantization
(FVQ) as a concrete realization based on dense tight-frame projections, parallel independent codebooks, and information-preserving synthesis, as illustrated in Fig.
3
.

Properties of FVQ.
FVQ implements the three design choices described above. First, parallel independent quantization assigns symmetric roles to all codebooks, avoiding the progressively weaker inputs induced by a residual hierarchy. Second, dense projections provide each codebook with a fixed-dimensional view derived from the full feature, so the information available to an individual codebook does not structurally diminish as

4
Experiments
4.1
Implementation Details
We report two training configurations: an industrial-scale configuration for the main experiments and a shared configuration based primarily on the LLaVA-OneVision data
(
Li et al., 2024
)
for the exploratory experiments in Section
2
and the ablation studies.
Model Architecture.
Our main model pairs Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
with an any-resolution visual tokenizer constructed by applying 16-codebook FVQ to Qwen3 ViT
(
Bai et al., 2025a
)
. To preserve a native next-token prediction setup with minimal modality-specific modifications to the LLM, we use standard 1D RoPE
(
Su et al., 2024
)
in the LLM and omit the DeepStack connections from Qwen3 ViT. Unless otherwise specified, the exploratory and ablation experiments use Qwen3-1.7B and vary the quantization configuration according to the experiment.
Training Schedule.
Both configurations follow four stages. Quantizer training learns the visual tokenizer by reconstructing frozen visual features. Alignment stage freezes both the tokenizer and the LLM and optimizes the newly initialized visual token embeddings and merger to align the discrete IDs with the language embedding space. Pre-training and supervised fine-tuning both keep the tokenizer frozen and jointly optimize the LLM, visual token embeddings, and merger, using context lengths of 8K and 16K and maximum image resolutions of 1024px and 2048px, respectively.
Training Data.
For the main experiments, quantizer training, alignment, pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning use 100B, 10B, 60B, and 30B tokens, respectively, drawn from mixtures covering STEM, OCR, interleaved image-text sequences, image captioning and text-only data. For the exploratory and ablation experiments, we train the quantizer on 50B tokens, use approximately 4B tokens for alignment, and adopt LLaVA-OneVision
(
Li et al., 2024
)
for pre-training and supervised fine-tuning.
Evaluation.
We evaluate general perception and reasoning on MMMU
(
Yue et al., 2024
)
, its more challenging and robust extension MMMU-Pro
(
Yue et al., 2025
)
, MMStar
(
Chen et al., 2024a
)
, and RealWorldQA
(
xAI, 2024
)
. We assess mathematical reasoning on MathVista
(
Lu et al., 2024
)
. For text recognition and text-centric understanding, we use OCRBench
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
, OCRBench V2
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
, and TextVQA
(
Singh et al., 2019
)
; for document and infographic understanding, we use DocVQA
(
Mathew et al., 2021
)
, InfoVQA
(
Mathew et al., 2022
)
, and OmniDocBench
(
Ouyang et al., 2025
)
, which evaluates document parsing across diverse PDF document types. We assess diagram and chart understanding on AI2D
(
Kembhavi et al., 2016
)
with mask, ChartQA
(

)

OCR & Doc & Chart.
Quantization is commonly thought to discard the high-frequency details required for OCR, document, and chart understanding, causing discrete-representation models to lag substantially behind continuous-representation models
(
Yu et al., 2026b
)
. Table
4
shows that our model substantially narrows this gap, achieving state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, performing comparably to Qwen3-VL-8B on OmniDocBench and DocVQA, and surpassing the continuous-representation models on both CharXiv tasks. These results suggest that weak fine-grained visual understanding is not intrinsic to discretization but instead reflects the information bottleneck imposed by an insufficient effective bit budget. By expanding this budget, FVQ alleviates the bottleneck and substantially improves fine-grained visual understanding, challenging the view that discrete visual representations are inherently ill-suited to OCR.

Conclusion
We revisit the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and show that feature reconstruction error does not reliably predict downstream understanding. Instead, effective bit budget emerges as a key determinant of semantic capacity. However, existing multi-codebook quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute diminishing semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this bottleneck, FVQ combines complementary projections with symmetric parallel codebooks and sustains gains at larger bit budgets. Moving beyond small-scale feasibility studies, our industrial-scale model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models and remains competitive with strong continuous-representation models, including on fine-grained OCR and document understanding. These results support discrete tokens as a scalable interface for large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

Design Requirements.
The analysis in Section
2.2
shows that increasing the number of codebooks expands the nominal bit budget, but does not guarantee a corresponding increase in effective semantic capacity. Design Summary.
FVQ directly realizes the three requirements above. Dense projections provide every codebook with a fixed-dimensional view of the full feature, the tight-frame analysis–synthesis pair preserves these views collectively before quantization, and parallel independent lookup gives all codebooks symmetric roles. Together, these properties allow the nominal bit budget to grow with
L
L
without structurally reducing the information available to newly added codebooks.
Appendix B
Related Work
B.1
Native and Unified Multimodal Modeling
Multimodal foundation models are moving beyond the conventional paradigm of attaching a vision encoder and lightweight adapter to a pretrained language model. Recent work pursues more native multimodal modeling along two complementary directions. The first adopts early-fusion pretraining, introducing multimodal data from the outset of language-model pretraining, as exemplified by Qwen3.5
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
and Kimi K3
(
Kimi Team et al., 2026
)
. The second integrates visual processing directly into the multimodal backbone, reducing the architectural separation between vision and language. EVE
(
Diao et al., 2024
)
, EVEv2
(
Diao et al., 2025
)
, Mono-InternVL
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
, and SenseNova-U1
(
Diao et al., 2026
)
pursue encoder-free or monolithic designs, while TML-Interaction
(
Thinking Machines Lab, 2026
)
combines encoder-free processing with early-fusion pretraining for real-time multimodal interaction. These approaches pursue native multimodality by changing when multimodal learning begins or where visual processing occurs.
A complementary line of work pursues unification at the representation level. Chameleon
(
Chameleon Team, 2024
)
and Emu3
(
Wang et al., 2024a
)
represent images as discrete tokens and model vision and language under a shared autoregressive objective. X-Omni
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
uses a shared semantic image-token space for understanding and generation, with a diffusion decoder translating predicted tokens into images. LongCat-Next
(
Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026
)
lexicalizes arbitrary-resolution visual inputs through hierarchical discrete codes, while UniAR
(
Peng et al., 2026
)
uses a shared visual tokenizer to connect multimodal understanding and generation. Beyond unifying understanding and generation, visual representations can also serve as intermediate computational states. Representation Forcing autoregressively predicts visual representations before pixels and retains them in context to guide pixel-space diffusion
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
. Context Unrolling enables explicit reasoning across multiple modal representations before producing predictions
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
. VoT generates discrete visual-plan tokens, such as objects and layouts, to bridge high-level semantics and pixel rendering
(
Sun et al., 2026
)
. Together, these works establish discrete visual tokens as a promising interface for native and unified multimodal models
(
Zhou et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Ma et al., 2025
;
Deng et al., 2025
;
Xie et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Zou et al., 2025
)
. Complementary work improves multimodal understanding through generative imagination for human–object interaction
(
Yuan et al., 2026b
)
and tool-assisted action recognition
(
Yuan et al., 2026a
)
. Our work addresses the representation bottleneck underlying this interface by studying what determines the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and how that capacity can be scaled.
B.2
Semantic Visual Representations and Tokenization
Pretrained vision-language encoders provide the semantic feature spaces that modern visual tokenizers seek to discretize. CLIP
(
Radford et al., 2021
)
learns transferable visual representations through contrastive language supervision, while SigLIP
(
Zhai et al., 2023
)
improves the scalability of image-text alignment through a pairwise sigmoid objective. SigLIP2
(
Tschannen et al., 2025
)
further strengthens semantic understanding, localization, and dense visual features.
More recent VLM-oriented vision encoders, including Qwen3 ViT
(
Bai et al., 2025a
)
, MoonViT-v2
(
Kimi Team et al., 2026
)
, and InternViT
(
Zhu et al., 2025a
)
, are trained on large-scale task-oriented multimodal data covering OCR, document understanding, and visual question answering. Compared with CLIP-style image-text alignment, this richer supervision yields more fine-grained visual representations that better preserve textual, spatial, and structural information.
These semantically structured continuous features provide a natural target space for visual tokenization. RAE
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
uses pretrained VFM features directly as continuous latents, demonstrating their suitability for reconstruction and generation. UniTok
(
Ma et al., 2026a
)
combines reconstruction with semantic supervision to support both understanding and generation. ViQ
(
Yu et al., 2026b
)
introduces text-aligned, position-aware quantization, while dRAE
(
Ma et al., 2026b
)
uses hyperspherical codes that better match the geometry of pretrained features.
Despite these advances, discrete visual representations continue to lag substantially behind continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. This persistent gap motivates us to study what governs the semantic information retained when continuous features are mapped to finite discrete indices. We isolate this process within a frozen VFM feature space and use downstream multimodal understanding to evaluate the resulting representations. Our analysis shifts attention from reconstruction quality alone to the semantic information carried by discrete indices.
B.3
Quantized Visual Encoders
Vector quantization maps continuous features to entries in a finite codebook
(
van den Oord et al., 2017
)
. Recent methods improve the optimization and utilization of this discrete space from different perspectives. FSQ
(
Mentzer et al., 2024
)
, LFQ
(
Yu et al., 2024
)
, and BSQ
(
Zhao et al., 2025
)
replace unconstrained learned codebooks with structured scalar or binary codes, while SimVQ
(
Zhu et al., 2025b
)
and IBQ
(
Shi et al., 2025
)
improve the learning and utilization of explicit codebooks.
A complementary line of work expands representation capacity through multiple codebooks. Residual vector quantization recursively encodes the residual left by preceding codebooks
(
Lee et al., 2022
)
, while product quantization partitions each feature into independent channel groups, as adopted by UniTok for visual generation and understanding
(
Jégou et al., 2011
;
Ma et al., 2026a
)
. However, their gains can saturate as the number of codebooks grows. Our work studies this limitation in semantic visual representations and presents FVQ as one approach to sustaining scaling through fixed-dimensional full-feature views and symmetric parallel codebooks.

C.1
Additional Experimental Details
Our model follows four sequential stages: tokenizer training, alignment, pre-training (PT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Tokenizer training initializes from Qwen3-VL-8B ViT and optimizes the input projection, codebooks, and feature decoder while keeping the tight-frame projections fixed, reconstructing frozen visual features for 100B tokens. Alignment freezes both the tokenizer and the LLM and trains the visual token embeddings and merger for 10B tokens. PT then unfreezes the LLM and jointly optimizes it with the visual interface for 60B tokens while keeping the tokenizer frozen. article.headline: FVQ：让离散视觉 token 追平连续表示
article.lede: 量化误差不能预测多模态理解表现，有效比特预算是关键；FVQ 用对称并行码本突破饱和，九项平均追平连续表示。
article.problem: 离散视觉 token 常被认为因量化误差而必然损失语义，连续视觉特征因此被视为下游性能的天然上界。作者以多模态理解为语义保真度的代理，发现重构误差相差一个数量级的离散表示反而理解更好：RVQ 奇数组 MSE 为 0.246、八基准平均 60.7，而单码本 VQ 的 MSE 仅 0.027、平均只有 51.2。真正的问题于是变成：决定离散表示语义容量的是什么。
article.method: 作者把现有量化器的饱和归因于新增码本信息量递减：RVQ 后续码本只编码更小的残差，PQ 则把特征切成越来越窄的通道组。FVQ 改用稠密投影把同一视觉特征映射成 L 个固定维度视图，用 QR 分解构造满足紧框架条件的分析算子，使合成端在量化前可精确还原特征，再由 L 个结构对称的独立码本并行量化。量化器训练完成后冻结，VLM 阶段只把离散索引映射到新初始化的 token embedding。
article.results: 在码本大小固定为 16,384 的对比中，FVQ 在 L=16（B=224 bit/ patch）时八基准平均为 65.3，超过连续 QwenViT 的 64.6，而 RVQ 与 PQ 在同样 16 码本下分别停在 64.0 和 64.3。工业规模模型以 Qwen3-8B 配 16 码本 FVQ，在九指标平均上比 UniAR 高 22.8%、比 Emu3-Chat 高 59.2%。具体到单项，MMMU 64.3、MathVista 77.4、RealWorldQA 72.0、OCRBench 867、DocVQA 95.4、CharXiv 86.1/49.3，其中 MathVista 与 CharXiv 两项优于 Qwen3-VL-8B 的 77.2 与 83.0/46.4。跨编码器消融中，MoonViT-v2 平均从 38.7 升至 61.1，SigLIP2 从 44.7 升至 53.9。
article.why_it_matters: 若离散 token 能在理解任务上追平连续特征，视觉与语言便可共享同一个 next-token 预测接口，直接继承 LLM 的架构与扩展配方。论文把「有效比特预算」而非重构误差立为可扩展的设计维度，为原生多模态基础模型给出了一个明确的优化目标。
article.limitations: 结论主要建立在单个 8B 规模模型上，且在 MMMU（64.3 对 69.6）、OCRBench（867 对 896）、ChartQA（83.9 对 89.6）等多项仍落后 Qwen3-VL-8B，所谓「有竞争力」是接近而非全面追平。高分辨率长文档、手写表格等细粒度示例为作者手动挑选，原文明确说明不构成统计证据；此外码本大小固定、靠增加码本数量扩展，量化器训练需 100B token，成本门槛不低。
article.figure_caption_zh: FVQ 总览：量化器训练阶段用多组稠密投影生成同一视觉特征的互补视图，由独立码本并行量化并经紧框架合成重建；随后的 VLM 训练阶段冻结量化器，只把离散索引映射到新初始化的 token embedding。

figure.caption: Overview of FVQ. During quantizer training, multiple dense projections produce complementary views of the same visual feature, which are quantized in parallel by independent codebooks. The selected codewords are combined through tight-frame synthesis for feature reconstruction. In the subsequent VLM training stage, the quantizer is frozen, and only the resulting discrete indices are mapped to newly initialized token embeddings for multimodal understanding. The nine-metric average is computed over MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, OCRBench/10, ChartQA, CharXiv-DQ, CharXiv-RQ, DocVQA, and InfoVQA.
